The final nail in the coffin came when Burnham’s own domestic intelligence chief cautioned against exaggerating “Russian influence” on Brexit, arguing that debating the influence of “Russian trolls” on the vote “play[s] into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.”
However, Burnham couldn’t be faulted for his timing and opportunism. As he spoke of Russian bots and influence campaigns in Parliament on Monday, Zelensky, his Polish and Baltic backers, and his army of internet supporters claimed that a Ukrainian strike on a Yandex data center in Russia the previous day had wiped thousands of “Russian bots” from social media.
As it turned out, none of this was true. The strike interrupted the activity of Yandex’ web crawler bots, which archive websites for search users, but with the help of an AI-created graph and some creative interpretation of the word “bot,” the hoax made it all the way to the Warsaw Security Forum.
French riots spread
French students took part in a fifth wave of demonstrations this week, which they say are aimed at securing more school funding and better learning conditions. Every wave of protests thus far has descended into rioting and vandalism, and this week’s marches were no different, with participants torching cars and battering police officers with cobblestones and fireworks in Paris.
RT’s Nadege Abderazzak watched heavily armored police baton-charge crowds of rioters in the French capital on Wednesday, noting that officers now outnumber protesters two-to-one at some rallies.
With French President Emmanuel Macron determined to increase military spending and continue arming Ukraine, France’s financial situation is in dire straits, and right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is on track to win the country’s next presidential election.
Meanwhile, Albanian students have taken a page out of their French counterparts’ book. After large protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha over corruption allegations, a crowd of students breached the fence of the Education Ministry in Tirana on Wednesday and torched the building.
Rama’s response has also drawn from the Western playbook, with the Albanian PM accusing protesters of waging “hybrid war” against the country.
What we’re watching
Zelensky may be in Trump’s bad books, but he can still count on the support of Macron, Burnham, and the rest of his European backers, whom he met in Brussels on Thursday and Friday. In his address to the European Council on Friday, the Ukrainian leader asked for another “70 billion euros” for ammunition, missiles, and air defense. Should Ukraine “fall,” Zelensky warned, another 20 million Ukrainian migrants will flood into the EU.
We’ll be keeping an eye on what kind of promises the cash-strapped Europeans make after this blatant shakedown.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will fly to Tehran on Monday for talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi. The two diplomats are expected to focus on de-escalating the simmering US/Iran conflict in the Middle East, and any progress on this front will likely be reflected in global energy markets.
Lavrov will also meet Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic on Friday, ahead of critical parliamentary elections on October 25. Amid student protests, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic called the election early and stepped down to run as prime minister, a high-stakes move that turned the vote into a referendum on his nine years in power. With pro-Western students and right-wing ‘patriotic’ forces squeezing Vucic from either side, we’ll be keeping an eye out for polls, protests, and interference from the usual suspects.
For more on all of these stories, stick with RT.

articles.title: Belgium triples planned F-16 deliveries to Ukraine, pledges 10 jets by year-end
articles.body:
Belgium plans to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026, Prime Minister Bart De Wever announced on 16 October, raising the expected number from three amid delays in transferring the aircraft.
The expanded commitment comes as Ukraine faces sustained Russian drone and missile attacks and needs additional combat aircraft to strengthen its air defenses.
De Wever made the announcement at a press conference in Brussels alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Anadolu Agency reported. He said Belgium’s deliveries had fallen behind schedule because its new US-made F-35 fighter jets arrived later than expected.
Belgium also discussed supplying more ammunition for Ukraine’s F-16s.
F-16 deliveries delayed by F-35 schedule
“We will deliver 10 this year,” De Wever said, explaining that delays in receiving Belgium’s F-35s had held up the transfer of its F-16s. The new aircraft are now beginning to arrive, allowing Belgium to move forward with deliveries to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy confirmed that Kyiv expects additional F-16s from Belgium by the end of the year and thanked Brussels for the agreement.
The announcement marks an increase from Belgium’s previously reported plan to send three F-16s to Ukraine by the end of 2026. The new figure would more than triple the number expected under that earlier commitment.
F-16s to help counter Russian jet-powered drones
De Wever said Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets and described the F-16 as one of the few weapons capable of effectively countering Russian jet-powered drones.
The aircraft can also intercept cruise missiles and other aerial targets, while carrying out electronic warfare and combat missions. Ukraine received its first F-16s in 2024 after allies agreed to supply the aircraft and train Ukrainian pilots.
Belgium rushes three F-16s to Ukraine as Russia expands its drone and missile assault
Belgium discusses ammunition and financial support
Zelenskyy and De Wever also discussed supplying additional ammunition for Ukraine’s F-16s, including 20 mm rounds produced by Belgian defense company FN Herstal.
The leaders also reportedly discussed Ukraine’s financial needs, though neither provided details on potential next steps. Belgium remains at the center of discussions over frozen Russian assets, as Brussels hosts Euroclear, which holds a large share of the immobilized funds.

articles.title: Musk pushed Trump to slow Starlink in Ukraine, weakening air defenses as Russian drones attacked cities – The Telegraph
articles.body:
Elon Musk approached US President Donald Trump with a proposal to limit the speed of Starlink satellite communications in Ukraine, disrupting Kyiv’s ability to counter Russian drone attacks, The Telegraph reported on 16 October, citing four sources familiar with the discussions.
The restrictions had immediate consequences for Ukraine’s defenses, forcing some drone missions against Russian positions to be called off and threatening the ability to intercept Russian jet-powered drones as they targeted Ukrainian cities at the time.
According to The Telegraph, Trump agreed with Musk’s suggestion, paving the way for the Pentagon to impose restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s satellite network used by Ukrainian forces.
The report contradicts Musk’s public claim that the US military and ultimately Trump were responsible for deciding any limits on the system. However, Trump denied that either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing access, while an anonymous US official told AFP that the president had not requested the reduction in service.
The reported restrictions come amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The episode has raised concerns about Ukraine’s dependence on privately controlled communications infrastructure and the risk that changes to US support could weaken its battlefield capabilities.
Starshield restrictions hampered Ukraine’s drone defenses
Starshield is the military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet network. It allows Ukrainian drone operators to maintain communications with aircraft moving at high speeds, supporting both defensive interception missions and strikes against Russian targets.
The speed limit imposed on Ukrainian drones using Starshield was around 160 kph, making it difficult for them to intercept Russian jet-powered drones and missiles traveling at roughly twice that speed.
According to The Telegraph, a senior source said Musk had become concerned about potential backlash from European consumers following the restrictions. A high-ranking European official and two Ukrainian sources reportedly corroborated the account that Musk and Trump were both involved in the decision.
The Pentagon has not publicly explained the restrictions. The report’s account also remains disputed: Trump said on 16 October that he did not believe either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing access, while an anonymous US official cited by AFP said the president had not requested the reduction.
“Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
Ukraine says Starshield capabilities are being restored
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 16 October that restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system had disrupted several military operations, including efforts to intercept Russian jet-powered Geran drones attacking Ukrainian cities.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not use Starlink to support attacks inside Russia, but relied on the system to intercept drones targeting civilians, conduct mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory, and deliver food and water to frontline troops using drones.
“When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept a certain number of jet-powered ‘shaheds,’ [Gerans - ed.]” Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that Ukrainian forces had lost the ability to carry out some operations while the restrictions were in place.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was in contact with partners and had received signals from the White House that the capabilities would be restored. However, he stressed that speeds had not yet returned to their previous levels, although restoration was underway.
Europe warns against dependence on Musk’s network
The latest episode has renewed European concerns about relying on Musk and SpaceX for critical communications infrastructure. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned Musk on social media that European customers were watching his actions, The Telegraph reported.
The European Union is developing its own satellite communications system, IRIS², intended to provide an alternative to Starlink, according to The Telegraph. The system is planned to become operational by 2030, leaving Ukraine and European governments dependent on existing providers in the meantime.
The report adds to concerns that decisions made in Washington or by private technology providers could directly affect Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.

articles.title: Trump says will not use ground troops or nukes on Iran
articles.body:
Overnight in the region, US president Donald Trump said he "would not use" nuclear weapons against Iran and did not see "putting US troops on the ground"
Fighting in Yemen rages, with focus around Taiz and hits on Sanaa and Aden. Yemen's government reported that the prime minister and cabinet survived a Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, but at least five were killed and 16 wounded according to Yemen’s health minister
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria
And so we begin our live coverage....
Yemeni Army: 16 Houthis killed during clashes south of Taiz
The Yemeni government forces announced the killing of 16 members of the Houthi group and the injury of others, during confrontations on the Al Shaqab front, south of the city of Taiz, after confronting a massive attack launched by the group that lasted about eight hours, according to what was reported by the Taiz Axis Media Center.
The center said, in a statement, that government forces, backed by popular resistance, "were able to break the Houthi attack and prevent the attackers from achieving any field progress on the front," which it described as the southern gate to the city of Taiz.
The statement did not provide additional details regarding the losses of government forces or the nature of the weapons used in the confrontations.
President Donald Trump said the US may have to target Pickaxe Mountain, a site linked to Iran's nuclear program, as he aims to ensure Tehran does not get a nuclear weapon.
"Their nuclear is buried under millions of tons of mountain. Now we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there. We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast," Trump said in an interview with Newsmax on Thursday night.
Trump did not say if he had authorized the use of GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother ofall bombs," against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites. He did say the MOAB bomb was not a nuclear bomb.
Yemeni army targets a Houthi tank northwest of Taiz
This morning, the warplanes of the Yemeni Armed Forces targeted a tank belonging to the Houthi group in Ghurab School, northwest of the city of Taiz, according to what was reported by the Taiz Axis Media Center, affiliated with the government forces.
The center said, in a brief statement, that the air strike targeted the Houthi tank, without providing additional details regarding the extent of human or material losses resulting from the targeting.
The war in Yemen has intensified around Taiz. [Getty]
Gains in tackling malnutrition in Gaza remain fragile and could be undermined by disruptions by Israel to supplies entering the Palestinian enclave, the UN children's agency UNICEF said on Friday, urging that all crossings remain open.
Israel said on Wednesday commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza because of what it claimed as a dispute over taxes between local merchants and militant group Hamas.
That has cut off a vital source of food and other goods in a territory where most depend on humanitarian assistance after three years of war, repeated displacement and stringent Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries.
Although an alleged ceasefire has improved aid access and reduced large-scale fighting, humanitarian agencies say ongoing Israeli strikes, continued displacement and widespread destruction have left civilians highly vulnerable.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said the flow of both commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.
“The impact on children obviously will be felt if this situation is not resolved," he said. "We can't go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require."
Saudi-hosted 2028 Olympics qualifier in BMX cycling canceled
A BMX cycling qualifying event in Saudi Arabia for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics was canceled Friday after deadly missile attacks from neighboring Yemen.
The Urban Cycling World Championships were due to be staged Nov. 3-7 in Riyadh, where the city’s airport has been bombed in the past week by the Houthi rebel group.
"The decision follows a joint assessment of recent developments in the region and their impact on the logistical organisation of the championships," the International Cycling Union said in a statement announcing the events "will not proceed."
Earlier Friday, the Australian cycling federation pulled its team citing travel advice about "the unpredictable security situation, with military strikes and reprisal attacks occurring across the country, including Riyadh."
"In light of these developments, AusCycling cannot justify exposing our athletes and staff to these risks," its statement said.
Doha supports Lebanon at this 'dire hour': Qatar PM
Qatar's PM and FM Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani said that Doha is in "solidarity with the Lebanese people in this dire hour, not only for Lebanon but for this entire region."
Speaking in Beirut at a media conference with Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, he said that Qatar Energy seeks to establish a "massive" solar plant in Lebanon to alleviate its decades-long energy crisis.
Sheikh Al Thani also stressed Qatar's "clear position in support of Lebanon’s sovereignty, stability, and unity."
"We also renew our commitment to stand by the Lebanese people," he said, before adding that Beirut should start reconstruction plans.
💥💥💥Photojournalist @HeidiPhotos is in a Ramallah hospital after being wounded by Israeli West Bank settlers while on the job. @FPAIsPal https://t.co/j7Voj2fEi3
Iran's navy said on Friday that it had detected an oil tanker on fire as it attempted to cross a prohibited area east of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf of Oman, according to state media.
The navy described the tanker as "violating", saying it had switched off its tracking systems. It gave no indication of what had caused the fire.
The navy said uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas created insecurity and posed significant risks to other vessels.
Norwegian teen sentenced for UK murder plot linked to Iran
A Norwegian teenager who planned to commit murder in Britain after being recruited by a Swedish organised crime group linked to the Iranian government was on Friday sentenced to 20 years' detention.
Johannes Natland, now 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, northern England, in March 2025 with two firearms and ammunition in his possession.
Natland was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group used by the Iranian state and sanctioned by both Britain and the United States, prosecutors said.
He admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder and claimed he did not intend to carry out the plan.
But he was convicted in July after a retrial and was sentenced at London's Woolwich Crown Court to detention for 20 years.
Natland was the latest young adult to stand trial in Britain and elsewhere over serious criminal acts allegedly carried out after being recruited online for money, often as an unwitting proxy for a foreign state.
China: Israel should stop settlements in West Bank
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Israeli President Isaac Herzog that Israel should stop and reverse its "forced establishment" of West Bank settlements, China's foreign ministry said in a statement on Friday.
China has consistently held that the Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century, Wang told Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan, the ministry added.
Iran army chief: Hormuz closed until US respects rights
Iranian army's commander-in-chief Amir Hatami claimed on Friday that the Strait of Hormuz "is under the full supervision" of Iran and "remains closed until the enemy respects the rights of the Iranian people".
Israeli settlers injure US journalist in occupied West Bank
Clad in black and their faces masked, dozens of militant Israeli settlers burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians in a coordinated attack on Friday on a West Bank village's annual harvest that injured at least two people including a journalist.
Some 80 settlers, some of them carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill above a terraced olive grove where villagers from Abu Falah had gathered to pick ripe fruit, a cherished annual tradition in Palestinian life, Reuters witnesses said.
The settlers took positions in front of the terraced lanes of olive trees. Some of them used slings to launch rocks towards Palestinian villagers, who descended towards the bottom of the hill before picking up and throwing stones to defend themselves.
The attack continued after the military's arrival, with Israeli soldiers firing tear gas in the direction of the Palestinians who had dodged the jeeps. The sound of live gunfire could be heard in the area, and a Reuters photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a gun.
Palestinian medics said two people were injured and taken to hospitals in the area of Ramallah. One of them was Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with the Washington Post. The newspaper did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
American @washingtonpost journalist Heidi Levine was just severely beaten by settlers in Abu Falah. Videos coming in a minute.
Iraq's Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein has said that the country’s losses from the war between the US and Iran have reached $60bn.
The Iraqi News Agency quoted a Foreign Ministry statement as saying that "the continuation of the US-Iranian conflict has caused significant economic losses".
France's Macron to visit Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain and Qatar
French President Emmanuel Macron will travel to Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar to meet the leaders of these countries from 19 October to 21 October, his office said on Wednesday.
He plans to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and its impact on energy prices, the statement said.
Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to 'ecocide'
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression".
Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required "international solutions".
"What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian told a nature summit in Armenia attended by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Settlers attack occupied West Bank's olive harvest
Palestinian media outlets report that the Palestinian Red Crescent has treated a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man who sustained injuries from an Israeli settler attack in the Ramallah area.
Separately, Palestinian media outlets report that Israeli settlers attacked olive pickers, also in the Ramallah area.
How Green Party insiders aided media's Zionism witch hunt
Media attacks on the UK Greens and Zack Polanski over anti-Zionism echo the playbook used to silence criticism of Israel during Corbynism, writes Alex Foley.
The Israeli army says it will launch strikes across south Lebanon, warning that explosions will be heard Western Galilee and central Upper Galilee due to strikes.
Israel has been continual attacking south Lebanon despite an alleged ceasefire.
Three years into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, people living with chronic illnesses are struggling to access the medicines, tests and routine treatment they need to stay alive. For patients with diabetes, heart disease, kidney failure and cancer, shortages of essential drugs, medical equipment and fuel have turned the management of everyday conditions into a daily struggle for survival.
Across Gaza, disrupted medical care means patients are increasingly unable to monitor their conditions, attend follow-up appointments or complete essential treatment.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Lebanon's president on Thursday that he should not return several hundred kilograms of explosives seized by Lebanese authorities from Hezbollah, a US official said.
"He urged President (Joseph) Aoun to hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question," the official told reporters on condition of anonymity.
The Iran-backed militant group acknowledged on Thursday that a 500-kilogram shipment of explosives belonging to it was seized last week by Lebanese authorities, saying it was intended for "the resistance."
"The vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance" against Israel, Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah had said, adding that the group requested the release of those arrested over the seizure and demanded the return of the shipment.
Rubio also raised the issue of Lebanon's 1955 boycott law, which bans direct relations with Israel and "deter steps towards peace."
Rubio "emphasized that the law is impractical and urged direct military-to-military communication between Lebanese and Israeli forces for deconfliction," according to the US official, adding it "would help to reduce miscalculation and to advance sequenced implementation" of the framework agreement.
Saudi Arabia: 2027 Asian Cup preps continuing as planned
The local organising committee for the 2027 Asian Football Cup in Saudi Arabia said on Friday that preparations for holding the tournament are proceeding according to the specified schedule, despite the doubts surrounding sporting events in the Kingdom in the wake of the recent attacks.
Earlier this week, AFC President Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said the federation was "in no rush to make a decision" about postponing the tournament.
Israel claims commercial goods not entering Gaza over tax
Israel on Thursday claimed commercial goods usually delivered into Gaza by private merchants had not entered the beleaguered territory for days because of Hamas threats and a taxation scheme, an accusation the group rejected.
In a letter to international representatives involved in implementing the ceasefire, Israel said merchants reported that Hamas demanded about 10,000 shekels ($3,200) for every truck into Gaza and that traders sell around 30 percent of goods in cash instead of bank transfers.
Israel also cited reports that Hamas security personnel had arrested the son of a merchant who refused to comply with the demands, prompting traders to suspend operations out of fear for their safety.
Hamas rejected the allegations in a letter addressed to mediators including Egypt, Qatar and Turkey, saying it "categorically" denied imposing taxes or government fees on commercial trucks.
It said it had not collected taxes or fees on commercial activity in the past three years of war because of the humanitarian and economic conditions in Gaza.
Hamas said the 10,000-shekel figure referred to a "voluntary community initiative" by Gaza's businesspeople to put money into a "national fund" for relief projects, while the transaction requirement was to inject "cash liquidity" into the territory.
The Trump administration has issued fresh Iran-related sanctions targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities, according to a notice posted on the US Department of Treasury website on Thursday.

articles.title: Black Sea Attacks Push Bulgaria to Seek NATO Aircraft and Missiles, Former Leaders Urge Action
articles.body:
Black Sea Disruptions Leave Bulgarian Steel Plant Without Billets
The crisis in the Black Sea has disrupted raw material supplies to Bulgaria’s ferrous metals industry, forcing a plant in Debelt to operate only two weeks a month
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said Bulgaria had asked NATO for aircraft, air defense and counter-drone systems, and air patrols as attacks on vessels in the Black Sea intensify, while former prime ministers, ministers, military officers and diplomats issued an appeal urging the country to strengthen its defenses and coordinate more closely with European Union and NATO allies.
Speaking to journalists, Stoyanov said attacks in the Black Sea were growing more intense by the day, with strikes in Romanian territorial waters highlighting the need to modernize Bulgaria’s armed forces and expand their defensive capabilities. BGNES reported his remarks.
“We have requested aviation, surface-to-air missile systems, counter-drone systems, and air patrols - essentially, the entire spectrum of available assets,” Stoyanov said, explaining that the requests were also intended to demonstrate a strong presence in the region.
The minister said it remained unclear what assistance Bulgaria would receive. Romania and the Baltic states had similar needs, he added, while European partners were paying increasing attention to Black Sea security.
“I hope for a swift response and a strengthening of our capabilities,” Stoyanov said. He stressed the need for a common action plan and said a meeting was expected soon involving the defense ministers of Turkey and Romania and the chiefs of defense of all three countries.
Stoyanov said absolute security in the Black Sea could not be guaranteed even with allied forces and equipment deployed in the region. Both Russia and Ukraine possess advanced technology, he noted, yet drone and ballistic missile attacks continue.
“100% security is impossible,” the defense minister said, adding that the aim was to reduce the danger as much as possible.
Bulgaria is using its available forces and equipment for surveillance and countermeasures, Stoyanov said. The country currently has two reconnaissance systems monitoring its maritime territory, with a third expected to be deployed by the end of the year. He said the new system had never been used elsewhere.
The minister also discussed the operation to recover the vessel Chelsea 3, which was suspended the previous day because of bad weather. The ship is anchored about 10 kilometers east of Lozenets, and the operation is due to resume when conditions improve, allowing it to be towed to the port of Burgas.
“We hope that useful information can be retrieved from Chelsea 3, but the Ministry of Defense is not conducting the investigation,” Stoyanov said.
Separately, an open appeal signed by former Bulgarian President Rosen Plevneliev, former prime ministers Ivan Kostov, Boyko Borissov, Kiril Petkov and Nikolay Denkov, former ministers, senior retired and reserve military officers, diplomats and public figures calls for urgent action to address growing security threats in the Black Sea region.
Published in Sofia on October 15, 2026, the appeal is addressed to Bulgarian citizens, the National Assembly, the government, the European Union and NATO. Its signatories urge President Rumen Radev and the government to defend national security, strengthen the armed forces and work more closely with Bulgaria’s allies.
The appeal cites repeated drone attacks on commercial vessels near Bulgaria and Romania, including in Romanian territorial waters, as well as subversive operations attributed to Russian intelligence services in Bulgaria and Romania in recent years. The signatories describe these incidents as evidence of expanding risks to Bulgaria and the region, affecting not only shipping but also citizens, critical infrastructure and national sovereignty.
The document acknowledges that assessments may differ over whether the incidents represent a new stage of escalation, preparations for a wider confrontation or the early signs of such a conflict. However, the signatories say the broader trend of rising military risks in the Black Sea is clear.
They insist that each incident must be investigated and responsibility established on the basis of evidence, but argue that uncertainty over who carried out an individual attack cannot justify failing to prepare.
“The lack of a definitive attribution for any specific strike cannot serve as a justification for inaction or a failure to prepare,” the appeal states.
The signatories express concern that Bulgaria is confronting these threats with armed forces they consider insufficiently prepared and political leaders who, in their view, have not demonstrated the resolve needed to protect national security and citizens’ interests. They also warn of a campaign intended to spread fear and paralyze society.
“The Black Sea is turning into a war zone. Bulgaria must be prepared to defend itself,” the appeal declares.
The authors reject the argument that Bulgaria can avoid being drawn into the war by maintaining good relations with the Kremlin or distancing itself from Ukraine, the EU and NATO.
“Peace is not guaranteed by the hope that Putin will spare us if we distance ourselves from Ukraine, the European Union, and NATO,” the document states.
Instead, the signatories argue that peace depends on combat-ready armed forces, effective security services, modern surveillance systems, credible deterrence and close cooperation with Bulgaria’s European and NATO allies. They stress that preparing to defend the country does not mean seeking war or intending to attack another state, but ensuring that aggression does not reach Bulgarian homes.
The appeal urges citizens to demand evidence of the state’s ability to protect them rather than accept political assurances that the country will remain safe through its relations with Moscow. It also warns that keeping a low profile, relying on promises or expecting goodwill from Russia could allow further provocations and attacks.
The signatories say stronger Bulgarian defensive capabilities and greater support from the EU and NATO would make deterrence more credible and improve the prospects for preserving peace. They warn against waiting for another ship to sink, critical infrastructure to be attacked, violence to occur or lives to be lost before responding to the risks.
The document calls on the government to prioritize national security over immediate political considerations and take concrete steps, including unequivocally condemning the escalation of Russian military activity in the Black Sea, improving surveillance and defense of Bulgarian airspace and maritime territory, accelerating the development of counter-drone capabilities and coordinating the work of the armed forces, security services and civilian institutions.
It also calls for closer cooperation with allies to protect commercial shipping, ports and critical infrastructure, including energy facilities, and for the government to prepare for future threats rather than simply assess past incidents. The signatories urge Bulgaria to draw extensively on Ukraine’s experience in countering unmanned systems.
The appeal also asks the EU and NATO to make Black Sea security an immediate priority and strengthen coordinated defense along the alliance’s eastern flank. It calls for integrated maritime and aerial surveillance, timely intelligence sharing, joint capabilities to counter aerial and maritime drones, and specific measures to protect shipping, ports and energy infrastructure.
Bulgaria, the authors say, should take the initiative and participate actively in these efforts rather than become a weak link in collective allied defense. They urge citizens to hold politicians accountable and the government to act.
The signatories also identify the upcoming presidential elections as an opportunity to bring questions of security, solidarity with allies and Bulgaria’s place in European politics to the forefront of public debate.
The appeal remains open to professionals with experience in foreign policy, defense and security who wish to add their names.
Among its signatories are former President Rosen Plevneliev and former prime ministers Boyko Borissov, Ivan Kostov, Kiril Petkov and Nikolay Denkov.
The former ministers who have signed are Anyu Angelov, Asen Vassilev, Atanas Zapryanov, Boyko Noev, Valentin Radev, Velizar Shalamanov, Gergana Pasi, Daniel Mitov, Korman Ismailov, Lidiya Shuleva, Meglena Kuneva, Nadezhda Neynski, Nikolay Nenchev, Nikolay Svinarov, Rumyana Bachvarova, Solomon Pasi, Todor Tagarev and Traycho Traykov.
The military signatories include retired and reserve officers Lieutenant General Chavdar Chervenkov, Major General Stefan Dimitrov and Brigadier General Dinko Ivanov.
Diplomats and public figures who have joined the appeal are Valeri Rachev, Vesela Cherneva, Dimitar Ivanovski, Elena Poptodorova, Ivan Anchev, Ilian Vasilev, Orhan Ismailov, Radan Kanev, Stefan Tafrov and Stoyan Stalev.
The appeal was signed in Sofia on October 15, 2026, and addressed to Bulgarian citizens, the National Assembly, the government, the European Union and NATO.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would adjust its deterrence and defense posture if necessary after discussing Black Sea security and recent attacks on commercial shipping with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Romanian President
Bulgaria’s National Assembly has approved the purchase of five additional IRIS-T SLM air defense systems from Germany, in a deal worth more than 900 million euros that will be financed through the European Union’s SAFE instrument
Two foreign nationals aged 21 and 20 have been detained over the deliberate burning of Starlink antennas at a secret facility near Sofia, Bulgaria in what authorities are investigating as a terrorist attack
Romania has proposed that Bulgaria join it in asking NATO to establish a military command in the Black Sea, while Sofia and Bucharest are also preparing to seek a dedicated discussion of regional security at the upcoming EU summit following a series of dr
Bulgaria’s State Agency for National Security (SANS) does not rule out future acts of sabotage on Bulgarian territory, its chairman, Plamen Tonchev, told the National Assembly during a hearing on the suspected arson of antennas near Sofia intended to conn
Bulgaria plans to request membership in a NATO initiative to counter low-altitude aerial threats by October 30, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told Parliament during a hearing prompted by a question from MP Hamid Hamid about the country's participation
Bulgaria Honors Tsar Samuel with Grand State Ceremony in Sofia
Bulgaria Is Disappearing: Nearly 2 Million People Lost in 30 Years

articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
The Houthis continue to strike Saudi Arabia despite Riyadh’s threats of a forceful response and promises to enlist outside partners to defend the kingdom.
By targeting airports and oil infrastructure, Ansar Allah is seeking to raise the cost of Saudi involvement in Yemen’s conflict and force the kingdom’s leadership to reconsider the terms of a settlement.
The latest wave of Houthi attacks has targeted facilities of particular importance to Saudi Arabia. On the evening of October 13, a strike hit Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, home to the company’s key management operations. The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire, though miraculously no one was killed.
Ansar Allah also claimed strikes on an oil refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport. The choice of targets suggests the Houthis want to put virtually all of the kingdom’s oil revenue at risk and disrupt its international air connections.
These targets also suggest that the movement is trying to influence Saudi leaders’ decisions directly. Oil infrastructure generates government revenue, airports connect the country to the outside world, and confidence in the kingdom depends on the security of both. Even limited damage can therefore produce an impact far greater than the cost of the weapons used.
What is driving the conflict?
The Houthis have their own history of confrontation with Saudi Arabia. The movement emerged in northern Yemen, fought a series of wars against the central government between 2004 and 2010, and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Its rise was rooted in Yemen’s political system, local conflicts, and the collapse of state institutions. Iranian support strengthened an already established force with its own social base and political objectives.
The Saudi intervention in 2015 cemented Riyadh’s position as the movement’s principal foreign adversary. For the kingdom, the aim was to prevent a hostile force from consolidating power along its southern border and to support Yemen’s internationally recognized government. For the Houthi leadership, the war became both a threat to its survival and a rallying cause. Invoking foreign aggression allowed the movement to portray its struggle for domestic supremacy as a defense of national sovereignty.
That logic remains relevant to the current escalation. Saudi support for an offensive by Yemeni government forces threatens the Houthis’ territorial gains and bargaining position. Striking deep inside the kingdom allows them to raise the price of that support. Their apparent calculation is to make continued Saudi involvement in the war carry a recurring cost on Saudi soil.
The movement’s demands are concrete: an end to strikes, limits on assistance to its Yemeni adversaries, the lifting of transportation and trade restrictions, and agreements on revenues and payments. These issues were under discussion long before the latest escalation. The framework for a roadmap presented by the UN in December 2023 included a nationwide ceasefire, payment of public-sector salaries, the resumption of oil exports, and an easing of restrictions on Sanaa airport and the port of Hodeidah.
By increasing Riyadh’s costs, Ansar Allah hopes to extract concessions and retain control of the territory it has seized. A ceasefire on those terms, however, would consolidate the movement’s position without resolving how power should be shared in Yemen.
Attacks on Saudi Arabia also serve Ansar Allah’s domestic political interests. The movement uses its ability to strike deep inside the kingdom to bolster its standing among supporters. Confrontation with Riyadh also allows the Houthis to cast themselves as Yemen’s defenders against foreign intervention and use that claim to justify their bid for power.
Iranian military and technological assistance has undoubtedly expanded Houthi capabilities considerably. But the relationship with Tehran does not erase Ansar Allah’s own interests in Yemen’s power struggle or its confrontation with Saudi Arabia. Reducing the movement’s actions to the execution of Iranian orders fails to explain either the conflict’s local roots or the Houthi leadership’s objectives.
A more accurate description would be a partnership with unequal resources in which the Yemeni side retains substantial autonomy. Weakening Saudi Arabia may serve both partners’ interests, but their preferred terms for ending the war may differ. Ansar Allah must consider conditions on Yemen’s battlefields and the survival of its own rule. Agreements between Iran and outside powers therefore do not guarantee an automatic halt to Houthi operations.
The economics of war
The development of domestic missile production and an expanding network for procuring components make it harder for Riyadh to bring Houthi attacks to an end. If the movement can replenish its arsenal from several sources, restricting Iranian supplies will have only a partial effect. An agreement with Tehran alone would therefore be insufficient to secure Saudi facilities. Much will depend on whether the Houthis themselves believe continued strikes serve their interests.
Nor do the Houthis need to match Saudi Arabia in the quantity or quality of their weapons. They can choose their targets and pause between attacks, while the kingdom must continuously defend airports, oil facilities, and cities across a vast territory. Even a single hit can disrupt a facility’s operations, trigger flight cancellations, or bring business activity to a halt. Purchases of American air defense systems reduce that threat but do not eliminate it. Riyadh’s problem is that military superiority has yet to deprive its adversary of the ability to inflict economically painful blows. That is precisely the capability the Houthis are trying to turn into negotiating leverage.
Saudi military spending exceeds $82 billion per year, yet the kingdom still struggles to protect its infrastructure from Houthi attacks. This exposes the gap between the cost of the weapons it has purchased and their effectiveness in this particular war. Advanced fighter jets and missile defense systems give Riyadh a considerable advantage, but detecting small drones and low-flying cruise missiles requires extensive radar coverage and rapid information sharing between units. Without those capabilities, expensive equipment cannot reliably detect and engage targets in time.
In a prolonged confrontation, the disparity in weapons costs also becomes significant. According to cited estimates, a Patriot interceptor costs more than $3 million, while some Houthi drones cost just $15,000–25,000. Defenders have to use such interceptors against cheap aircraft to protect far more valuable assets. But sustained defensive operations deplete stocks that cannot be replenished quickly, particularly amid strong global demand for air defense systems. This gives the Houthis an opportunity to wear down the kingdom’s defenses even when most of the aircraft they launch fail to reach their targets.
Technical difficulties are compounded by the structure of the Saudi armed forces. The separation of the regular military and the National Guard has historically served, in part, to protect the monarchy against a coup. But separate chains of command and highly centralized decision-making can hinder coordination and limit commanders’ initiative. Another weapons purchase, then, will not solve the problem on its own. Even additional detection and interception systems will deliver limited results if information arrives late and coordinating a response takes too long.
The Houthis can reasonably expect these shortcomings to take time to address, leaving them able to continue inflicting painful blows in the meantime. Domestic production and broader supply networks help sustain that campaign. The movement does not need to destroy major industrial facilities or shut down air travel altogether; a recurring threat is enough to make airlines reconsider routes, investors postpone decisions, and Saudi leaders spend more on protecting infrastructure.
Will help come from abroad?
Statements by Türkiye and Pakistan expressing their readiness to defend Saudi Arabia do not yet provide grounds to expect either country to enter the war fully, much less fight the Houthis inside Yemen. At an October 5 meeting, the parties to the Mecca Agreement announced that they would provide forces and equipment for the kingdom’s defense. The political weight of those promises, however, will depend on whether the allies can actually reduce the number of attacks and the damage they cause. As long as the strikes continue, Houthi leaders may view such declarations as rhetoric unlikely to be followed by a dangerous expansion of the war.
Ankara’s position reinforces that calculation. Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan outlined possible assistance with air defense, electronic warfare, and technical support, while explicitly ruling out Turkish troops taking part in offensive operations on foreign soil. Türkiye has thus set clear limits on its role from the outset.
Pakistan also has reasons to avoid direct intervention. Joining the war in Yemen would mean additional military spending and the risk of worsening relations with neighboring Iran. It would therefore be premature to expect Islamabad to take on the task of defeating the Houthis on Riyadh’s behalf. Its commitments to the kingdom leave room for a role limited to defending specific facilities and providing military assistance.
A similar distinction applies to the American position. Intelligence sharing and targeting assistance support Saudi operations, but they do not mean Washington is willing to stop the attacks at any cost. The Houthis appear to be counting on precisely these limits to outside involvement. Their bet is that the kingdom’s allies will help it defend itself but will be reluctant to become embroiled in a prolonged war to achieve Saudi objectives in Yemen.
Until that support produces a substantial reduction in attacks, threats to bring in allies may carry little weight with Ansar Allah.
***
The Houthis are seeking to demonstrate that continued Saudi intervention will bring losses that neither a vast defense budget nor foreign partners can prevent. If that pressure prompts Riyadh to scale back assistance to their adversaries or accept settlement terms favorable to them, the movement will have an opportunity to translate its battlefield gains into lasting political advantages.
Such an outcome would also benefit Iran by weakening Saudi Arabia’s position. Its most immediate consequence, however, would be to strengthen Ansar Allah itself in the struggle for power in Yemen.

articles.title: Bulgaria Asks NATO for Air Defense After Ship Attack
articles.body:
Bulgaria has asked NATO for aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone equipment and air patrols, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Oct. 16, as drone strikes on merchant ships creep toward the country’s Black Sea coast.
Stoyanov told reporters that Sofia requested “the entire spectrum of available assets” to show a strong allied presence in the region, according to Bulgarian outlet Novinite.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He said it is still unclear what help Bulgaria will actually receive.
Stoyanov said Romania and the Baltic states have similar needs, and that defense ministers from Turkey and Romania, along with the chiefs of the general staff of all three countries, are expected to meet soon. He also cautioned that absolute security in the Black Sea cannot be guaranteed, even with allied forces deployed.
Earlier this week, Stoyanov said Bulgaria would deploy two additional drone systems and more missile systems to the Black Sea area, Newsweek reported, citing Bulgarian news agency BTA.
The request follows a turbulent fortnight off Bulgaria’s coast. On Oct. 6, drones hit two commercial ships, the Alfa Watan and the Able, in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew went missing, while the Able’s 18 crew members were rescued. It was the first such attack in the economic zone of a NATO member.
A week later, on Oct. 13, the Ukrainian-owned, Malta-flagged cargo ship Chelsea 3 was hit by three drones roughly 18 nautical miles off the coast near Byala. Its crew survived. Prime Minister Rumen Radev said a second vessel was struck and sunk about 17 nautical miles off the village of Krapets, and Reuters said 11 sailors were missing.
Moscow Airports Suspend Flights Again Amid Drone Alerts
Radev said Bulgaria lacks solid evidence to accuse any specific party but suggested that Russia benefits from the attacks. He summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who said she had no information on Russian involvement and did not rule out a third-party provocation, according to ARY News. Ukraine claims that Russia is responsible.
The Oct. 6 attack came a day after a drone strike sank the Turkish-owned grain ship Royad Mammadov off Romania, killing two crew members. The Romanian Naval Authority said the incident occurred in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, outside its territorial waters.
President Volodymyr Zelensky blamed Russian drones, though Romanian authorities have not officially confirmed a drone strike.
Bulgaria’s shift
Calls for NATO help are coming from a government that has distanced itself from Kyiv.
Radev, a former president and long-time critic of military aid to Ukraine, won the April 19 parliamentary election in a landslide. On June 9, Stoyanov said Bulgaria would send no more weapons to Ukraine, adding Bulgaria had approved 13 military aid packages since 2022.
On July 14, Radev said Bulgaria would no longer take part in the Coalition of the Willing that seeks to provide postwar security guarantees to Ukraine; he has halted government-supplied military aid since taking office but has not stopped commercial arms sales to Kyiv.
Speaking at the NATO summit in Ankara earlier that month, Radev said Bulgaria had exhausted what it could give from state stockpiles but could still repair Ukrainian military equipment.
Sofia also reportedly vetoed EU sanctions on Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church and a confidant of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and sought the removal of oil billionaire Vagit Alekperov from the lists. Radev argued that religion should stay separate from sanctions policy.
Producer of Soviet-standard ammunitions
Bulgaria is not a military heavyweight, but it matters to Ukraine for what it can produce.
Because of its communist-era industrial base, it is one of the few countries outside Russia that can produce Soviet-standard munitions, and output surged after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Emilian Gebrev, owner of arms maker Emco and a survivor of two nerve-agent poisonings, said that Russian military intelligence agents repeatedly sabotaged his facilities. Bulgarian prosecutors have charged six officers serving in Russia’s Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU) in connection with the incidents.
Geography matters too.
Bulgaria borders neither Ukraine nor Russia, but it holds a strategic position on the Black Sea. With Russia bombing Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, Kyiv increasingly relies on Danube River ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
Romania’s foreign ministry says, per Maritime Executive, that between 20% and 30% of globally traded wheat and grain transits the corridor. That makes the waters off Bulgaria both a lifeline for Ukraine’s exports and a growing test of whether NATO can protect shipping in its own backyard.

articles.title: US Senators Seek Probe Into Ukraine Starshield Disruptions As Zelenskyy Attends EU Summit
articles.body:
BRUSSELS -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, has no interest in peace talks and criticized a US deal with Moscow on diesel exports, saying it will hand more money to the Kremlin to fund its war against his country.
Speaking during a European Union summit in Brussels on October 16, Zelenskyy also said that speeds of US company SpaceX's satellite communications, crucial for Ukraine's defense, had not returned to previous levels but were "being restored" after having slowed in recent days.
EU leaders signaled support for Zelenskyy and Ukraine at the summit, which came amid a new flare-up of tensions between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump, who has stepped up pressure on Kyiv to reach an agreement to end the full-scale war Putin launched in February 2022.
"Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form," Zelenskyy said at a press conference. "He’s playing with words.... Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war."
Russia has rejected repeated calls for a full cease-fire and has appeared to ignore what Trump said on October 11 was a limited truce barring attacks on energy infrastructure, as its forces hammer Ukrainian cities, power plants, and other facilities with winter on the way.
Disruptions to the Starshield satellite system, the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX, left Ukraine particularly vulnerable earlier in the week. Starshield is overseen by the US government, and Ukraine uses it for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes, and interceptor drones.
For a few nights, speed limits in the system “were lower and when that happened, we were unable [to shoot] down jet-powered Shahed drones” Zelenskyy said, describing the situation as “very painful and very unpleasant." There were numerous casualties ion Kyiv and elsewhere as intensified attacks.
"Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," Zelenskyy said.
The satellite problem added to concerns in Ukraine after Trump announced on October 9 that he and Putin had agreed by phone to a deal that would send Russian diesel to world markets including the US, where high fuel prices are adding to challenges facing Trump's Republican Party ahead of midterm Congressional elections on November 3.
At the press conference, Zelenskyy said that "cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal." He said it would "never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets. But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war."
Trump has repeatedly called on Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian refineries, blaming those attacks -- and not the decreased energy flows from the Mideast resulting from the US-Israeli war with Iran that began in February -- for high diesel fuel prices.
On October 10, Trump said that Kyiv "better damn well" stop hitting Russian refineries and that Ukraine should "get a new president," blaming Zelenskyy for the lack of a peace agreement.
Trump, who made ending Russia's war on Ukraine a priority when he started his current term in January 2025, told US media outlet Newsmax on October 15 that peace between Russia and Ukraine would only be possible if Zelenskyy left office.
"Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with," he said in an interview. "He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. No, I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Trump said, adding that he believes both leaders wanted peace but found Zelenskyy more difficult to negotiate with than Putin.
Russia, among other demands, has said Ukraine must hand over the portion of the eastern Donetsk region that Moscow's forces have been unable to capture in years of very deadly fighting. Ukraine says that is unacceptable, signaling it could agree to a cease-fire that would leave the front lines in place as talks commenced.
Speaking at what Russian media said was a command post on October 16, Putin said he had instructed Russian forces not only to drive Ukrainian troops out of regions Moscow baselessly claims as Russian territory, but also to establish a "security zone" beyond those regions. He said Russian control of that zone would not be subject to negotiation.
Separately, Putin ordered Russian forces to continue their "massive and coordinated strikes against enemy targets."
In an interview published on October 15 by the Financial Times, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian energy facilities because Moscow had not halted its own strikes. "We're done," he said after stating that Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian refining operations for three days.
Zelenskyy also told the British newspaper that the satellite communication slowdown was described to Kyiv as a technical glitch even though it remains unclear who authorized the restrictions, whether they affected commercial Starlink or Starshield, and whether Washington also reduced intelligence support to Kyiv.
US news outlet Axios, citing unnamed sources, reported that the White House told Ukraine it does not control SpaceX. Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS" -- meaning the US president.
Asked about the matter on October 16, Trump told reporters, "It wasn't me. And I don't think it was Elon." According to Reuters, he also said he has a good relatonship with Zelenskyy.
At the press conference a few hours earlier, Zelenskyy seemed careful to avoid criticizing Trump directly, saying he had had “a couple of meetings with the American President and we are always finding topics for discussions and for making decisions.”
He also said Kyiv still was talking with the US negotiation team and that they would meet “at a certain level in the coming days.”
European leaders pledged support for Kyiv, even if few concrete measures appeared to be forthcoming.
Speaking ahead of the summit, European Council President Antonio Costa reaffirmed that the EU's support for Ukraine was stronger than ever, stressing that this was no time to withdraw assistance or ease sanctions on Russia.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen added that the EU had supported Trump's proposed energy cease-fire, but Russia had failed to respect it "for a single minute." She added that EU sanctions would remain in place until Russia stopped the war and that Brussels was preparing another round of sanctions on Moscow.
Zelenskyy used his meeting with the European leaders to seek air-defense support ahead of the winter. Speaking about the US-made Patriot missiles, the Ukrainian leader said “Most of PAC-2- and PAC-3 are now being sent to the Middle East. It’s an open secret we are not a priority destination for these systems.”
He added that his EU counterparts received “a bare minimum” of what Kyiv’s needs this winter adding that there are enough PACs in Europe for Ukraine to go tough this winter.”
Asked in Brussels whether Ukraine had resumed targeting Russian refineries, Zelenskyy said only that he “usually doesn’t comment details about our operations.”
Meanwhile, overnight Russian attacks injured five people in Ukraine's central Cherkasy region, where a drone strike set fire to an apartment building in Uman, regional officials reported on October 16.
Lutsk, in Ukraine's Volyn region, was left without electricity following a Russian drone attack, according to city authorities.
Earlier in the day, Russian authorities said their defense forces had repelled a Ukrainian drone attack targeting heating infrastructure in the Vladimir region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin also reported that 94 Ukrainian drones had been shot down near the capital over period of eight hours, while four were downed over the Leningrad region, according to the regional governor.
All four Moscow airports were temporarily closed amid the drone attacks, with flights diverted to other cities, Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency reported. An air raid alert was also declared in the Leningrad region.
In Washington on October 15, a bipartisan group of nine US senators called for an investigation into the disruptions to Starshield.
"We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical US-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks," they said in a letter to the Defense Department's inspector general.
The senators urged an immediate probe to determine whether any US officials "directed, authorized, approved, or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements, warning capabilities, or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine."
Separately, Pope Leo spoke by phone with Putin on October 16, expressing "deep concern" over the humanitarian situation in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents remain trapped amid landmines and face starvation in the largely destroyed urban area.
The Vatican said that during the call, the pontiff called for a truce to allow the delivery of first aid and food supplies and to facilitate the voluntary evacuation of the civilian population. The Kremlin said Putin supported the initiative to deliver supplies and was ready to "cooperate on this matter."
Ukrainian volunteers who spoke with RFE/RL earlier this year said Oleshky is an important staging ground for Russian attacks on parts of southern Ukraine. They said local residents had effectively been turned into "human shields" by Russian forces operating in the area.
According to Ukrainian authorities, Kyiv has sought to establish a humanitarian corridor linking Oleshky with government-held territory since the spring, but Moscow has not agreed to the proposal.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1695: Ukraine’s war budget has $52 billion hole as West ties aid to reforms
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine’s military now orders supplies based on real front-line data, not guesswork, lawmaker says. Shift comes under new commander-in-chief. Ukraine’s new commander-in-chief, Drapatyi, is centering the army on soldiers’ lives and real front-line needs, a lawmaker believes.
“Operation to strike Russian targets deep in swamps continues”: Ukrainian Commander Madiar says his unit hits 7,306 Russian troops in first half of October, up 59% on August. The pace held through weather that usually grounds drones, says Robert “Madiar” Brovdi, who calls the trend the opposite of de-escalation.
Ukraine’s Navy says it hit six Su-34 bombers at a Russian airbase with Neptune missiles—the jets that drop glide bombs on Ukrainian towns (updated). Footage from Borisoglebsk showed a large fire at the base after Russian officials declared a missile alert, though the damage has not been independently confirmed.
Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles. The pause was meant to seal a US-announced energy truce, but Russia kept hitting power plants while Ukraine lost early warnings and drone connectivity.
To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets. The crews fight under Air Force commands, using interceptor drones and automated turrets.
Intelligence and technology
Posting strike videos online may help Russia tune its drones’ optical targeting. Moscow now pays people to film hits, Ukrainian adviser warns. Russia is collecting footage of its Geran attack drones hitting Ukraine, probably to test the optical target-recognition systems that guide them in their final seconds.
Ukraine’s shell factories outpace state orders, arms company chief says: Kyiv spent five months buying from them this year, leaving six to produce. Private plants were built under Russian fire with no state investment, says the head of Ukrainian defense maker Ukrainian Armor
Ukraine’s hobbit-named robot fired on targets up to 1.3 km away in a demo for border guards. First reported carrying a wounded soldier, Ukraine’s Frodo robot has now fired for a border guard brigade—built, its maker says, to hit and run.
Musk pointed at the US military over Ukraine’s satellite limits. Now a US official says the administration had nothing to do with them. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says it is in talks with partners and SpaceX to maintain stable service and prevent sudden restrictions on satellite services used by its military.
International
Ukraine and Japan plan prefabricated backup crossings for Kyiv’s bridges: 720 meters of structures already delivered. The fifth phase of the Emergency Recovery Program, recently signed by the two countries, allocates $15 million for Ukraine’s infrastructure needs.
After Trump, Musk tells Ukraine’s president to go. Zelenskyy says he won’t resign and will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian. The Ukrainian leader told British broadcaster Piers Morgan that this refusal is why some “big guys” want him replaced.
US weighs relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, days after freeing Russian diesel. Officials say only unsanctioned oil would sail, but Reuters says Trump’s diesel push could pressure them to let Russian fuel aboard.
Ukraine’s war budget has $52 billion hole, and army needs $45 billion more on top. The West won’t send Ukraine the billions it needs until Kyiv delivers the reforms it promised.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russian drone cuts down unique energy line tower over Dnipro River in Kyiv. It can’t be rebuilt, and world is queuing for more power equipment. Ukraine’s grid operator Ukrenergo is already starting work on workarounds, but calls drones that cut down towers a new challenge.
Two tankers burn off Romania’s Sulina as Bulgaria says it lacks proof Russia is behind the Black Sea ship attacks. Seven crew members of a San Marino-flagged chemical tanker were still missing hours after it caught fire at anchor off the mouth of the Danube.
Russia’s largest drone attack on Kirovohrad Oblast since the full-scale invasion kills three in Kropyvnytskyi. Drones struck critical infrastructure, transport companies, logistics sites, and homes across the central Ukrainian oblast, with its capital taking most of the damage.
On Monday she sat in her cousin’s Kyiv apartment, and by Wednesday a Russian strike had left a hole where the window was. Her cousin, his girlfriend, and an aunt survived inside, and rescuers lifted them out 15 minutes after the blast.
A Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, Ukraine’s largest painting, in the section depicting the future. Its artist spent nearly two years creating it. The museum is weighing whether to restore the burned section or keep the fire’s traces as a reminder of the war.
Political and legal developments
Hungary held $82 million in cash and gold from Ukraine for months. Now, it faces torture complaints in Europe’s top court. Hungarian forces stopped two Oschadbank vehicles in March, carrying cash and gold from Austria to Ukraine.
Ukraine detains a gas station worker and a Telegram commenter suspected of scouting targets for Russian strikes. One was allegedly reached through a former classmate in Russia, and the other allegedly took orders from a female handler there.
Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies, whose independence EU made condition for membership, have clawed back $5.1 million for state budget. Detectives found that a regional branch’s inaction had put millions at risk.
Read our earlier daily review here.
Read Also
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1696: Romania blames Russia for drone attacks on ships off its coast and calls for a joint NATO Black Sea command
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1694: Starlink cap cripples Ukrainian drone missions as Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, ordered the cut
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1693: Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before air raid sirens, as fears grow that the US could cut launch warning data

articles.title: Putin Doesn’t Want Talks ‘in Any Format,’ Zelensky Says, Urges NATO to Take Drone Threats Seriously
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has no interest in peace negotiations in any form, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, warning European and NATO countries that Moscow’s ambitions extend well beyond Ukraine’s borders.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels Friday, Oct. 16, Zelensky dismissed the Kremlin’s portrayal of its strikes on Ukraine as merely retaliatory, describing it as a “parody” of a genuine willingness to see the war end.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Putin wants to destroy us. He does not respect us, our sovereignty or our territorial integrity. He truly believes that we are not a country, not a nation,” Zelensky said.
“Do you really believe that the eastern part of our country is enough for him [Putin]? Then why, when the full-scale invasion began, did he go for Kyiv? Is that Donbas? No, it is the capital. Without the capital, there is no state,” he continued.
The war could spill beyond Ukraine’s borders
In recent months, Russia’s escalating hybrid campaign – from espionage, cyber attacks and drone incursions – has increased to the point that several EU members are saying that the continent is already at war with the Kremlin.
Russian diplomats have made serious threats to the Baltic states in particular, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed that European preparations for a possible war with Russia could provoke one.
2 Killed, 6 Injured in Russian Strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Region
“This position could turn out to be a self-fulfilling prophecy,” Lavrov said during the 81st United General Nations Assembly (UNGA) in New York late September, where 51 countries have separately signed a joint letter urging Moscow to agree to an immediate ceasefire.
So, it does not come as a surprise that Zelensky also questioned where Russia would stop should it achieve the military objective it set in Ukraine.
He pointed to the growing number of Russian drones crossing into European and NATO airspace, accusing European governments of avoiding responding forcefully to individual incursions out of fear of escalation.
In his view, the countries will practically be forced to take the threat seriously once Russia begins using ballistic and cruise missiles, alongside drones to violate NATO’s airspace, as it already does in Ukraine.
His warning came a day after Romania said Russian drones had entered its airspace three times in less than 24 hours, as attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea killed eight people.
Diesel deal could open the door to wider sanctions relief
Zelensky criticized US President Donald Trump’s diesel agreement on Oct. 9 with Moscow that allowed imports of Russian diesel to enter the global markets. Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
He warned that the deal could set a precedent for further concessions, predicting that gas deals would follow, gradually extending sanctions relief to Russia’s banking system, chemical industry and sanctioned individuals.
Ukraine had no choice but to oppose such steps diplomatically, since no one else would defend Kyiv’s interests, Zelensky said.
Trump’s move came while Ukraine’s negotiating delegation was holding talks with Trump’s administration in Miami, hoping to reach a breakthrough and end Russia’s aggression.
Only three weeks earlier, on Sept. 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law. His latest decisions appeared to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s military-industrial complex, as well as networks close to Putin himself.
A bipartisan group of 12 US senators signed a joint letter on Oct. 13, urging Trump to rescind his diesel agreement with Putin, calling it a gift to Moscow and a betrayal of Ukraine.
Starlink speed still not fully restored, Zelensky said
Addressing recent restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals, Zelensky said the service had not been switched off but slowed, preventing Ukrainian forces from shooting down a number of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones that target civilians.
He rejected claims that Ukraine uses Starlink for attacks inside Russia. Instead, he said, the system supports interceptor drones, mid-range strikes on Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory, and drone deliveries of food and water to soldiers who spend weeks or months on the front line. All three were disrupted while the restrictions were in place.
According to Zelensky, speeds are now recovering but have not returned to previous levels.
The restrictions took effect overnight on Oct. 13-14 after the US aerospace giant’s CEO Elon Musk tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour) without prior warning.
Musk claimed that speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals are set by the US military, including Trump himself, not the company.
Washington has not taken responsibility for the restrictions.
