articles.title: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.
The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump.
Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”
Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.
Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.
Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.
“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”
Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.
Trump said on Friday he did not think either he or Elon Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starshield access and that any limits were not imposed by the US.
Starshield is produced by Musk’s SpaceX but controlled by the US government.
Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.
Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 across Ukraine on Friday, hitting two shopping centres and temporarily power to more than 1 million people, officials said.
When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.
According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.
The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.
The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.
Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.
“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.
The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.
Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.

articles.title: Chief of General Staff of Poland Inspects Turkish SRBM TAYFUN System Amid Search for Long-Range Missiles
articles.body:
During a visit to Turkey, General Wiesław Kukula, Chief of the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces, visited facilities of the ROKETSAN Group, where he familiarized himself with the Turkish TAYFUN SRBM.
This was reported by the press service of the Polish Armed Forces.
In addition, Polish military officials were shown the TRG/TRLG families of guided rockets, which align with Poland’s concept for developing the capability to deliver high-precision strikes deep into enemy territory.
Poland also expressed interest in multi-layered air defense technologies, particularly the ALKA system, which combines laser weapons with electronic warfare capabilities, as well as the PUSU anti-drone solutions and the SUNGUR man-portable air defense system (MANPADS).
“The visit was part of an effort to familiarize ourselves with modern technologies and areas of development in operational capabilities that are important for the transformation of the Polish Armed Forces and the strengthening of the country’s defense potential,” the ministry emphasized.
Poland aims to develop the capability to deliver high-precision strikes at ranges of over 1,000 kilometers. The country is considering strike drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles as potential weapons.
According to Brigadier General Grzegorz Potuszki, head of the Planning and Programming Directorate for the Development of the Polish Armed Forces, the Polish Army is currently capable of striking ground targets at a range of approximately 300 kilometers using American ATACMS missiles and South Korean CTM-290 missiles. However, the experience of the Russia-Ukraine war has demonstrated the need to use high-precision weapons at significantly greater ranges.
ROKETSAN is actively developing the TAYFUN family of ballistic missiles. The first tests of the missile took place in October 2022—the missile struck a target 561 km away after a 458-second flight.
Subsequent tests took place in June 2023 from the Rize-Artvin airfield in the northeast of the country. The tests confirmed the missile’s combat capabilities and marked another step toward the mass production of the new weapon.
In July 2025, ROKETSAN unveiled the TAYFUN Block-4 short-range ballistic missile for the first time. According to unofficial reports, its range is approximately 1,000 km.
According to the company, the TAYFUN Block-4 is an improved version of the previous model and features an increased range and higher speed, allowing it to effectively penetrate missile defense systems.
The missile weighs about 7.3 metric tons, is approximately 10 meters long, and has a diameter of 610 mm. According to the company, this is the first Turkish ballistic missile capable of striking targets at a range of several hundred kilometers at a speed exceeding Mach 5.

articles.title: Ukraine Plans More Powerful Drone Campaign to Paralyze Russian Airports – The Atlantic
articles.body:
Ukraine is preparing to escalate its campaign to disrupt Russian airports, deploying AI-guided drones capable of evading air defenses and striking aviation infrastructure directly.
The operation, codenamed “M&Ms,” was developed under former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and envisioned using small, low-cost drones capable of navigating and identifying targets without human operators, according to two sources familiar with the plan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The drones would carry detailed maps and images of designated targets, allowing their onboard computers to compare live camera footage with stored data. Once a target was identified, a drone would dive into it and detonate without requiring further confirmation from an operator, the report said.
The upcoming operation is expected to be significantly more aggressive, with drones that do not depend on US intelligence and could soon enter mass production, Ukrainian officials told The Atlantic.
The Ukrainian official also said a drone prototype had already been used in combat in the Donbas, although development is ongoing. The drones have not yet been deployed against Russian airports.
The current campaign has already disrupted air travel across Moscow. Between Oct. 3 and 9, Russian airports canceled 345 flights and delayed nearly 4,000, with some passengers facing waits of 10 hours or more.
On Oct. 10, another 692 flights were delayed and 93 canceled. On Oct. 14, 238 flights were delayed and 124 canceled. Moscow’s airport network was shut down for an average of around three hours daily, according to the report.
22 US Lawmakers Press Trump to Enforce Russia Sanctions Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
Even Russian President Vladimir Putin’s plane was reportedly unable to land in Moscow on Oct. 9 while returning from Turkmenistan, as two of the capital’s four airports were closed for seven hours during a drone attack.
Prolonged airport shutdowns could force international carriers, including Turkish Airlines and Emirates, to reconsider flights to the Russian capital, disrupting a key connection between Russia’s political elite and the outside world.
The plan was reportedly presented to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in early 2026. Although he raised concerns about risks to civilian aircraft, passengers and airport workers, he allowed preparations to continue, according to The Atlantic’s earlier report.
Trump’s energy ceasefire fails to stop Russian attacks
The planned escalation comes amid growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Last week, on Oct. 9, Trump announced an agreement for Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, drawing criticism from US lawmakers and European allies.
Zelensky described the deal as a “simple victory” for the Kremlin in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday.
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Zelensky said.
He also accused Trump of taking Russia’s side in the war, arguing that Washington should remain neutral rather than favor Moscow.
“This is our country, our body, our home, our children,” Zelensky said. “That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side.”
Trump called for a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure and announced what he called a mutual energy ceasefire.
However, Russia continued striking Ukrainian cities and energy facilities, with missile and drone attacks leaving hundreds of thousands of people without electricity.
Ukraine had temporarily suspended strikes on Russian refineries at Washington’s request. Kyiv argued that any energy truce must apply to both sides, rather than restrict Ukraine’s ability to retaliate while Moscow continues attacking its power grid.
On Oct. 14, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times that Kyiv would no longer observe the pause in refinery strikes.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Oblast early on Oct. 15, triggering a fire at the facility about 300 kilometers (186 miles) southeast of Moscow.
Later that day, Trump called Ukraine’s decision to resume refinery strikes a “disgrace,” accusing Kyiv of driving up global energy prices in an interview with Newsmax.
“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said when asked about the renewed attacks.
Energy analysts, however, say Trump’s deal to resume Russian diesel exports is unlikely to significantly lower fuel prices.
The main driver of the global price surge has been the US-Israel war with Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump also portrayed Zelensky as a greater obstacle to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine than Putin.
“It should end soon. I think they actually both would like to see it end,” Trump said. “But I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
Zelensky met NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels on Oct. 15 and held talks with European leaders ahead of the EU summit, seeking continued military and political support for Ukraine.
“Don’t attack us. Don’t kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel,” Zelensky said in an Oct. 11 interview with ABC News, outlining Kyiv’s position on a reciprocal energy ceasefire.
Kyiv prepares to escalate airport campaign
Trump, however, has not publicly objected to Ukrainian attacks on Russian airports or data centers, which Ukrainian forces targeted last week, The Atlantic reported.
When Trump first called Zelensky last month, he reportedly suggested that Kyiv could strike targets other than oil refineries.
“There are many other targets,” Trump said.
According to The Atlantic, Trump is becoming less interested in mediating between Moscow and Kyiv and increasingly appears to be pursuing a deal on the Kremlin’s behalf.

articles.title: EU summit: Zelensky brings begging bowl to Brussels under Trump cloud
articles.body:
EU summit: Zelensky gets promises but no money – As it happened
Vladimir Zelensky has emerged from the EU summit in Brussels with fresh promises of support but no deal on the additional €70 billion ($79 billion) he is demanding for Ukraine. Instead, European leaders tasked the European Commission with finding ways to meet Kiev’s growing financial needs, leaving the question of who will foot the bill unanswered.
The Ukrainian leader arrived in Brussels following a bitter public falling-out with US President Donald Trump over Washington’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel supplies. His demands have put further pressure on Kiev’s European backers, who are already struggling with soaring energy costs, strained budgets and the prospect of a difficult winter.
- Zelensky rejected the arrangement, saying he felt “betrayed” by Trump and called the US president’s decision “weak.”
- Trump then called for Ukraine to get a “new president,” and questioned Zelensky’s willingness to reach a settlement with Moscow.
- Zelensky announced continued refinery attacks and complained of restrictions on American intelligence support and Starlink services.
- On Thursday, Kiev hit a refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Region, despite Washington’s clearly expressed expectations and objections.
- Trump called the attacks a “disgrace” and accused Zelensky of “driving up fuel prices for everyone.”
- On Thursday night, after Zelensky arrived in Brussels, Trump went hard in an interview with Newsmax. “He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t,” Trump said, adding that Zelensky was harder to deal with than Putin. He also alleged that US missiles supplied to Kiev had been sold on the “open market.”
- Washington also announced it would prioritize its own munitions stocks over others. “Once we are really stocked, we will start letting our allies buy them from us,” Trump said.
The summit also failed to break the deadlock over frozen Russian sovereign assets held in Belgium. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz continued to push for the funds to be used to support Kiev, despite his unpopularity at home, while flatly rejecting a US proposal to include them in a peace settlement. After the talks, Merz acknowledged that “there were no decisions, but there was an exchange of views,” warning that the €90 billion loan already agreed for Ukraine “will not be enough.”
This live feed has now ended.
- 16 October 2026 16:01 GMT Merz’s insistence on continuing to bankroll Ukraine drew a sharp response in Germany, where AfD co-leader Alice Weidel contrasted his appetite for further funding with skyrocketing costs at home. “Diesel €2.25 [per liter], drinks 30 cents more expensive, cigarettes soon €12 – and Merz wants to pump even more tax money into Ukraine, because it’s still not enough and never will be,” she wrote on X, pledging that the AfD would end this “policy against our own people.” Her party and the left-wing BSW had previously called for Germany to follow Trump’s example and strike its own diesel deal with Moscow, arguing that sanctions had “failed across the board” and that regular citizens have ended up absorbing the cost. Deputy BSW leader Claudia Wittig insisted that Berlin should go further than a one-off fuel agreement and resume regular imports of Russian oil and gas to help rescue German industry.
- 15:56 GMT After all the applause, embraces, and promises of unwavering support, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed the summit had achieved exactly nothing on Ukraine, and that “there were no decisions, but there was an exchange of views.” He also confessed that the €90 billion loan already agreed for Kiev “will not be enough” and that EU members will need to empty out their pockets once again while the European Commission assesses how much more is needed. Merz also found room to endorse Ukrainian strikes on Russian communications and energy infrastructure, describing them as “right, reasonable, and understandable.” Finding agreement on Europe’s own finances, however, has proved difficult, Merz admitted, stating it was impossible to predict whether leaders would reach a budget deal. Discussions could continue at an additional November meeting and at December’s regular summit, he said.
- 15:35 GMT “Not one more Euro for Ukraine!” the leader of the French right-wing Les Patriotes party Florian Philippot wrote on X in response to Zelensky’s gargantuan €70 billion EU funding demand. “That means 13 billion to be paid by France: RUIN! Meanwhile, they want to stop reimbursing medicines here, delink pensions above 1260 euros per month,” the politician wrote, demanding a “STOP” to giving money to Ukraine.
- 15:00 GMT Zelensky says he cannot accept Washington’s diesel deal with Moscow, but a pause in refinery attacks apparently does have a price – satellite coverage allowing Ukrainian forces to strike deeper into Russia. The Ukrainian leader warned in Brussels that diesel agreements could lead to gas deals and further sanctions relief. Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reports that he agreed to a proposed 100-day halt in refinery strikes in exchange for extending Starlink coverage by 300 km, supposedly to allow Kiev to target Russian launch systems. The offer was reportedly brought to Kiev by two Republican senators last week. Read here what the offer really means. At the same time, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas pointed out at the summit that while the bloc can bankroll Kiev, it cannot offer an alternative to Starlink.
- 14:46 GMT Zelensky’s updated €70 billion demand has prompted EU leaders to ask the European Commission to find other ways to cover Ukraine’s estimated funding gap next year, according to four of the bloc’s diplomats. The suggested options include tapping frozen Russian assets, using unused SAFE defense loans and issuing more common debt – reportedly the likeliest route, repeating the approach behind the €90 billion loan already being disbursed. The idea of seizing frozen Russian assets still faces Belgium’s resistance and warnings of legal and financial fallout. More joint borrowing would put another bill on Europe’s books, and EU member states are already struggling with energy costs and competing spending demands. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was even more categorical about increasing spending on the bloc, telling reporters after the summit that “Sweden is not an ATM for the European Union budget.” The Commission is expected to present its options at the informal EU summit in Dublin on November 13. For now, leaders have agreed that someone should work out where the money will come from.
- 13:54 GMT Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker questioned Ukraine’s shifting financial demands ahead of the summit and demanded to see the actual numbers before dishing out any more funds to fill Zelensky’s ever-growing budget hole. “So many numbers are swirling around that you have to put them in order… you have to make it transparent, where this hole comes from,” he said. Ukraine’s proposed budget put next year’s shortfall at roughly $40 billion. The country’s prime minister subsequently cited needs exceeding $52 billion, plus $45 billion in off-budget military requirements. In his Friday address, Zelensky put the number at a staggering €70 billion in additional financial and military support, far exceeding Brussels’ previous estimates; it would come in addition to the €90 billion support loan slated to be rolled out this year and next year. The requests come against a familiar backdrop of corruption investigations, including an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom linked to Zelensky’s former business partner Timur Mindich, and more recent cases involving inflated defense construction contracts. Even Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko has apparently gotten sick of the embezzling, asking this week where the billions allocated for energy infrastructure defense have actually gone.
- 13:50 GMT Zelensky expressed horror and shock at the prospect of Russia getting its frozen foreign assets back, begging the Europeans to hand them over to Kiev before that happens. “Ukraine would like to receive these funds in some kind of format,” he said, insisting that Russia should not have an opportunity to influence future discussions about its own reserves. He also thanked the EU for last year’s €90 billion bailout, before making clear he doesn’t intend to stop dipping into their pockets. The appeal follows reports that US negotiators proposed releasing some of the frozen Russian assets as part of a peace settlement. European officials have rejected the initiative and have revived, yet again, the debate on how to appropriate the funds. “The frozen assets are there: that’s what should be used for supporting Ukraine. Simple,” Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said. Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen called them “the most obvious place to look,” with Kiev estimating a $78 billion funding black hole next year. However, “simple” has yet to convince Belgium, which has repeatedly blocked the previous scheme, warning that appropriation could trigger enormous legal liabilities and undermine confidence in Europe’s financial system. Moscow has condemned confiscation as theft and threatened retaliation.
- 12:41 GMT In the final question of the press briefing, Sky News decided to take part in the Zelensky show and give him a clippable moment. “Are you a scapegoat for Trump’s midterm troubles,” the outlet’s reporter asked. Zelensky said nothing, glanced at his notes, and said “that is my answer,” prompting laughter from the press room.
- 12:07 GMT Asked about Trump finding him harder to negotiate with than Putin, Zelensky turned the answer into another objection to Washington’s diesel deal, complaining that gas agreements could follow, then banking arrangements, and further Russian sanctions relief. Zelensky then returned to the familiar claim that Putin would move beyond Ukraine and threaten NATO as justification for continued pressure on Russia. Moscow has repeatedly denied plans to attack the bloc, dismissing the allegation as a pretext for European rearmament and continued funding for Kiev. A number of EU military officials have also cited a lack of evidence for any such plans.
- 11:51 GMT Zelensky offered a teary-eyed explanation of Ukraine’s use of Starlink, claiming its drones are primarily used for interception and deliveries of food and water. In the same breath, however, he acknowledged that the restrictions had also disrupted medium-range strikes. He denied using the network for attacks deep inside Russia, but complained that lower speed limits had deprived Kiev of other strike capabilities. Musk has said Starlink should serve civilian and defensive purposes, describing offensive operations as “inappropriate for a commercial company.” Zelensky said partners had promised to restore the capabilities, although the previous speed limits had not yet been fully reinstated.

articles.title: Why a new US–Israeli war against Iran could carry enormous risks
articles.body:
In recent days, three developments have emerged as key preliminary indicators that the US may be preparing to step up its military campaign against Iran. First, the dispatch of a third aircraft carrier strike group alongside additional American forces toward the waters surrounding Iran; second, the directive from the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) to achieve full operational readiness; and third, the continuation of economic pressure, sanctions, and blockades, alongside disputes over the Strait of Hormuz and diplomatic friction surrounding negotiations.
While these developments clearly signal an expansion of military options and an intensification of coercive pressure, they do not, on their own, constitute definitive proof of an executive decision to launch a broad war. This new force posture serves at least three strategic functions: deterrence, diplomatic leverage in negotiations, and operational preparation of a military option. Consequently, while a war posture increases the statistical probability of conflict, it does not in itself demonstrate a definitive decision to enter a major war.
Military power is not measured solely by the quantity of aircraft carriers, planes, or missile launchers. Rather, sustained combat power is a function of the equilibrium between consumption capacity, stockpiles, production, replenishment, human resources, logistics, and the ability to absorb the total costs of warfare.
Consequently, transforming a military posture into a major war requires the simultaneous presence of at least four structural capacities.
First, a sufficient reserve of munitions and weaponry must exist to execute initial operations and sustain subsequent engagements against Iran—a country that possesses the largest and most diverse missile arsenal in the region.
Second, robust equipment replenishment capacity is required, ensuring that if missiles, ammunition, aircraft, defence systems, or command assets are consumed or destroyed during hostilities, military industries can replace them at a commensurate rate—an outcome that appears practical implausible for the US regime.
These two requirements would appear to be unachievable at the moment. An April 21 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies shows that in four out of the seven key categories of munitions analysed, expenditure during the 40-day conflict likely exceeded half of pre-war inventories, and replenishing some of these stockpiles could require between one to four years.
Alongside the depletion of ammunition stockpiles, the Ramadan War has imposed tangible costs upon the air fleet of the hostile United States administration. According to an official report by the US Congressional Research Service on 5 October, at least 81 US military aircraft, including fixed-wing planes, helicopters, and unmanned systems, have been destroyed or damaged.
Third, sufficient human resource and logistical capacity must exist to sustain long-term operations at a vast distance while simultaneously maintaining the US regime’s existing military commitments and global readiness across other regions.
Fourth, the capacity to absorb the economic and geopolitical fallout must be present, including the ability to withstand spikes in energy prices, supply chain disruptions and diminished oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz, fiscal strain, the depletion of strategic reserves, vulnerable military bases, and domestic political pressure ahead of the November elections.
Iran’s ability to disrupt confidence at the world’s primary energy chokepoint has become a strategic lever that substantially raises the cost of any military adventure for the global economy and decision-makers in Washington.
The cumulative weight of munitions constraints and the economic variables examined places enemy decision-makers before three plausible strategic trajectories:
In the first scenario, the American and Zionist regimes rely on the continuation of a heavy military posture, economic sanctions, maritime pressure, intelligence operations, and cognitive warfare without initiating a major new conflict. Operationally, this option is entirely feasible. Its primary appeal for Washington lies in avoiding further depletion of its vulnerable stockpiles of Patriot, THAAD, and Tomahawk missiles, as well as preventing additional aircraft losses. Nevertheless, evidence suggests that this path is not without cost or hazard: maintaining a state of neither war nor peace entails persistent insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz, oil flows remaining below normal capacity, recessionary pressure on global energy demand, continuous attrition of forces deployed to the region, and increasing difficulty in managing unintended maritime incidents.
In the second scenario, the US/Zionist axis considers executing limited, phased air and missile strikes against specific targets—including Iranian military, missile, nuclear, or energy infrastructure—rather than entering directly into an all-out war; an option cited by Axios sources as one of the plans under active consideration. Although the presence of three aircraft carrier strike groups and current stockpiles render such strikes operationally viable in the short term, the central dilemma of this scenario remains escalation control. When an actor initiates a limited attack under the assumption that the opponent’s response will remain bounded, it exposes itself to inadvertent escalation due to asymmetrical perceptions of thresholds and the absence of unilateral control over the defender’s decisions.
The third scenario—direct entry or a gradual slide into a full-scale regional war—represents the most costly and perilous trajectory facing the US regime and the genocidal Zionist entity. Should such a scenario materialise, the conflict is unlikely to remain unidimensional. Operationally, it could encompass, simultaneously or sequentially, high-intensity air combat, mass missile exchanges, severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, cyber operations, and strikes against enemy regional bases and energy infrastructure across the broader region. In such a context, a punitive operation could rapidly degrade into a multi-front war of attrition.
Alongside military variables, the autumn political and electoral calendar constitutes another factor influencing calculations regarding the timing and ceiling of escalation. The deployment of a third aircraft carrier and 10,000 additional troops toward the waters surrounding Iran coupled with the Pentagon’s directive to US Central Command to complete operational preparations explicitly demonstrates that the timing of potential operations within Washington and Tel Aviv’s decision-making circles is being weighed against the November congressional mid-terms, as well as the Zionist parliamentary elections scheduled just one week prior.
A further dimension concerns apprehension over Iran’s potential capacity to sever subsea internet cables, thereby completely severing connectivity across the Arabian Peninsula as well as the aggressor Zionist state, and disabling all exchange and financial markets dependent on this network infrastructure. Crucially, through the establishment of its National Information Network and its relative independence from western-dominated internet financial transactions, Iran has shifted the balance in this domain to its own strategic advantage.
From the standpoint of deterrence theory, inflicting costs that outweigh the scale of the initial strike often serves as a rational mechanism to fundamentally reshape the adversary’s cost-benefit calculus regarding subsequent actions. Given Iran’s documented capabilities, should such a miscalculation be committed by the US or the Zionist regime, a plausible strategic posture for Tehran would involve launching a multi-domain, asymmetrical, and extensive response designed to defy containment or mitigation. Consequently, even a limited military strike would impel Iran to formulate a response that far exceeds the initial scale of aggression. This underlying logic of an escalatory response to limited warfare significantly raises the calculative risks of any new military venture.
The principal danger in the current security environment is not necessarily a pre-planned decision to wage an all-out war, but rather the escalation—whether intended or unintended—of a small war into a major war through crisis instability.
If the deployment of military force as a pressure tactic leads to a miscalculation and a limited strike, and that limited strike is met with an asymmetric, multi-domain response, a cycle of reciprocal retaliation will take hold. This chain reaction could impose a war whose full consequences its initiators lack the capacity to absorb.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
articles.body:
In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
No matter how European leaders pledge to support Ukraine come hell or high water and let the taxpayers foot the bill, the cold hard fact is that there are things no euros can buy, such as US intelligence and satellite communications.
Kiev’s critical reliance on American space capabilities came to the fore this week when the long-standing feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky flared up again. Trump, who had struck a diesel supply deal with Russia, called Zelensky a hindrance to peace who should be replaced. Zelensky called Trump a weakling who had betrayed Ukraine, if not in those exact terms.
According to lamentations from Kiev corroborated by media reporting, the White House put a chokehold on the Zelensky government by suspending early warning about incoming Russian ballistic missiles and temporarily suspending access to Starlink satellite internet for fast-moving objects – such as drones used in Kiev’s “middle strike” operations inside what Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine.
It’s not like Kiev was not warned. During a meeting in Miami last week, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly told the Ukrainians the diesel deal announcement was coming and that Kiev should not have ignored Trump’s multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accounts shared with Axios and Reuters suggest the Americans were polite enough not to say “what a nice deal to get intelligence and internet you have; it would be a shame if something happened to it.” But they mentioned “all that the US has done for Ukraine.” The Ukrainians did take it as a threat.
Here are the alternatives Kiev would have, should Trump push the issue further.
No match for US intelligence
Intelligence that European NATO members can provide is a far cry from what the US has been delivering for years. Already, early warning about Russian ballistic missile launches has stopped coming, just as Zelensky is complaining.
The US operates the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS), whose backbone is six geosynchronous orbit satellites equipped with thermal sensors that detect launch signatures, complemented by two active and two reserve payloads in a highly elliptical orbit.
SBIRS helps identify and estimate the trajectory of a weapon, but has limited ability to track missiles after the intensive boost phase. But knowing one is incoming helps ground and airborne radar systems that guide interceptor missiles.
Other NATO members rely on SBIRS intelligence and never thought they would need their own alternative.
Satellites operated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the Air Force’s electronic reconnaissance aircraft, such as the RC-135U Combat Sent, also collect intelligence about Russian air defense systems. It’s unclear how much data it shares with Kiev, but the media has said the US helps plan Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia to minimize Moscow’s ability to intercept.
European NATO members do have some similar capabilities, including France’s three CERES electronic-intelligence satellites, the UK’s three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, and Germany’s SARah radar-reconnaissance space program, but there is only so much they can do to measure up to the world’s largest military spender.
OneWeb not to rule them all
On the connectivity side, Starlink and its military twin Starshield remain the most capable today. It has over 11,000 satellites in low Earth (LEO) orbit that can use lasers to route traffic between each other, boosting their bandwidth.
The Starlink Mini terminal weighs just 1.1 kg and has an integrated antenna, making it usable even on even smaller military drones. Even larger variants are compact, which makes them harder to spot, and they typically consume under 100 watts of power – both valuable features in frontline applications.
The most direct non-US alternative is Eutelsat OneWeb, which already complements Starlink access in Ukraine. It only has 600+ satellites in its constellation, but nevertheless offers a high-speed connection.
However, OneWeb’s orbital component “remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, told Reuters.
OneWeb ground hardware is likewise no match for Starlink in price, size, or appetite for energy. The relatively small Hughes HL1100W terminal weighs over 10 kg and consumes around 130 watts, though there are efforts to produce smaller and less power-hungry equipment.
Kymeta Corporation announced a OneWeb terminal in March whose 100-watt consumption it said was optimized for mobile platforms. Its “compact and lightweight design” means it weighs less than 11 kg, and the producer itself is Redmond, Washington.
Dark horses in orbit
In September, EU co-founder Luxembourg announced the successful launch of the final three of a planned 13 satellites of its O3b mPOWER communication system. The low number is misleading, since the constellation is being positioned in medium Earth orbit and requires fewer satellites for coverage.
The trade off is latency, which is higher by an order of magnitude compared to LEO-based systems, but Luxembourg’s system is still good enough for some military applications and is used by NATO.
O3b mPOWER’s potential for Ukraine’s war effort is limited due to its coverage, which is between 50° north latitude and 50° south latitude. Luxembourg is right on the northern border of the band, but a large part of Ukraine, including Kiev, is outside of it. As they say, geography is destiny.
GOVSATCOM, the EU’s program to band together communication satellites owned by several member states, is somewhat of a dark horse, but public data suggests its capabilities are too limited to replace Starlink.
Amazon Leo is currently in limited preview, but it’s hard to expect an American company and a major Pentagon contractor to publicly defy Trump at Brussels’ call. Russia’s in-development Rassvet system is obviously not an option.
The EU’s proposed IRIS² system is years away from being operational, as is Canada’s Telesat Lightspeed.
In short, should Ukraine lose Starlink, in the short term Europe cannot replace it, as EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.

articles.title: Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
articles.body:
Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
It is the first time the president has definitively addressed nuclear weapons, but he did not deny US could use ‘mother of all bombs’.
United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future.
In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax.
The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Here’s what we know:
What did Trump say?
Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.
He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said.
He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”.
Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.”
Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran.
Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.
Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop.
When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory.
What is the ‘mother of all bombs’?
The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters.
It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said.
“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.”
However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access.
What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons?
Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.
Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran.
In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait.
He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.
Experts widely interpreted his statements as a threat of nuclear destruction, but one that still failed to force Iran to the table.
Although Trump largely moved away from his sabre-rattling rhetoric in the following weeks, he reiterated at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month that he could “annihilate” Iran. He also told the assembly that he believed a deal would emerge after the midterms.
What is a ‘tactical’ nuclear weapon?
“Tactical” nuclear weapons (TNW) are smaller nuclear munitions designed for the battlefield as opposed to strategic nuclear munitions designed for mass destruction.
Some perceive TNWs as having a lesser impact than an atomic bomb, but experts warn that their names are misleading and they can nevertheless be devastating. Their explosive yield, between 0.3 and 50 kilotons, can impact areas within a 500-600km radius.
The US dropped a 15-kiloton nuclear bomb on Hiroshima, meaning that weapon would today be considered a TNW. The US, North Korea and Russia have TNWs in their arsenals, although no country has ever used them. TNWs are not subject to any international treaties and are largely unregulated.
What might another US attack on Iran look like?
With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.
The US could also continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports, while providing escorts for commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has vowed to respond to escalatory strikes by targeting oil and digital infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states.
Senior defence officials have also warned that Iran will invade its neighbours if the US launches a ground operation, although Trump appears to have ruled that out.
Earlier in the war, he hinted at the possibility of sending ground forces to retrieve some 400kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington and Israel claim Tehran has hidden underground.
Trump’s phone calls in March to Kurdish militia groups fighting Iran provoked speculation that Washington could coordinate with them for an invasion, although that did not happen.

articles.title: Russia still parks its best bombers in the open. Ukraine has spent a year knocking out the air defenses that were supposed to protect them
articles.body:
- An overnight raid by the Ukrainian navy reportedly destroyed four Russian air force Sukhoi Su-34 fighter-bombers
- A barrage of Long Neptune cruise missiles struck the parked aircraft at a base in western Russia
- Observers blamed poor airfield procedures, and also lamented a lack of air defenses
Overnight on 14 and 15 October, the Ukrainian navy fired a clutch of Long Neptune cruise missiles at Borisoglebsk air base in Voronezh, in western Russia some 260 km from the border with Ukraine.
The results were devastating. The ground-launched Neptunes struck the tarmac where six Russian air force Sukhoi Su-34 fighter-bombers were parked nearly wingtip to wingtip in uncovered positions.
Satellite imagery from the morning of 15 October depicted piles of smoldering wreckage. The navy said it hit all six jets. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said four Su-34s were destroyed and a further two were damaged. "I thank the warriors of the Ukrainian navy for their precision!" he wrote.
The jets, he said, were loaded with aerial bombs and ready for new strikes on Ukraine. An analyst reading the imagery counted wreckage of two to four aircraft and two empty spots where damaged jets had been moved.
An Airbus Pléiades satellite image from 11 October, four days before the strike, showed the six Su-34s on open aprons. Next to them were structures that the Russian independent outlet Istories said looked like anti-drone nets or their frames. Nets can snag a small drone. A cruise missile goes through.
At roughly $50 million apiece, by the Ukrainian Air Force's estimate, the four destroyed jets alone cost Russia some $200 million. The twin-engine, two-seat, supersonic Su-34 is the Russian air force's best fighter-bomber. Almost every day, Su-34s lob KAB precision glide bombs at Ukrainian troops and civilians.
In nearly 56 months of hard fighting in Russia's wider war on Ukraine, the Russians have now lost no fewer than 37 Su-34s destroyed, with several more damaged, by open-source counts. Sukhoi continues to deliver new Su-34s in small batches, the latest handed over on 7 October, helping the Russians sustain their overall inventory despite heavy losses.
They've still got plenty of Su-34s, but that doesn't mean the Russians shouldn't worry. As long as they're parking warplanes out in the open within range of Ukraine's best deep strike munitions, those planes are vulnerable to attack. Russia's air defenses are spread too thin to intercept every Ukrainian munition.
The strike may also hit the Russian air force's training pipeline. Borisoglebsk air base is home to the 160th Aviation Training Regiment. The regiment operates Yakovlev Yak-130 trainers for more basic flight training plus—for more advanced training—front-line combat aircraft including Su-34s, Sukhoi Su-35s, and Sukhoi Su-30s.
Russian bloggers are aghast, according to a round-up of posts on Russian social media by analyst ChrisO_wiki. "How is it that, four years after the start of the Special Military Operation, there are no protective structures for aircraft at airfields located within range of Ukrainian air strikes?" blogger Ramsay wrote. "And where did the billions of rubles allocated for their construction go?"
Trending Now
"Much can be said about the need to build a sufficient number of concrete shelters at all airfields," blogger Vladimir Romanov pointed out. "Reality shows that, to date, sufficient measures have not been taken."
“Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare”: Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September, and winter will make it worse, analyst says
Close parking
Ramsay asked why the Su-34s were concentrated in one area, apparently so that ground crews could quickly service all of them with a single ground power unit, a mobile generator that starts an aircraft's systems before flight. "How is it that the APA, a utilitarian piece of equipment, has become so scarce that it forces an entire group of combat aircraft to be parked in a single area, making them an ideal target for attacks?"
The best defense is an active one, however, the Fighterbomber channel stressed. "Protecting aircraft by the usual method of moving them out of the line of fire at such ranges from long-range strike systems won’t work here; the only way to defend against them is with a full-scale, echeloned air defense system—both ground-based and airborne."
Ukrainian planners know this. Which is why, for more than a year now, they've been systematically striking Russian radars, surface-to-air missile batteries, and mobile air defense systems. By March, Ukrainian forces were “collaps[ing] the layered defensive architecture that the Russian integrated air defence doctrine depends upon to function,” according to an in-depth investigation by Tochnyi.info.
The strikes on Russian air defenses—at least 492 of them between June and early March—are part of a carefully scripted plan. Destroying the right air defenses faster than the Russians can replace them has the effect of “facilitating strikes on more critical targets deep within Russian territory,” Tochnyi.info explained.
The critical targets include air bases such as Borisoglebsk and the expensive warplanes parked on its tarmac.
Read Also
- Russia is losing the Black Sea grain war it started. Its answer is to sink civilian ships off Romania and Bulgaria
- Russia is back at Dobropillia a year after it failed there. Now it’s the southern jaw of a pincer on Donbas’s last big free cities
- Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won.

articles.title: Trump criticizes Ukraine's resumption of refinery strikes, calls Zelenskyy difficult negotiator – media
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump criticized Ukraine's decision to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries and described Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as a more difficult negotiating partner compared to Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, making the statement in an interview with Newsmax television channel on Thursday.
"Now, if you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace... there are many other targets to hit," Trump said.
According to the head of the White House, strikes on refineries producing diesel fuel harm the global energy market. Trump seeks to reduce energy prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3, 2026, including through an agreement with Putin regarding the purchase of Russian diesel. Assessing the prospects of ending the war by the end of his term, the U.S. President expressed confidence that hostilities should end soon, but questioned the Ukrainian leader's readiness for compromises. According to Trump, negotiating with Zelenskyy is harder than with Putin, while mutual personal hostility between the two leaders presents an additional obstacle to a settlement.
Furthermore, the American president spoke in favor of holding elections in Ukraine, questioning the level of public support for the current government amid ongoing missile strikes on residential buildings. He also criticized his predecessor Joe Biden for providing Kyiv with multi-billion-dollar military aid and stated that the current administration is replenishing its own stockpiles of Patriot anti-aircraft missile systems and Tomahawk cruise missiles at record speed, after which Washington will permit allies to purchase these arms.
Separately, Trump reported that his administration is holding talks with Russia and China regarding the reduction of nuclear arsenals. According to his assessment, the U.S. ranks first in the world in nuclear capability, Russia second, while Beijing is currently less inclined toward denuclearization due to a lag that it could close within five to six years. The American president did not specify a timeframe for these negotiations.
On Thursday, Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil infrastructure following a three-day pause that Kyiv agreed to after Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. A senior Ukrainian official confirmed a drone attack on an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region, located approximately 290 km southeast of Moscow, where a fire broke out.
Previously, Ukraine fully agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's proposal for an energy truce and did not attack any energy facilities in Russia in response to their strikes.

articles.title: Restrictions on Starlink: Consequences for Ukrainian Drones and the Search for Alternatives
articles.body:
On the night of October 14, SpaceX, at the request of the White House, unilaterally and without warning imposed restrictions on Starlink accounts with special Starshield military accounts for Ukraine.
Starshield is a secure version of the Starlink satellite communications system, developed for the needs of government, military, and intelligence agencies and managed by the U.S. Department of Defense.
It first became known in December 2024 that the Armed Forces of Ukraine had gained access to the secure U.S. military satellite communications network Starshield. According to sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu, the current contract for the service is valid through April 2027 and is funded by Germany.
Communications began to drop out at varying speeds, ranging from 72 to 161 km/h, on various unmanned platforms and across different units. On October 15, the speed threshold for SpaceX’s military communications system was raised to 160 km/h, but as of October 16, its operation had still not been fully restored.
Kirill Lyukov, head of the unmanned technologies department at the Serhiy Prytula Charitable Foundation, told Militarnyi that communication issues with Starlink terminals have been reported since the night of October 14 across the entire combat zone, in the temporarily occupied territories, and in Ukraine’s rear regions. At least three units reported regular loss of connection at speeds of 75 km/h.
According to him, afterStarlink was blocked for Russians in the temporarily occupied territories, additional restrictions were imposed, causing the terminals to lose connection at speeds averaging over 70 km/h. To identify military users, special accounts are used for which this restriction has been lifted. This allows the Ukrainian Defense Forces to operate at higher speeds both in the temporarily occupied territories and in areas under Ukraine’s control.
Lyukov speculates that the restrictions on Starlink may be linked to political pressure from the U.S. presidential administration on Ukraine regarding the demand not to strike Russian oil refineries. At the same time, he emphasized that Starshield’s operations do not affect such strikes, since these facilities are located on Russian territory, where Starlink has been and remains unavailable to the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
He also does not rule out the possibility that a software glitch was the cause. According to him, as of the evening of October 14, Starlink terminals with Starshield accounts had begun to resume normal operations.
As the 1st Unmanned Systems Battalion High-Altitude Predators of the 59th Separate Unmanned Systems Assault Brigade named after Yakov Handzyuk told Militarnyi, the situation caused by the Starlink restrictions is complex but under control.
“We all knew that sooner or later this day would come. There are systems that don’t require Starlink,” the military personnel noted.
According to the military, the unit is switching to radio communications and drones capable of flying in autonomous mode. The restrictions on Starlink did not affect the operation of reconnaissance UAVs, UGVs, and bomber drones, but they did complicate the use of strike drones.
“A Starlink-equipped strike drone: at 80 kilometers [per hour]—that’s it, the connection drops out. There’s nothing you can do about it. Plus, there’s the problem that during a catapult launch and so on, there’s immediate high acceleration. And, basically, the drone is uncontrollable—it’s carried along, and [it] crashes,” a unit representative explained.
At the same time, reconnaissance drones can continue operating with Starlink at speeds of up to 80 km/h. After launch and reaching a circular trajectory, they establish satellite communication and carry out their missions.
According to other reports, the operation of high-speed interceptor drones and even certain models of bomber drones has also been affected.
According to military officials interviewed by Militarnyi, the reduction in strike drone activity will allow the enemy to step up its logistics. The situation is further complicated by bad weather and thick autumn fog.
At the same time, there are solutions that could operate using alternative communication systems. In particular, the military has submitted requests to procure strike drones that use radio communication and an automatic guidance system.
“Solutions, in principle, exist. The main thing is for the command to respond now and procure the equipment we need to somehow bridge the entire gap. Let’s hope that this [Starlink] will eventually be restored,” the military emphasized.
In response to a request from Militarnyi, Deviro noted that the company was one of the few that, even in the early stages of Starlink’s mass deployment, emphasized the temporary nature of this window of opportunity.
“Of course, we ensured that Starlink could be used in our products, but developing our own communication solutions—particularly Mesh technology—remained one of our priorities,” Deviro explained.
The company believes that technological independence and the ability to adapt to changes on the battlefield are more valuable than reliance on a single solution, even a highly effective one.
Deviro attributes the popularity of Starlink for middle-strike systems primarily to its ease of use and speed of integration. By the time the technology was actively being implemented, the terminals had already become widely adopted within the military, and personnel had practical experience working with them.
Cost was also a key factor: under certain conditions, Starlink provided a high-quality communication channel at a relatively low price compared to certain specialized radio systems. Furthermore, satellite communications long reduced dependence on the limitations of traditional radio channels in the face of electronic warfare (EW) operations. The combination of these advantages made Starlink attractive for both reconnaissance and strike drone systems.
According to Deviro’s assessment, there is currently virtually no direct alternative to Starlink that would provide a similar combination of accessibility, cost, ease of use, and infrastructure. At the same time, other technological solutions do exist: large-scale work is underway to test, refine, and integrate both new and existing communication technologies.
The company explains that due to the dynamic nature of modern warfare, a technological advantage today does not guarantee it will be maintained tomorrow. Component manufacturers, unmanned system developers, the military, and the country’s military-political leadership are becoming increasingly aware of this.
Deviro specifically emphasized the need to avoid dependence on a single technology, regardless of its current effectiveness. To achieve this, manufacturers must constantly collaborate with the military, seek new solutions, test them in practice, and adapt their approaches as quickly as the war demands.
Andriy Rymaruk, Deputy Director of Ukrspecsystems, noted in a comment to Militarnyi that the company has focused, continues to focus, and will continue to focus primarily on the development and production of systems with radio modems. According to him, these systems operate independently of external technical, diplomatic, or political factors.
Rymaruk explained that by using radio communication as the system’s primary channel, the company’s systems continue to conduct reconnaissance and strike targets at depths exceeding 200 km. In particular, he described the recent destruction of an “expensive and rare radar system” at a depth of 226 km by a unit of the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade.
⚡️Уразили РЛС «Небо-У» у ростовській області
Рота дальнього ураження 429 бригади «АХІЛЛЕС» уразила РЛС «Небо-У» на аеродромі «Міллерово» у ростовській області. Орієнтовна вартість «Небо-У» – $100 млн.
Встановлюємо вогневий контроль над військовим аеродромом «Міллерово» у… pic.twitter.com/qQEQq4MsWA
— 429 окрема бригада БпС «АХІЛЛЕС» (@achilles_429) August 27, 2026
In addition, the use of radio communications allows Ukrspecsystems’ drones to operate over Russian territory, where Starlink does not function, as well as to strike and disable ballistic missile launchers.
Andriy Shevchenko, Managing Director of Helsing in Ukraine, told Militarnyi that the restrictions on Starlink have demonstrated the critical importance of autonomy for modern defense systems. According to him, military technologies must remain effective regardless of decisions made by external suppliers.
It is precisely based on this principle that Helsing developed the HX-2. As Shevchenko explained, the drone does not depend on Starlink and uses radio communication that operates effectively under enemy electronic warfare (EW) conditions. It also features visual navigation without GNSS and automatic target acquisition. At Helsing, autonomy is viewed as the foundation of the product’s operation, enabling the military to continue carrying out missions even when conventional communication and navigation systems are unavailable.

articles.title: Poland provided secret military aid to Ukraine, Zelenskyy hints amid air defense shortages
articles.body:
Ukraine has received undisclosed assistance from Poland as it struggles to defend against increasingly intense Russian drone and missile attacks, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hinted during a meeting with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Brussels on 15 October, Radio Svoboda reported.
Ukraine’s air defense needs are greater than at any point since 2022, as intensified Russian drone and missile attacks strain existing systems and expose shortages of interceptor missiles. With US support increasingly uncertain amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington, European military aid is becoming more critical to Ukraine’s ability to defend its cities and infrastructure.
Zelenskyy thanked Warsaw for its support, suggesting that some assistance had to remain confidential. He also specifically mentioned 20 mm ammunition, which Ukraine needs to defend its cities against Russian attacks.
“Sometimes this has to stay between the two of us,” Zelenskyy said, thanking Tusk for the aid.
European support increasingly important amid US rift
Ukraine is facing mounting pressure on its air defenses as Russia increases the scale of its aerial attacks. Ukrainian forces are also struggling with shortages of interceptor missiles, particularly Patriot missiles needed to counter Russian ballistic strikes, leaving the country vulnerable to further attacks.
The need for additional support comes amid growing uncertainty over US assistance under President Donald Trump. Washington has taken steps that have strained ties with Kyiv, including easing some restrictions on Russian fuel and pressing for an energy ceasefire that Ukraine says Russia has continued to violate.
Recent disruptions to US-linked intelligence and satellite support have also raised concerns about Ukraine's ability to detect and counter Russian attacks.
As uncertainty over Washington's role grows, European military assistance is becoming increasingly important for Ukraine's defense.
White House ordered limits on Ukraine’s military satellite service — Reuters. Who made the decision remains unclear
Defense cooperation continues despite political tensions
Tusk reaffirmed Poland's commitment to supporting Ukraine, saying Kyiv could count on Poland and the European Union. He also opposed easing EU sanctions against Russia, arguing that Europe should not take steps that help Moscow finance its war.
The meeting also came amid strained relations between Kyiv and Warsaw over historical disputes. However, Poland's government has maintained that these disagreements should not undermine military support for Ukraine, whose ability to resist Russian aggression is closely tied to Poland's own security.
