articles.title: Zelenskyy says Starlink speed restrictions hamper Ukraine’s military, humanitarian operations
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that the Starlink system had not been completely switched off in Ukraine, but speed restrictions affected the country's ability to use it for certain military and humanitarian purposes.
Speaking at a briefing on the sidelines of the EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelesnkyy said the Defense Ministry remained in contact with partners and that he received indications from the White House that services would be fully restored.
He claimed Ukraine was not using Starlink to conduct deep-strikes against targets inside Russia, but relied on the system to operate interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
He said the restrictions also affected Ukraine's ability to carry out medium-range strikes against military targets.
Starlink-enabled drones, he said, were used to deliver food and water to Ukrainian personnel in positions exposed to enemy drone attacks.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine receives information from the US specifically about Russian ballistic missile launches, while dozens of countries also share intelligence with Kyiv.
He said Ukraine receives PAC-2 and PAC-3 air defense missiles from the US through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, with European countries financing the deliveries.
“So it's no gift. It's not for free,” he said, acknowledging that Ukraine is not currently a priority destination for the missiles, as many are being sent to the Middle East.
The Ukrainian leader criticized the recent US-Russia diesel deal and the prospect of lifting sanctions, saying Kyiv had not been informed in advance.
Ukraine, he said, proposed an energy ceasefire and offered the US to provide Kyiv with anti-ballistic missiles to protect energy infrastructure for the duration of the arrangement. “Don't give too many. Give us for the period you'll need for the duration of the diesel deal. I have not received that,” he said.
Responding to Donald Trump’s remark that he was more difficult to deal with than Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy said negotiating with the US president was easier than dealing with the Russian leader.
He said ending the war remained his priority but accused Putin of showing no genuine desire for negotiations. He warned that concessions on sanctions could eventually lead to broader agreements with Moscow, including in the energy, chemical industry and banking sectors.
“In my view, we cannot perceive diesel deals, these arrangements. We cannot accept them because then there will be gas agreements. I'm sure of that,” he said.
Zelenskyy also rejected the notion that the war was solely about control of the Donbas region, saying Ukraine’s national existence was at stake. “The issue is not withdrawing from Donbas. It's the issue of our country's existence,” he said, arguing that Moscow’s objectives of the war extend beyond eastern Ukraine.
He said European countries understood the risks posed by Russia, and urged partners to continue supporting Kyiv.

articles.title: From the sell-off of the Soviet defense industry to domestic ballistic missiles: what Ukraine lost and is restoring
articles.body:
From the sell-off of the Soviet defense industry to domestic ballistic missiles: what Ukraine lost and is restoring
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has a powerful missile legacy; however, after the collapse of the USSR, a significant portion of the industry's production capabilities and technological potential was lost. Modern developments are paving the way for the restoration of Ukraine's own ballistic missile capabilities.
For decades, Ukraine lost defense enterprises, technologies, and engineers, even though after the collapse of the Soviet Union it inherited a powerful missile industry. Now, amid a full-scale war, the country is trying to restore these capabilities. UNN, together with experts, examined why Ukraine lost part of its industrial potential and how difficult it is now to rebuild its own missile school.
Two years to develop a ballistic missile
After decades of decline in Ukraine’s defense industry, the country developed its own FP-7 ballistic missile in a short period of time. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced its first combat use on October 1, 2026.
According to its CEO, Iryna Terekh, Fire Point created the missile in just two years.
When it comes to the development timeline for what one might call a conventional ballistic missile, it generally takes around 15 years on average, although it can range from 7 to 30. Before the FP-7, the shortest recorded development time for a ballistic missile was 7 years, whereas we reduced it to two
She said that the team worked intensively, sought to optimize the development process, and move to testing as quickly as possible. Some solutions had to be invented anew.
The CEO of Fire Point also noted that the company financed the development with its own funds.
The development of the FP-7 in two years shows that Ukrainian companies are capable of rapidly creating complex missile technologies even amid a full-scale war. It is now important to build on this result: establish serial production and continue developing the technologies.
But why does Ukraine have to restore its missile industry amid a war at all, if it once had a powerful industrial base and participated in the creation of strategic missile systems?
What Ukraine inherited after the collapse of the USSR
After the collapse of the USSR, Ukraine inherited part of the Soviet defense industry. The country had design schools, production facilities, engineers, and experience working on complex technological projects.
At the same time, military experts note that the inherited industry was not fully autonomous. According to defense industry expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi, Ukraine received "fragments of broken production chains without a closed cycle and a specific pool of customers"—mostly authoritarian countries in the Third World, while no one even attempted to integrate into the U.S. or European markets.
After gaining independence, Ukraine needed to restructure this system to meet its own needs, determine priorities for developing the army, and create conditions for modernizing enterprises. However, for decades the defense industry did not receive sufficiently consistent support, while a significant part of state policy focused on using resources that were already available.
Military expert Ivan Stupak believes that Soviet stockpiles largely created a false sense of adequacy.
Until 2013, there was a department for surplus property, which was simply sold off. I knew people who worked at "Ukrspetsexport," and they told me: "We sold a tank to Pakistan, sold a plane somewhere else—everything is fine, we are making money." And these huge stockpiles created the illusion that we did not need to do anything
According to him, the country had technical developments that it could have used to advance its own missile programs, but it failed to do so in time.
How selling off assets turned into the loss of technologies
The problem was not only that Ukraine failed to create enough new weapons. The production capabilities themselves gradually weakened: enterprises lost orders, equipment became outdated, cooperative ties collapsed, and skilled workers left the industry.
Defense industry expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi attributes this to the lack of a long-term defense strategy and the state’s inability to restructure the inherited industry for new conditions.
In his assessment, some enterprises found themselves in a situation where they had to maintain production without stable orders or clear development prospects. This led to bankruptcies, the loss of equipment, and a reduction in technological capabilities.
The main problem of those twenty years was the absolute absence of a state defense doctrine. Instead of modernization and a transition to domestic production cycles, the country lived in an infantile illusion of security under the umbrella of the Budapest Memorandum, selling off Soviet arsenals for pennies and sincerely believing that it would never again need an army or defense industry
One of the most difficult consequences was the loss of specialists. Engineering expertise is developed through years of practical work, and without stable production, young specialists have no opportunity to gain experience and learn from their senior colleagues.
Money can buy any five-axis machine tool or build a clean hangar, but it is impossible to instantly restore the culture of chemistry, materials science, and solid-state physics. Over these two decades, we completely destroyed specialty chemicals and propellant production: the Shostka giants ("Zirka" and "Svema") deteriorated to such an extent that the country lost the complete production cycle for creating nitrocellulose, artillery propellants, and solid rocket fuel—something that cannot be restored without decades of chemical schools. We completely buried our own military microelectronics and microwave technology (ultra-high frequencies): plants such as Lviv's "Polaron," Kyiv's "Saturn," and Zaporizhzhia's "Gamma" no longer grew crystals or produced componentry for radars and active radar homing heads, which left us dependent on imports even for basic sensors. This was compounded by the degradation of specialty metallurgy: the loss of technologies for precision casting of monolithic blades for aircraft and gas-turbine engines, as well as special armor-grade and heat-resistant titanium alloys
According to him, another consequence was the loss of schools of large-scale engineering design.
Mykolaiv's heavy shipbuilding disappeared forever: along with the bankruptcy of the Black Sea Shipyard and the Shipyard named after the 61st Communist, the school of calculating and welding ocean-class hulls, aligning shaft lines, and coordinating thousands of suppliers for cruisers and aircraft carriers also died. Aircraft manufacturing at Kharkiv's KhAZ and Kyiv's "Aviant" lost the culture of serial assembly: one may have the brilliant Antonov design bureau, but if a plant produces one aircraft in ten years, engineers forget how to organize a serial takt-time assembly line
He emphasized that this concerns not only equipment and infrastructure, but also the experience passed from one generation of engineers to the next.
The main irreparable loss is "shop-floor memory." If the chief metallurgist or optical-mechanical alignment technologist at the Arsenal plant retires without passing the nuances on to an apprentice, the technology dies forever. And it is impossible to train a chief designer of a missile system or a developer of a thermal-imaging array with money—you need 15–20 years of continuous practical work on actual serial products for that
How to develop Ukrainian missile manufacturing
Restoring lost production capabilities is very difficult. Experts note that this requires not only engineering solutions, but also stable funding, long-term state orders, specialist training, and a clear strategy for developing the defense industry.
Military expert Ivan Stupak emphasizes that the full-scale war has forced Ukraine to accelerate weapons development. However, speed must not replace a systematic approach: defense technologies require long-term investment, and the result cannot always be achieved within a single budget year.
The defense industry does not work in such a way that you provide money today and go to a store tomorrow to buy a missile. You can invest in 2026 and see the result only in 2032
In his opinion, Ukraine needs a mechanism to support promising military developments modeled on the American DARPA agency, which funds research and development in defense technologies.
We have a great many talented people who can create extraordinarily interesting things. The main thing is to provide them with funding and ensure its stability
At the same time, Anatoliy Khrapchynskyi believes that restoring Ukraine's defense industry depends not only on financing individual enterprises but also on changing state policy. In his opinion, Ukraine needs to move from situational decisions to a long-term strategy that would provide for the development of private defense companies, the localization of critical components, and cooperation with European and American manufacturers.
True independence is not only a final break with moscow, but also a rejection of the role of an eternal supplicant with an outstretched hand before Western partners. We need our own agency: an aggressive focus on private defense tech, a rigorous review of the ineffective state sector, rapid localization of critical components, and parity-based integration into European and American production chains as an equal partner hardened by a major war
Fire Point could become one example of such development. Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation, suggests that the company could become the foundation for further development of Ukraine's missile program and the creation of an entire family of ballistic missiles. He noted that the company is gradually expanding its areas of work—from drones and cruise missiles to ballistic weapons.
International cooperation could play a special role. Anton Zemlyanyi notes that Fire Point's plans to establish joint ventures with European manufacturers could help scale up production, attract partners, and reduce the risks of Russian strikes on production facilities. In the future, this could also open up new opportunities for integrating Ukrainian developments into European defense programs.
However, in the analyst's opinion, Ukraine should not build its missile program around a single manufacturer alone.
I would also not rule out other manufacturers, including state-owned ones. It is in Ukraine's interests to have several capable producers of missile weapons rather than depend exclusively on a single private company. This would create a broader production base, strengthen competition, and reduce risks for the missile program as a whole
Ivan Stupak emphasizes that the main lesson of previous decades is the need to invest continuously in one's own defense industry rather than remember it only when the country finds itself facing a large-scale military threat.
If you do not finance your own army, you will then have to stand for a year asking other countries for help. And there may not be another opportunity to do so

articles.title: Ukraine has run out of missiles for Patriot air defence systems – WP
articles.body:
Ukraine has run out of missiles for Patriot air defence systems – WP
Ukraine has completely exhausted its stock of interceptor missiles for the US-made Patriot air defence systems.
Source: The Washington Post, citing two Ukrainian officials and a NATO representative
Details: According to one source, Ukraine had only 10 Patriot missiles left as of 7 October.
"These were used up during the attacks. Currently, there are only a couple remaining," a Ukrainian official said.
Quote: "A second person familiar with Ukraine's deteriorating air defence situation said the country is out of the sophisticated weapons, which are critical to shooting down incoming Russian ballistic missiles."
Details: A Ukrainian official stressed that "the situation is extremely tense".
CNN reported earlier that Ukraine had run out of Patriot missiles. According to its source, the shortage of ammunition was the reason Ukrainian air defences had been unable to intercept Russian ballistic targets during the latest large-scale attack.
Global missile stocks have been rapidly depleted by the war in the Middle East, launched by US President Donald Trump. In the first month of the war with Iran alone, the US used more than 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors.
Washington has made accelerating production a priority, but manufacturing a single missile can take up to 36 months.
Until now, missiles for Ukraine have been supplied through the PURL programme The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme allows NATO allies to finance purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine , under which European countries pay for US-made weapons.
A senior NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the programme remained operational and that "air defence munitions like Patriot interceptors continue to flow".
However, a Ukrainian official raised concerns about the nature of the deliveries.
"Since May, supplies have been irregular, and right now no one can say with any certainty or guarantee that a delivery will actually arrive," the official said.
Background:
- Throughout the summer and autumn of 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly urged Ukraine's partners to urgently increase supplies of missiles for Patriot air defence systems. In August, he stressed that Ukraine needed between 300 and 360 Patriot missiles to get through the winter safely. Meanwhile, Western deliveries had fallen sharply, from 675 missiles in 2023 to 364 in 2025, with only 264 planned for 2026.
- Meanwhile, according to reports in the media, the governments of Greece and Spain would rather keep Patriot missiles nearing the end of their service lives in storage than transfer them to Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges EU not to ease sanctions against Russia during leaders' meeting
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday urged the EU not to ease sanctions against Russia, stressing the need for a “strong” 22nd sanctions package from the 27-member union.
Speaking on the second day of an EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy accused his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin of seeking to “drag out” the Ukraine war into next year, saying Europe must be ready for this.
“I urge you not to ease sanctions against Russia or anyone linked to it. Putin uses every trick he can find to get money for making more weapons,” Zelenskyy said, noting Ukraine has warned that sanctions relief will result in others taking advantage.
The Ukrainian leader argued that the diesel deal between the US and Russia will never be enough to offset the impact of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz on global markets, but will rather “put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
He stressed the need for a strong 22nd EU sanctions package, particularly calling for sanctions against all involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles, advanced communications systems and drones.
Zelenskyy said the financial cost of the ongoing conflict for Ukraine will be €155 billion next year and it needs at least €70 billion more for spending, including in terms of defense purchases.
He stressed the need to deal with Russian frozen assets, as well as called on European leaders to use every opportunity to strengthen air defense, emphasizing the need for a winter package consisting of 300 Patriot interceptors against Russian ballistic missiles.
“We are grateful that the EU is moving toward us. Four EU accession clusters have already been opened this year. And we need to open the remaining two by the end of the year. We are ready,” Zelenskyy said, calling on the union to keep Ukraine and Moldova's membership processes tied together.
Defining unity in Europe as a target for Russia, Zelenskyy said that in spite of disagreements and their differences, all of them seek a security system in Europe that “really works and can deal with today’s threats.”
“So, as we work now to finally stop Putin, to stop his war, we are doing this not just for Ukraine alone. We are working for security guarantees for all of Europe. For guarantees that this war will not be passed down to our children,” he said.
He expressed gratitude to those supporting Ukraine and those trying to keep Europe and the US together. “Putin will listen to America if America really turns up the heat on him and makes one thing clear -- either he chooses peace, or he gets no more money for his war,” he said.
Zelenskyy arrived in Brussels on Thursday to attend the European Council summit and hold a number of talks on the sidelines of the event.
Zelenskyy met with the presidents of the European Council and European Commission, as well as held talks with the Hungarian, Finnish and Swedish prime ministers on Friday.
On Thursday, he met his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Belgian King Philippe, and the prime ministers of Belgium, Denmark, and Poland.

articles.title: Russia plans winter strikes to cut off electricity, heat, and water in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa to force Ukraine’s surrender, NYT reports
articles.body:
Russia plans winter strikes to cut off electricity, heat, and water in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa to force Ukraine’s surrender, NYT reports
Russia expects to force Ukraine to capitulate this coming winter by disabling its energy system, particularly by leaving Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa without electricity, heat, or water, The New York Times reported. The newspaper reviewed a Russian government plan that Ukraine intercepted and showed to its European allies in September.
According to the plan, Russia would need about 70 ballistic missiles, 720 long-range drones, and 150 guided aerial bombs to cut off water, electricity, and heat to Ukraine’s three largest cities. Russian military planners believe a month of strikes at that intensity would destroy Ukraine’s energy system.
With the war now in its fifth year, previous attacks have left Ukrainian power plants unable to operate at full capacity, and each new strike quickly knocks them offline, the newspaper reported. Before the war, for example, the three combined heat and power plants supplying Kyiv had a total generating capacity of about 1.3 gigawatts. That has now fallen to about 500 megawatts.
If Russia’s plan succeeds, Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa could lose 90% of their power generating capacity and see heat supplies cut by 90%, disrupting water and sewage systems, according to the newspaper.
Russia’s confidence that the plan can work stems largely from Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, particularly Patriot interceptor missiles, without which Ukrainian forces are virtually unable to defend against ballistic missiles.
Analysts agree that Moscow now has a better chance of succeeding in its air campaign than at any other point in the war. Ukraine’s missile defenses have been depleted by cuts in American aid, Russia’s missile and drone arsenal has grown more powerful and effective, and years of strikes have left Ukraine’s energy infrastructure far more vulnerable.
This makes Moscow extremely unlikely to agree to any version of the energy ceasefire Kyiv has repeatedly proposed. “The only card they have to pressure the Ukrainians are these air attacks. They don’t have anything else,” Harry Nedelcu, a director at the consulting firm Rasmussen Global, told The New York Times.
But history shows that such bombing campaigns, which devastate economies and civilian life, usually fail to force an enemy to surrender, the newspaper reported. The United States failed to achieve its aims this way in Vietnam, during the Persian Gulf War in the early 1990s, and in the current war against Iran.
“Punishing the adversaries’ civilian population and trying to break its will has a very poor historical track record for coercing it to concede defeat,” Seth Jones, a military expert at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, told the newspaper.

articles.title: Zelensky imposes refinery deal demand – WSJ
articles.body:
Zelensky imposes refinery deal demand – WSJ
Vladimir Zelensky is open to stopping attacks on Russian oil refineries for 100 days in exchange for a 300 km extension of Starlink satellite internet service coverage for the Ukrainian military, the Wall Street Journal has said.
The report comes as US President Donald Trump has ramped pressure on Zelensky to end the strikes, which he blames for surging global energy prices. In his interview with Newsmax on Thursday, Trump called Ukraine’s actions “a disgrace.”
In an article published the same day, the WSJ said that Republican Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer brought the deal to the Ukrainian leader during their visit to Kiev last Friday. The outlet claimed that it was told by unnamed sources that Zelensky had agreed to the proposal.
The extended Starlink coverage should help Ukraine target missile launchers inside Russia, according to the report.
Kiev, which is experiencing an acute shortage of US-supplied Patriot air defense missiles, has been struggling to contain Russia’s large-scale missile and drone strikes against military-related infrastructure across Ukraine. Moscow says the raids are being carried out in response to Ukrainian terrorist attacks on civilian targets in Russia, including energy facilities.
The Ukrainians, who have relied heavily on Starlink during the conflict with Russia for battlefield communications and controlling drones, have been “terrified” by the slowdown of satellite internet provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company this week, the WSJ said.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders complained that Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working when UAVs flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. According to Reuters, the order to slow down the service came directly from the White House. Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink’s speed has increased over the last couple of days, but the restrictions haven’t been fully lifted yet.
Earlier this week, Zelensky confirmed reports that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev if it kept ignoring Trump’s demands to cease energy strikes inside Russia. Officials in Kiev also complained about receiving no advance warning from the Americans before Russian missile strikes.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Russia was unaware of the Starlink slowdown for the Ukrainians, noting that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.”
Last month, Peskov warned that allowing Starlink to be used to facilitate strikes deep into Russian territory would be “a very harmful, potentially dangerous and misconceived step.”
The American authorities apparently don’t require consent from Musk to expand the coverage of Starlink’s military component, known as Starshield, for Ukraine. The SpaceX CEO said earlier this week that its systems “are owned and controlled” by the US government, with the Pentagon and the US president deciding on the limits on their speed or usage.
On Sunday, Musk backed Trump’s suggestion that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” In a comment to a White House video with the US president’s criticism of the Ukrainian leader, the entrepreneur said that “Zelensky has gone too far.”
Zelensky reportedly wanted to personally discuss the expansion of Starlink coverage with Musk during his US visit to Washington in July, but the SpaceX CEO turned down the meeting.

articles.title: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed refinery strikes “a disgrace” after Russia’s 39-missile strike on its energy sites
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries a disgrace in an interview with Newsmax and questioned President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s will to settle the war on 15 October. His statements came after he made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel back into the US ahead of the mid-term elections in the US.
Kyiv says its long-range strikes have knocked out more than half of Russia's refining capacity, one of the few levers it controls on Moscow's war income, according to Ukraine's Defense Ministry. This is part of efforts to reduce the aggressor's capabilities to launch assaults, including the latest, during which four Russian regions fired 39 Iskander-M, North Korean KN-23, hypersonic Zircon, and supersonic anti-ship cruise Oniks missiles, Zelenskyy said.
Trump criticizes Zelenskyy over oil prices while remaining silent on Russian strikes
Earlier, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine stopped refinery strikes for three days to meet US wishes after Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October. At the same time, Russia struck a Kharkiv heat-and-power plant within hours of the announcement, he emphasized.
Meanwhile, in the interview with Newsmax, Trump said Zelenskyy is only pushing world oil prices higher.
“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” he said.
He added that Ukraine has other options: “There are a lot of targets that you can hit.”
At the same time, Trump didn't say a word about Russian strikes on Ukraine's civilian buildings and power infrastructure ahead of the winter.
Trump compares Zelenskyy to a circus showman
The US leader said he is “not a big fan” of Zelenskyy. He claimed both sides “would like to see it end,” but that he finds Zelenskyy “more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
US weighs relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, days after freeing Russian diesel
He also said that he believes the depletion of US ammunition stockpiles is linked to the aid provided to Ukraine under the Biden administration, rather than the war with Iran.
Ukraine has repeatedly offered to help the US counter Iranian drones during the operation. The New York Times reported that a Ukrainian team departed the day after the US made such a request.
Nevertheless, despite Kyiv’s offers and actions, Trump once again compared Zelenskyy to P. T. Barnum, the 19th-century American circus showman, saying that he received a tremendous number of Patriots and Tomahawks.
However, there is no public confirmation that Tomahawk missiles were transferred to Ukraine during the Biden administration.

articles.title: Trump calls Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries a 'disgrace'
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has sharply criticised Ukraine for resuming attacks on Russian oil refineries, calling the strikes a "disgrace", as reports emerged that the White House had ordered restrictions on a satellite communications system essential to Ukrainian military operations.
According to a Reuters report, citing two US officials and a Western official familiar with the matter, the instruction to limit Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield service originated inside the White House.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The order was communicated to senior Pentagon officials, although the sources did not identify who authorised it.
Starshield, a military-grade satellite network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX, supports Ukrainian battlefield communications and drone operations. Ukrainian officials reported this week that satellite receivers installed on fast-moving equipment had stopped functioning, disrupting drone strikes against Russian positions and operations to intercept incoming Russian drones.
A Ukrainian Defence Ministry source told Reuters on Thursday that the receivers had resumed working while moving, but only at speeds below 160 kilometres per hour.
A senior US official denied that Trump had personally requested the restrictions. The White House did not clarify whether another administration official had issued the order.
The disruption comes amid mounting tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
In an interview with Newsmax aired Thursday, Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of contributing to rising global fuel prices by targeting Russian refineries.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said, arguing that attacks on diesel production facilities threatened supplies needed by the United States and other countries.
Trump also renewed his criticism of Zelenskyy, saying he considered the Ukrainian leader more difficult to negotiate with than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine resumed refinery strikes on Thursday following a three-day pause intended to accommodate Trump's calls for an energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy ended the suspension after Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite a ceasefire announcement made unilaterally by the US president.
The breakdown followed Washington's controversial agreement with Moscow to ease sanctions in exchange for additional Russian diesel supplies. Under the arrangement, Russia is expected to release more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel onto US and international markets.
Zelenskyy has criticised the deal, warning that renewed energy revenues could help finance Russia's continuing invasion. Some US lawmakers have raised similar concerns.
According to sources cited by the The Financial Times, Washington had threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and weapons procurement arrangements unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries.
European leaders have meanwhile reaffirmed their support for Ukraine. Following talks with Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron said France remained committed to helping Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and protecting its civilian population and infrastructure.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also posted a message following discussions with European leaders in Brussels. Addressing Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian people in a post on X, Tusk declared: "YOU ARE NOT ALONE".
HT

articles.title: Belgium to transfer 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by year-end – PM De Wever
articles.body:
Belgium plans to transfer ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026, Prime Minister Bart De Wever announced after a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels, according to The Brussels Times, citing a statement from the prime minister.
"We will deliver 10 this year," De Wever said, explaining that delays in the delivery of F-35 fighter jets had affected the timeline for transferring the Belgian F-16s to Ukraine, but that the new aircraft are already beginning to arrive.
According to the prime minister, the fighter jets will help Ukraine defend itself against Russian drones. He emphasized that Ukraine urgently needs combat-ready aircraft and confirmed Belgium's readiness to make its contribution.
Belgium delayed the transfer of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine due to the postponement of the delivery of American F-35s, which are intended to replace the aging aircraft. During a meeting with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, Prime Minister De Wever also discussed the supply of Belgian-made ammunition for the F-16s and reaffirmed the need for continued financial support for Ukraine from the European Union.
"I made it clear that, as far as I am concerned, the European Union must continue to support Ukraine. I have a clear view of how this can be done. I have not yet discussed it, but I think it will come up tomorrow and I am prepared for that," he said.
As reported on Thursday, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy was granted an audience with King Philippe of Belgium, during which the president emphasized the importance of supporting Ukraine and its air defense system, as well as supplying Ukraine with F-16 fighter jets. Prior to this, Zelenskyy held a series of meetings with representatives from NATO, Poland, and France.

articles.title: Russia Builds Massive Jet Drone Launch Base Near Ukraine in Just Six Weeks
articles.body:
Russia has nearly completed a massive new launch base for jet-powered attack drones in its southwestern Rostov region in just six weeks, satellite imagery analyzed by Reuters shows, as Moscow ramps up attacks that are increasingly difficult for Ukraine to intercept.
The facility near Millerovo, roughly 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles) from a Russian air base, has grown from an empty field into a complex covering about 0.9 square kilometers (0.3 square miles) – roughly the size of 126 soccer pitches – between Aug. 31 and Oct. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Defense experts say the site is designed to launch Russia’s latest jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, which can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (373 miles per hour).
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, identified eight launch platforms along the facility’s western edge. Two already had launch rails installed, according to Reuters’ analysis of satellite imagery.
The base could be operational within weeks, if not sooner, Monnik said.
“The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” he said.
Russia ramps up faster drone attacks
The construction comes as Russia sharply increases its use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine, with Kyiv and the surrounding region among the hardest-hit areas.
Russian use of the faster drones increased roughly sixfold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data.
White House Ordered Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield, Disrupting Drone Defense – Reuters
Unlike slower, piston-powered drones, jet-powered models are harder to stop with relatively inexpensive interceptor drones that Ukraine has increasingly relied on to counter Russian attacks.
With the full-scale war in its fifth year, Ukraine expects Russia to intensify drone and missile strikes this winter, putting additional pressure on its air defenses.
The new facility could potentially launch 100 or more jet-powered drones in 24 hours, depending on available supplies and operational requirements, Monnik said. Russia typically launches its drones in smaller waves throughout the day.
New base could be harder for Ukraine to hit
The new site is located close to Millerovo air base, home to Russia’s 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
DroneSec assessed that the launch facility likely falls within the air-defense coverage of the military air base, potentially making it more difficult for Ukraine to strike.
The rapid expansion of Russia’s drone-launch infrastructure also poses a potential challenge for NATO countries, which face growing concerns over Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions.

articles.title: Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is ‘disgrace’, Trump says
articles.body:
EU leaders rally around Zelensky as Trump calls Ukrainian strikes on Russia a ‘disgrace’
- EU leaders backed Zelensky in Brussels as Trump called Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace” and warned of pressure on energy prices.
- Ukraine faces heavy Russian attacks, winter power cuts and uncertainty over US support, while Europe says it must fill gaps in air defence, funding and intelligence.
- Europe lacks a quick Starlink replacement, and leaders are split over new money for Ukraine, which still faces a large 2027 budget gap.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – European Union leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelensky at a summit on Oct 16 as US President Donald Trump fired another salvo at Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”.
The EU is hosting Zelensky in Brussels at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
Trump blindsided Zelensky last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
Facing US midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
The US has also struck a diesel deal with Russia, angering Ukraine and European allies.
“We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don’t see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That’s why we have to prepare for the winter,” Zelensky said as he arrived at the summit, hugging many of the leaders as he met them.
“The winter package is not only energy, it’s also air defence and funding.”
In the latest attacks, Russian drone strikes on the city of Kharkiv killed three people, while strikes elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.
In an interview, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for 2027.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.
“We have a lot of gaps to fill, and this is a European mission to fill the gaps that Ukraine needs.
“Because always, at the start (and) at the end of every conversation, people need to be reminded that we are sitting in a warm room, lights are on, heating is on, the coffee is warm, and we cannot get tired of the war in Ukraine, because they are fighting... for us.”
No ready-made European alternative to Starlink
Ukraine’s leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used by Kyiv for battlefield communications and drone operations.
A source in Ukraine’s defence ministry said on Oct 15 that Starshield receptors were only working at speeds of up to 160kmh, complicating their use for military missions.
A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.
Europe does not have a ready-made alternative to Starlink, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can’t replace this capability,” said the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
“We are working on the new sanctions package to put the pressure on Russia, and we of course hope that we do this with all our partners around the world.”
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.
While EU leaders hit out at the US deal to buy Russian diesel, they are also grappling with how to tackle energy prices that have soared since the Iran war, exposing divisions between member states on day one of the summit on Oct 15.
Zelensky told Reuters earlier in October that Ukraine had agreed a plan with European partners that would allow it to close a US$27 billion (S$34.5 billion) deficit in its military spending for 2026, allowing it to order the drones needed to continue fighting at the start of 2027.
However, Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said recently Ukraine still faced an unfunded budget gap for 2027 of US$32.6 billion – and that does not include an estimated US$40 billion in direct military supplies from allies.
“I am unhappy with the number of countries that have been willing to pledge new financial support to Ukraine,” said Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten.
Sounding a more sceptical note, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker urged caution in the debate over making new, far-reaching financial commitments to Ukraine.
“There are so many figures being bandied about that we now need to put them into context, explain them and make it clear where this shortfall is coming from. I’m surprised too,” he said. REUTERS

articles.title: Zelenskyy confirms Starlink speed restrictions hindered interception of jet-powered Shaheds
articles.body:
Zelenskyy confirms Starlink speed restrictions hindered interception of jet-powered Shaheds
Ukraine was unable to intercept jet-powered Shahed drones to protect civilians because Starlink connection speeds had been reduced.
Source: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking after meetings on the sidelines of the EU leaders' summit on 15-16 October, as reported by European Pravda's correspondent in Brussels
Details: Zelenskyy added that the reduction in Starlink speeds had also prevented Ukraine from striking military targets in occupied territories and delivering water and food to Ukrainian troops.
He also stressed that the Armed Forces of Ukraine do not use Starlink to conduct long-range strikes on Russian territory.
"We use [Starlink] to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that strike our civilians and kill our families. We use specialised interceptors that move at high speeds. Interceptor drones that operate specifically with Starlink," Zelenskyy said.
He pointed out that Starlink had not been switched off, but its connection speed had been reduced.
Quote: "When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept some of the jet-powered Shaheds… In other words, we were unable to use a tool to protect civilians. This is very painful and unpleasant."
Details: The president explained that jet-powered Shaheds fly at speeds of more than 400 km/h, while the Starlink restrictions had reduced the equipment speed available to Ukrainian troops intercepting Russian drones to 70 km/h.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine uses Starlink for mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in temporarily occupied territories, but the reduction in connection speeds had prevented it from carrying out those operations as well.
In addition, Starlink is needed to deliver water and food to Ukrainian troops who spend weeks or months on the front line in areas under the Russians' full drone surveillance.
Zelenskyy noted that the Defence Ministry is in daily contact with the United States and had recently received information that the connection speed had been resumed.
"If that is the case, we are very grateful," the president added.
"We approached SpaceX and the White House to ask them to enable this capability," Zelenskyy said, noting that Ukraine has not received a positive response to its request.
Background:
- Reuters previously reported that the order to restrict the use of the Starshield satellite system, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone control, had come from the White House.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation and report back to Congress on the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- Axios previously reported that Trump's administration supposedly had nothing to do with the incident. Washington attempted to shift responsibility to SpaceX, saying the White House does not control the company's actions.
- Zelenskyy publicly described the communications restrictions as a mistake that would lead to casualties and destruction.

articles.title: Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
articles.body:
Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
TEHRAN – In the new international order, the concept of “power” is no longer defined solely by the number of nuclear warheads, overseas military bases, or classical security alliances; rather, the new geometry of global power is shaped by the capacity of supply chains, currency exchanges, infrastructure investments, and economic interdependence.
Within this novel framework, China has managed to elevate its position from a mere trading power in the late twentieth century to a “structural actor in international crisis management”—an actor whose primary tools for intervening in crises are not missiles and sanctions, but economic integration and financial leverage.
The defining distinction of China’s approach to international crises is rooted in the theory of “developmental peace” as opposed to Western “liberal peace.” Beijing believes that the primary root of many geopolitical conflicts and security instabilities in the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia lies not in a vacuum of Western democracy, but in poverty, a deficit of infrastructural development, and a lack of connection to global markets. Therefore, Beijing utilizes initiatives such as the Belt and Road and strategic energy partnerships as efficient tools to contain security shocks. When countries share tangible, mutual economic interests in the continuity of joint projects, the cost of escalating tensions and war increases dramatically for them.
A concrete and successful example of this strategy can be seen in Beijing’s historic mediation between Tehran and Riyadh. Leveraging its immense weight as the largest buyer of Persian Gulf energy and the primary trading partner of both countries, China provided an economic-strategic platform for a political agreement without the need for ideological alignments. This model demonstrated that Beijing’s crisis management levers are built on a commitment to mutual interests and non-interference in internal affairs—a factor that has made Beijing’s model attractive and acceptable among the countries of the Global South.
Furthermore, in complex crises such as the war in Ukraine or tensions surrounding maritime security, China has managed—by relying on its position as a core commodity buyer—to prevent devastating fractures in the global energy and food markets. China’s policy is to maintain a balance between trade with Russia while simultaneously safeguarding Western markets; a strategy that prevents the deepening of acute international deadlocks and the uncontrolled spread of crises into the global economy.
Ultimately, Beijing has demonstrated that economic power is not merely a source of wealth, but a decisive lever for containing shocks and moderating geopolitical behavior. Although China’s cautious policy and avoidance of direct security guarantees may appear to limit its role in certain acute crises, an undeniable reality remains: in the current post-hegemonic world, no major international crisis can be managed, sustainably resolved, or contained without considering Beijing’s capacities, considerations, and economic levers.
Mahdi Zolfaghari is an Associate Professor at the Department of Asian Studies in Allameh Tabataba’i University

articles.title: ‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
articles.body:
‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
TEHRAN — The possible use of America’s largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran may offer President Donald Trump a dramatic display of military power, but it is unlikely to resolve the strategic predicament facing Washington, analysts have warned, arguing that a spectacular explosion cannot substitute for a viable path out of a protracted war.
CNN reported on October 14 that the US military had developed strike plans that could include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if Trump orders a resumption of combat operations. The report cited multiple US officials familiar with the planning.
The prospect of deploying the weapon has raised questions about whether Washington is seeking a decisive military outcome or a dramatic action that could allow the president to declare victory without achieving his stated strategic objectives.
 
Even within US military planning circles, doubts have emerged over the weapon’s effectiveness in changing the course of the war, CNN reported. Reuters subsequently reported the story, noting that it had not independently verified CNN’s account.
A dramatic explosion, but what strategic result?
Dani Citrinowicz, a former Israeli military intelligence official, told the BBC that even using the “mother of all bombs” would not force Iran to surrender.
“Even the use of the [mother of all bombs] will not force Iran to surrender; although such an attack could have psychological effects and give Trump an opportunity to claim an imaginary victory,” he said, according to the quotation provided in the BBC-attributed report.
The assessment points to a fundamental distinction between the destructive power of a weapon and its ability to achieve political objectives. A strike can cause extensive damage without compelling an adversary to accept the attacker’s demands or bringing a conflict to a favourable conclusion.
Sina Azodi, director of the Middle East Studies Program at George Washington University, similarly questioned the strategic logic behind the reported option.
“Trump has a strange fascination with the symbolic use of American military power and wants to advertise it on his personal social media account through a grand spectacle and a massive explosion,” Azodi said, according to the quotation provided.
He also highlighted the weapon’s limitations against deeply buried targets, noting that it detonates in the air and has limited capacity to penetrate far underground.
The distinction matters because the MOAB was designed primarily to produce devastating blast effects over a broad surface area. It is not the same as a specialised penetrator designed to attack deeply buried, hardened facilities.
In an October 15 Al Jazeera explainer, military analyst Elijah Magnier said that using the MOAB would not guarantee the destruction of Iran’s deeply buried nuclear installations and could amount to little more than “political theatre.”
A weapon cannot resolve a strategic deadlock
The reported plans have emerged as the Trump administration faces pressure to demonstrate progress in a war that has failed to produce a clear political resolution.
In a CNN broadcast on October 15, senior national security reporter Zachary Cohen said Trump and his advisers had spent months discussing options that could be presented to the American public as a “definitive end” to the war.
Cohen said the military had been tasked with developing fresh strike options amid the absence of a diplomatic resolution and growing unpopularity of the conflict.
He also reported that the administration’s stated strategic goals remained unfulfilled.
That assessment raises a central question: what would a MOAB strike actually accomplish that previous attacks and existing military pressure have not?
The bomb’s destructive capacity is not in dispute. The uncertainty concerns whether its use would change Iran’s calculations, compel Tehran to capitulate or create conditions for a durable settlement.
A dramatic strike might generate powerful images and headlines. But if it does not achieve its declared objectives, it could instead expose the gap between the administration’s military capabilities and its ability to translate them into a political outcome.
The limits of spectacle
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Its deployment would represent a major escalation, but its size alone does not make it an appropriate weapon for every target.
CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Colonel Cedric Leighton explained in a broadcast on October 15 that the MOAB is designed to inflict damage over a large surface area, whereas Iran’s hardened and deeply buried nuclear facilities present a different targeting challenge.
He contrasted the MOAB with the Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a different weapon specifically designed to attack hardened underground targets.
Leighton also questioned the suitability of the aircraft required to deliver the MOAB for the Iranian operational environment.
The technical limitations reinforce the broader strategic problem. A weapon capable of producing an enormous explosion is not necessarily capable of destroying every intended target, still less of compelling a country to surrender.
A face-saving exit is not the same as victory
The most consequential possibility raised by the reporting is that the proposed strike could be intended partly to shape the political narrative of the war.
CNN’s reporting suggested that the administration was examining military options that could enable Trump to present the conflict as decisively concluded. Such a scenario would make the distinction between a battlefield achievement and a politically useful declaration of victory particularly important.
Citrinowicz’s assessment, as quoted by the BBC, captures that concern: the attack might provide an opportunity to claim victory without necessarily producing the underlying result.
This is the danger of treating military spectacle as a substitute for strategy. An attack can be visually overwhelming and still leave the fundamental dispute unresolved.
For Washington, the question is not simply whether the United States can deploy a powerful bomb. It is whether doing so would bring the war closer to an outcome that can be sustained politically and strategically.
 
The quagmire remains
The possibility of using the MOAB does not, by itself, demonstrate that Trump has authorised such an attack. The reports describe contingency planning, not a confirmed decision to deploy the weapon.
Reuters said it could not independently verify CNN’s initial report. CBS News separately reported on October 15 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans for possible use of the weapon if ordered by the president.
If the bomb fails to achieve its intended military objectives, the administration could find itself confronting the same fundamental problem after an even more dramatic attack. If it is used primarily to create the appearance of a decisive outcome, the gap between the declaration of victory and the realities on the ground could become harder to conceal.
The “mother of all bombs” may offer Trump a spectacle of overwhelming force. But an explosion, however large, cannot by itself deliver a political settlement, compel an adversary’s surrender or guarantee a way out of war.
The real test is not the size of the blast. It is whether the strategy behind it can produce an outcome that military power alone has so far failed to secure.

articles.title: Of course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayal | Jonathan Freedland
articles.body:
Donald Trump must find it oddly frustrating. He keeps showing the world exactly who he is, and yet the world keeps refusing to believe it. As clearly as he can, he is announcing that he is not the leader of the free world, that he is not even a reliable member of the democratic west, that he is in fact an ally of its enemies – but the west, including Britain, either doesn’t fully get the message or can’t quite bring itself to draw the obvious conclusion.
Trump had another go this week, finding multiple ways to declare that in the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is no mediator or peace broker but a partner of Vladimir Putin. In fairness to him, the US president had loudly issued that declaration within weeks of his return to the White House when, in February 2025, he delivered an on-camera dressing down of Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, seeking to humiliate the Ukrainian leader by telling him “you don’t have the cards”, even as JD Vance demanded their visitor show gratitude. That should have made Trump’s position sufficiently plain, but in the past few days he has all but put it up in lights.
Earlier this week Ukrainian forces found that an essential piece of kit – a version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system used by Kyiv to guide its drones – was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph. That meant not only a sudden shrinking of Ukraine’s ability to strike behind the frontlines, but also the hobbling of an air defence system vital in protecting the capital from Russian jet-propelled drones. This was no technical hitch. Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is owned and controlled by the US government – and, as Reuters reported, the order to limit its use in Ukraine came from the White House. Put simply, Trump actively intervened in the war to weaken Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. “The decision will bring a lot of human losses,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan. “Of course, people will die.”
Trump’s move was hardly a bolt from the blue. This same week, Ukraine endured at least two nights of Russian bombardment without the usual advance warnings from the US of when or where Moscow was about to strike. Trump denied that he had broken off long-established intelligence sharing with Kyiv, but that’s exactly what it looked like.
All this followed the US president’s decision to break the international sanctions regime on Moscow, by agreeing to buy $4bn worth of Russian diesel oil. That volume will barely make a splash in the US market, where high diesel prices are imperilling the Republicans’ midterm chances in several rural states that rely on the stuff, but it will come as a welcome cash infusion for Putin’s war machine. Just as Russia’s military position was looking precarious, Donald Trump has come riding to the rescue. Throw in the US invitation to Putin to attend December’s G20 meeting at one of Trump’s golf clubs in Florida, and you have a US president who might as well be skywriting his support for Russia and his betrayal of Ukraine.
In Trump’s first term, much energy was spent trying to work out what dark secret lay behind this apparent affinity with Moscow. I tend to the view advanced by my expert colleague Luke Harding, who, when asked if Trump is a tool of the Russian intelligence services, answers with a question of his own: if Trump were a Russian asset, in what way would he behave any differently from the way he behaves now?
Whatever the motive, or whether, as Harding suggests, it’s some combination of greed, ideology, dictator envy and kompromat, the facts are unarguable. The most powerful member of the western alliance is, at best, an unreliable partner and, at worst, in league with the alliance’s chief enemy. Why this matters should not need spelling out, least of all in the week when the head of MI5 described Russia as “aggressor number one”. For years now, the Kremlin has demonstrated its willingness to attack Nato member states, usually in the form of hybrid or “grey zone” operations that are not overt acts of war but come instead with a patina of deniability. One study found that there have been than no fewer than “151 confirmed Russian-directed industrial sabotage incidents in Europe between February 2022 and February 2026”, while last weekend brought credible reports of a Russian intention to assassinate executives of key European defence firms.
What should the US’s erstwhile allies do about this new reality? The first task is to keep supporting Ukraine, all the more energetically given that Washington has, in effect, switched sides. The second is to avoid an error that is looming. The midterm elections, which are little more than a fortnight away, are expected to deliver big gains for the Democrats and a big blow to Trump. If Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress, plenty of European leaders will be tempted to exhale deeply, conclude that the orange storm has passed and that normal transatlantic service is about to resume. That would be a grave mistake.
For one thing, while the US president has been unbound by congressional restraint for most of the past two years, it’s not certain that a constrained Trump will be a tamed Trump. On the contrary, one Washington hand warns that he could become a “cornered animal”, even more extreme in the area where a president is freest to act, namely foreign affairs. Of course, Trump will be gone eventually, but there too lies the danger of false comfort. “This shift is permanent,” one former UK cabinet minister tells me. If nothing else, Trump has proved that Trump and Trumpism can happen: now we know that the western alliance is neither guaranteed nor unshakeable, but vulnerable to a change in the US political weather.
All of this means we are living in a newly dangerous world. Witness the richly reported new book War is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman, which lays bare quite how seriously leading policymakers rate the risk of a third world war. It’s an age in which we can no longer rely on others to defend us. The chilling lesson of the Starlink episode for those who depend on US hardware or software is that the US always retains an off switch. In other words, Britain and the rest of Europe have to be able to defend ourselves, with our own armies and our own arms.
The best time for governments to have made this case was the night of that shocking Oval Office scene with Zelenskyy last year. But the second-best time is now. When John Healey delivers his first budget on 28 October, this is the argument he needs to set out. As a former defence secretary, he is especially well placed to do it. The Labour manifesto of 2024 was written before Trump was re-elected, before anyone knew that in the great clash of our time the US was about to align itself with authoritarianism against democracy. Things have changed and that document can no longer be treated as holy writ. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in a changed and perilous world. Trump is telling us that in a crude, loud voice. We must listen.
- Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist
- US midterms: Trump, war and America’s future
   
On Thursday, 5 November join Jonathan Freedland, Devika Bhat, Professor Adam Smith in London and David Smith and leading US commentator Tara Setmayer live from the US to discuss the results and their implications for the future of Trump, the US and global politics.

articles.title: Russia’s Air Surveillance Takes a Hit as Ukraine Strikes $100 Million Nebo-U Radar
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Air Surveillance Takes a Hit as Ukraine Strikes $100 Million Nebo-U Radar
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Nebo-U long-range radar station in Krasnodar Krai overnight, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 16.
The strike targeted a 55Zh6U Nebo-U radar near the settlement of Magri in Russia’s Krasnodar Region during the night of October 16. A fire broke out near the facility following the attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Nebo-U is a three-dimensional VHF-band radar designed to detect and track aircraft, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles. The General Staff estimated the system’s value at approximately $100 million.
“Strikes on such systems reduce the enemy’s ability to control airspace and promptly detect aerial targets,” the General Staff stated.
Ukraine’s military did not disclose the weapons used in the strike or provide an assessment of the radar’s condition after the attack. It noted that operations against key Russian military facilities are continuing.
The strike follows earlier Ukrainian attacks on the same type of radar as part of an effort to blind Russia's air surveillance network.
On August 27, Ukrainian drones hit a Nebo-U station at the Millerovo military airfield in Russia's Rostov region, roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, from the front line.
The airfield serves as a launch point for Shahed-type attack drones and other strike and decoy UAVs used against Ukraine's eastern, central, and northern regions. That attack formed part of a broader campaign to establish sustained fire control over the site.

articles.title: Belgium To Transfer Ten F-16s to Ukraine by the End of Year
articles.body:
Belgium plans to transfer ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever made this announcement after meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels, according to a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty correspondent.
“We will transfer ten this year. We have a slight delay, but it’s not our fault—it’s due to a delay in the delivery of the F-35s. We must be able to fulfill our NATO commitments, so we need the aircraft. The F-35s are now starting to arrive, and this allows us to transfer the F-16s to Ukraine,” de Wever said.
He emphasized that Ukraine urgently needs the fighter jets, particularly to combat Russian jet drones.
“The jet-powered drones that Russia now possesses have given it an advantage in the drone war. And the F-16, with its 20-millimeter cannon, is one of the few types of weaponry that can be widely used to defend against them,” explained the Belgian prime minister.
According to him, Ukraine also needs air cover to protect grain exports through the Black Sea, as well as its energy infrastructure and bridges.
De Wever said he discussed with Zelensky the possibility of accelerating deliveries, as well as the transfer of 20-millimeter ammunition manufactured by the Belgian company FN Herstal.
“We can help him. We have that capability. In particular, we can help with 20-millimeter ammunition,” he noted.
In June, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken announced that by the end of 2026, the country would transfer seven F-16s to Ukraine, three of which are intended for combat missions and four for spare parts.
De Wever did not specify how many of the now-promised ten aircraft would be designated for combat use and how many for spare parts.
In May 2024, Belgium committed to supplying Ukraine with a total of 30 F-16 fighter jets by 2028. The overall plan calls for the transfer of 53 Belgian F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2029.
Initially, it was planned that Ukraine would receive the first Belgian fighter jets as early as 2024. However, the delivery was postponed due to delays in the arrival of American F-35s, which are set to replace the F-16s in the Belgian Air Force.
In early October, it was reported that Belgium’s transfer of three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine would take place immediately after the signing of an agreement with France on the transfer of technology to a third party.

articles.title: Belgium to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year, says premier
articles.body:
Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Belgium will deliver ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year to help strengthen its defense capabilities, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said Thursday.
Speaking at a press conference following the first day of an EU summit in Brussels, De Wever said he discussed Ukraine's military needs with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit.
"We will supply 10 this year. We have fallen a little behind because of delays with the F-35s, but those are now starting to arrive, which will enable us to send F-16s to Ukraine," De Wever said.
He stressed that Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets, describing F-16s as among the few weapons capable of effectively defending against "Russian jet-powered drones."
De Wever added that the two leaders also discussed the possibility of Belgium supplying ammunition for the F-16s, including some manufactured by Belgian defense company FN Herstal.
The leaders also discussed Ukraine's funding needs, although De Wever did not elaborate on the possibility of using frozen Russian assets held largely at Belgian-based Euroclear to support Ukraine.
Belgium previously opposed a proposal to use the frozen assets to finance a reparations loan for Ukraine, citing potential legal and financial risks.

articles.title: Russian drones kill three in Ukraine, cut power to 1 million as US, Russia seek further cooperation
articles.body:
Russian drones killed at least three people across Ukraine early on Friday, hit two shopping centers and temporarily knocked out power to over 1 million people nationwide after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.
A 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man died, and 12 more people were wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. He had earlier put the death toll at three.
Ukraine's energy ministry said its repair crews had restored power to over 1 million people who lost it in Russian attacks on Friday. It was unclear how many people were still without power.
Almost 300,000 remain temporarily without power
In the northwestern region of Volyn, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight others, according to Governor Roman Romaniuk. He said 370,000 people were temporarily without power in the morning, although 100,000 of them got supply back later on.
The blackout could last for at least 24 hours in Volyn's regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said on Facebook.
Romaniuk said that drone attacks continued throughout the day, striking a customs terminal and torching about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, which sits on a major trunk road from Kyiv to Poland.
Other attacks hit at least two shopping centers, one in the northern city of Sumy, which sits close to the front line, and one in the neighboring region of Rivne, officials said, the latest in a spate of Russian assaults on malls and markets.
Pictures from emergency services in Sumy showed blood spattered across the floor and shots of the center's damaged entrance.
Seven people were wounded by drones that hit a major shopping center and other sites in Rivne, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.
Ukraine's energy ministry said large parts of the city of Rivne and the surrounding area were without power after attacks on energy infrastructure there.
Russia, US to announce new joint initiatives beyond diesel deal
Russia and the United States will soon announce new joint initiatives beyond a recently agreed diesel deal, President Vladimir Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said on Friday.
Dmitriev said the two countries were discussing joint data center projects, including facilities that could use electricity generated by Russian nuclear power plants.
Dmitriev said that the projects would be launched before the end of what Moscow calls its "special military operation" in Ukraine.
Following a report in the Financial Times that the US had proposed European countries transfer some frozen Russian assets to a vehicle overseen by Washington to try to revive stalled peace talks, Zelensky said that Ukraine could not risk any deal being struck to return the assets to Moscow.
Ukrainians struggling with a fifth year of Russian attacks on their power grid and other civilian infrastructure have said they are appalled by Trump's decision to open the US market for Russian diesel. They have also condemned his attempts to blame fuel shortages caused by the Iran war on Kyiv's military strikes on Russian refineries.
"In my view, we cannot accept these diesel deals, these agreements, because gas deals will follow. I am absolutely certain of this. Sanctions will be lifted on other things as well after gas," Zelensky told reporters in Brussels.

articles.title: Belgium promises to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year
articles.body:
Belgium will deliver ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said at a press conference attended by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
“Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets and we can make our contribution,” De Wever said following a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the European Council meeting in Brussels.
"We will supply 10 this year. We have fallen a little behind because of delays with the F-35s, but those are now starting to arrive, which will enable us to send F-16s to Ukraine," the prime minister said. As Belgium is modernizing its air force with U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets, the country said it would transfer some of its F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine.
On Sept. 29, Zelensky said that Belgium will provide Ukraine with three U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets by the end of the year.
De Wever said that Ukraine urgently needed the fighter jets, as they were one of the weapons capable of defending Ukraine from "Russian jet-powered drones."
The Geran-5 jet-powered drone is Russia's latest attempt to force Ukraine to capitulate. Small, and with a tubular fuselage reminiscent of a missile rather than a drone, the Geran-5 flies higher, faster, and is significantly more difficult to shoot down. Russia's jet drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Zelensky and De Wever also discussed the possibility of supplying Ukraine with ammunition for the F-16s.
F-16s are used in both offensive and defensive operations. The aircraft have been used for intercepting Russian missiles and drones during aerial strikes against Ukraine. They can also be deployed to launch missiles at Russian positions along the front line.

articles.title: Sweden Sends Patriot Systems to Crete for Live-Fire Drills Ahead of Deployment to Poland
articles.body:
Swedish troops conducted their first live-fire drills with Patriot SAM systems on the Greek island of Crete ahead of deploying them to Poland as part of a NATO mission.
The Swedish Armed Forces reported this.
The live-fire drills took place on October 14 at the NATO Missile Firing Installation (NAMFI) range as part of the Spartan Arrow exercise. They involved personnel from Sweden’s 6th Air Defence Regiment (Lv 6) alongside German units.
During the exercise, Swedish gunners fired two GEM-T missiles from the Patriot system. One of the missiles successfully hit an aerial drone target.
According to SVT, each missile used costs more than 40 million Swedish kronor. This puts the total cost of the two interceptors fired at over 80 million kronor.
The Spartan Arrow exercise is organized by Germany, with Sweden taking part for the first time. The troops are practicing the deployment of air defense systems, coordination between allied units, and engagement of aerial targets in challenging conditions. Sweden has deployed more than 100 personnel to the exercise.
Live-fire drills are a mandatory part of assessing unit readiness under both national standards and NATO requirements. After successfully completing the tasks, the Swedish unit was cleared for its upcoming mission in Poland.
The Swedish Armed Forces noted the exercise tested the Patriot system’s full operational cycle, from transportation and deployment to live missile firing.
Militarnyi previously reported that Sweden plans to deploy Patriot systems and around 100 personnel to Poland to protect the logistics hub in Rzeszów, which serves as a key entry point for military aid to Ukraine.
The mission is expected to begin in early December 2026 and run through the end of the year, with the possibility of an extension into the first half of 2027.
The Swedish contingent will operate under NATO command and join the Alliance’s integrated air and missile defense system.
Sweden operates US Patriot systems under the national designation Luftvärnssystem 103. Their arsenal includes GEM-T missiles, designed to intercept aerodynamic targets, and PAC-3 MSEs, which can also be used against ballistic missiles.
