articles.title: SCALP, AASM Hammer, and Aster 30: France Has Granted Ukraine All the Promised Licenses
articles.body:
Ukraine has received all the licenses France promised for the domestic production of three types of weapons: Aster 30 air defense missiles, AASMHammer guided bombs, and SCALP cruise missiles.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the development.
In July, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the licensing agreement following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The agreement allows Ukraine to produce these weapons domestically under French licenses.
Ukrainian forces have been successfully employing Aster 30 missiles for an extended period as part of the SAMP/T surface-to-air missile systems supplied by France and Italy.
The modern Aster 30 Block 1 variant can engage aerodynamic targets, including aircraft, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), at ranges of up to 120 km and altitudes of up to 25 km.
In addition, the system can intercept tactical ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 30 km.
The French AASM Hammer is a guidance kit that converts conventional unguided Western-designed bombs into precision-guided munitions.
Unlike the American JDAM, AASM Hammer kits are equipped with an integrated rocket motor, enabling them to engage targets at ranges of up to 15 km when released from low altitudes and up to 70 km when released from high altitudes.
Currently, two versions are available: the Hammer 250, designed for 227 kg Mk 82 bombs, and the Hammer 1000, designed for 908 kg Mk 84 bombs. Both are available with different guidance systems.
The Franco-British SCALP EG / Storm Shadow is an air-launched cruise missile measuring 5.1 metres in length, weighing 1,300 kg, and equipped with a 450 kg warhead designed to destroy hardened, fixed targets.
The missile was developed by Matra and British Aerospace beginning in the late 1990s. It has been in service with France and the United Kingdom since 2003 and is manufactured by the MBDA consortium.
The French SCALP-EG and British Storm Shadow variants are essentially identical in design, differing primarily in their software and the specifics of their integration with carrier aircraft.

articles.title: AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
articles.body:
AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
TEHRAN— Hossein Taeb, head of Iran’s Basij Organization, says the use of artificial intelligence in defense and intelligence operations has improved the accuracy of target identification and precision strikes, highlighting the technology’s growing role in Iran’s military capabilities.
Speaking on Thursday at the first Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Conference in the southeastern city of Kerman, Taeb said AI had strengthened intelligence gathering and target assessment, adding that its applications had extended to the naval and aerospace divisions of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) and other branches of the armed forces.
Taeb also discussed 'the objectives of the US-Israeli war against Iran,' arguing that attacks on military commanders, scientists and air-defense systems were intended to weaken the country’s defenses and undermine the scientific foundations of its development.
Protecting Iran’s scientific capabilities
Referring to the 12-day war, Taeb said the simultaneous targeting of military commanders and scientists was part of a strategy to weaken Iran’s security infrastructure and damage the scientific capabilities underpinning its technological progress.
He said the campaign against Iranian scientists had failed to eliminate the country’s nuclear expertise. According to Taeb, the scope of attacks expanded during the 40-day war, extending to other scientific fields and claiming the lives of researchers.
Taeb argued that the objective of such attacks went beyond military damage, encompassing efforts to undermine public security and weaken the country’s capacity for scientific and technological advancement.
"Targeting one scientist would not halt the country’s progress, as more specialists would emerge to continue the work," he said.
AI and the changing landscape of military operations
Taeb described investment in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as a strategic decision for Iran’s future, calling for these priorities to be translated into practical action by government institutions, policymakers and leading experts.
He said AI had already produced tangible results in the defense sector by improving intelligence assessment and the accuracy of target identification.
He further said AI-assisted systems had improved the detection of military vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz and helped increase missile accuracy. Taeb argued that these capabilities had affected US military calculations and contributed to the relocation of American naval vessels farther from the area.
His remarks underscore the growing importance of AI-enabled intelligence, surveillance and targeting systems in contemporary military operations. Such technologies can help process large volumes of information, identify patterns and support faster operational decisions, although their effectiveness depends on data quality, system reliability and human oversight.
Taeb highlights disparity in military spending
Taeb also contrasted Iran’s defense resources with the much larger military budgets of the United States and Israel. He cited figures for US military spending and additional wartime funding requests, and said Israel had received $22 billion in additional US assistance for the conflict.
Despite Iran’s limited defense resources in foreign-currency terms, Taeb said the country had been able to withstand the military campaign. He argued that a comparable emphasis on scientific capability, technological innovation and strategic planning was necessary to sustain progress in the fields of AI and cybersecurity.
He called for artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to move beyond isolated technological initiatives and become part of a coordinated national strategy involving public institutions and the country’s scientific community.
The conference’s focus on young technology specialists, Taeb said, reflected Iran’s intention to expand its pool of skilled researchers and developers. In his view, strengthening domestic expertise in emerging technologies is essential not only to defense preparedness but also to the country’s broader scientific and technological development.

articles.title: “We Are Not the Number One Priority”: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Faces Severe Patriot Missile Shortage
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
“We Are Not the Number One Priority”: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Faces Severe Patriot Missile Shortage
Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its US-made Patriot air defense systems, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a briefing in Brussels on October 16.
According to Zelenskyy, most available supplies of these missiles have been directed to the Middle East for an extended period.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“There is currently a severe shortage. Most PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles have been going to the Middle East for quite some time. This is no secret,” Zelenskyy said.
“We are not the number one priority when it comes to the allocation of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles. Nevertheless, we are grateful for the number of missiles we can receive through PURL,” he added.
Despite the limited availability, Ukraine continues to receive some Patriot interceptors from the United States through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative. The program allows European partners to finance the purchase of US-made military equipment for Ukraine.
“We receive PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from the United States through the PURL program. Europe pays for them, meaning these are not free missiles or gifts,” Zelenskyy explained.
The Ukrainian president expressed gratitude to NATO, European countries financing the purchases, the White House administration, and the United States for their continued involvement in supplying air defense equipment.
With interceptor missiles remaining in short supply, Kyiv is also working with international partners to secure additional deliveries in smaller quantities.
“We are working with Europe and other countries around the world, gathering 2, 5, or 10 missiles at a time. However many we can agree on, however many of the necessary missiles we can obtain, that is how many we deliver to Ukraine to protect people,” Zelenskyy said.
The president emphasized that strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses remains particularly urgent as Russian attacks continue to threaten critical infrastructure across the country.
“Today, we are protecting infrastructure, primarily the energy sector. You are well aware of all these challenges,” Zelenskyy stated.
His remarks follow reports of an even more critical situation involving Ukraine’s Patriot missile stockpiles, with a source familiar with the matter telling CNN on October 15 that the country had completely exhausted its available interceptors.
According to the report, the shortage has significantly undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, raising concerns about the country’s vulnerability to further attacks.
The source told CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”

articles.title: Missiles hit Aden airport, Saudi coalition intercepts missile
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Missiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu
Missiles struck Aden International Airport in southern Yemen on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify those behind the attacks.
In Aden, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Iran-aligned Houthi group. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.
Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, where heightened regional tensions and security threats have raised concerns over the safety of shipping.
Brent crude briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, as worries over escalating Middle East tensions raised concerns about tighter global supplies.
Saudi Civil Defense authorities earlier issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Yemen's war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and forced the internationally recognised government south.
A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure. In recent days, the group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3.

articles.title: Ukraine expects an additional 10 F-16 fighter jets from Belgium by the end of the year — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine expects an additional 10 F-16 fighter jets from Belgium by the end of the year — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Belgium plans to transfer 10 F-16s to Ukraine by the end of 2026. The aircraft are already intercepting jet-powered Shaheds and strengthening air defense.
Belgium plans to transfer 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced this during his visit to Brussels, reports UNN.
Ukrainian troops are currently actively using these aircraft to intercept Russian jet-powered drones of the Shahed type, demonstrating high effectiveness.
Details
According to the head of state, F-16 fighter jets play an important role in countering Russian air attacks, in particular helping to destroy jet-powered variants of attack drones.
"F-16s are now helping greatly in repelling attacks by jet-powered Shaheds. We are working with Belgium to receive additional fighter jets as soon as possible," Zelenskyy emphasized.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, for his part, confirmed the intention to transfer 10 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of this year. According to him, the delivery of the aircraft had been delayed due to problems Belgium faced in receiving new American F-35 fighter jets. However, their arrival is now resuming, which will make it possible to accelerate the transfer of F-16s to Ukraine.
During the meeting in Brussels, Zelenskyy and De Wever also discussed the possibility of supplying additional ammunition for the fighter jets. The President emphasized that strengthening Ukraine's air defense remains one of the key priorities amid continuous Russian attacks.
It will be recalled
On September 29, Zelenskyy reported an agreement with Belgium to transfer three F-16 fighter jets by the end of 2026 under an expedited procedure. Ukraine also received urgent batches of ammunition for these aircraft from Belgium and other partners, including Spain.

articles.title: Zelensky's ask: 300 Patriot missiles, 70 billion euros, and Russian assets
articles.body:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky used his appearance at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels to list the main things Kyiv needs to survive the winter and beyond, but those asks won't come cheap.
"I am grateful for your support for Ukraine," Zelensky told EU leaders.
"Without a determined European Union capable of making strong decisions Putin would have gone much further by now," Zelensky said.
But with Russia ramping up its use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones to pummel Kyiv, and the U.S. taking steps to undermine Russia sanctions and Ukrainian security, Zelensky also came to the bloc with new requests for help.
read also
"We need a winter package... 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
The U.S.-made Patriot are considered the only technology currently capable of consistently taking down Russian ballistic missiles, and several European countries still hold stocks of them, such as Spain and Greece.
But for Spain, European diplomats have told the Kyiv Independent that there is a real fear that Madrid will not receive any more Patriot missiles in the future because of U.S. President Donald Trump's personal dislike for Spain's center-left Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
Greece on the other hand has a visceral fear that depleting its own supplies of Patriots might be perceived as a sign of weakness by neighboring Turkey, which Athens fears Ankara would act upon by annexing Greek islands near the Turkish coast.
Likewise, Ukraine's demand to "deal with the frozen assets," unsettles several countries around the table.
Using the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of Russian assets immobilized within the EU to support Ukraine came up in late 2025, but consensus on the idea was out of reach.
"We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war," Zelensky said.
Aside from the fears of holders of those assets, principally Belgium, about Russian retaliation for such a move, several European countries also fear that entering into such appropriations could fracture the global financial system, as countries move their wealth only into jurisdictions deemed friendly to them.
For Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, touching those assets remains very much a no-go.
"My personal view is that if you have immobilized assets, like in every war, even the Second World War, they were never touched. But at the end of a conflict, there's always a peace deal. And part of this peace deal is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever told journalists at a press conference during the night of Oct. 15.
"Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier? ... Yes, there are ... Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," De Wever said.
And the risk of Russia's assets being returned, despite some wishful thinking from the U.S. that Europe would hand them over, is nonexistent. The EU bound itself in December 2025, so that any vote to unfreeze the Russian immobilized assets must be unanimous.
"Nobody could ever dream of operationalizing those immobilized assets without unanimity here around the table," De Wever said.
On top of requesting the Russian assets, Zelensky also asked the EU to fill Kyiv's budget hole for 2027.
"The war will cost 155 billion euros ($174.5 billion) next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros ($78.8 billion) more from you," Zelensky said.
"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he added.
But the request for 70 billion euros comes only six months after the bloc approved a 90 billion euro loan to help Ukraine until the end of 2027. The idea was always that third countries would step in to help bridge the remaining gap, but so far only Norway has done so.
And the government has been notoriously unclear at communicating its financial needs, as noted earlier that day by Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
However, Zelensky's estimate of a 70 billion euro shortfall does match the estimated shortfall figure that a senior EU official familiar with Ukraine's financial situation shared with the Kyiv Independent.
On all three requests, even if they land on sympathetic ears, a decision would still not be expected the same day.
And because there is nonetheless a European consensus to support Ukraine, the demands are very likely to dominate discussions in Brussels over the next weeks.

articles.title: Putin says creation of ‘security zone’ along border will not be subject of peace talks with Ukraine
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that his country’s efforts to establish a “security zone” along its border with Ukraine will not be a subject of negotiations with Kyiv. 
In remarks to military commanders on a visit to a command post, Putin recalled that, following Ukraine’s incursion into Russia's border region of Kursk in August 2024, Russian troops were tasked not only with pushing Ukrainian forces out of its territory but also with creating a “security zone.” 
“Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border territories for the future, and we do not intend to make this a subject of potential peace negotiations with Ukraine,” Putin said, clad in military uniform. 
Addressing the commanders, Putin said this task is being “succesfully accomplished,” noting the effectiveness of strikes against Ukrainian military-industrial complex facilities and logistics centers. 
“In response to strikes by the Kyiv authorities against our industrial and fuel-and-energy facilities, the Russian Armed Forces continue to carry out strikes on enterprises of the military-industrial complex, as well as on infrastructure facilities in Ukraine,” Putin added. 
He said it is essential to continue delivering “massive, coordinated” strikes against such facilities. 
US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday a ceasefire on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine. Both countries, however, have since accused each other of violating the truce. 
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday said Ukraine will resume the strikes after a three-day halt. 
Meanwhile, the Kremlin said Russia was continuing contacts with the US concerning the truce. 
Last May, Putin ordered the creation of a “security buffer zone” along the border with Ukraine after pushing Ukrainian troops out of Kursk. 
In his most recent remarks, the president claimed Russia captured about 6,500 square kilometers of territory and took control of 310 settlements in Ukraine since the start of the year. 
He said the capture of the Donbas region remains as a key objective, claiming about 10% of the Donetsk region and about 16.5% of the Zaporizhzhia region still remained under Ukrainian control. 
Gerasimov briefing 
Separately, Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov, who briefed Putin on the front line situation, said Moscow has begun launching “massive” strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. 
“A list of these facilities has been established, along with the necessary complement of assets required to strike them,” Gerasimov said, noting that strikes are being carried out as well against strategically important bridges, railway infrastructure and data centers that “support the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.” 
Russia, he said, is also carrying to systematic strikes against Ukraine’s port and logistics infrastructure, which “led to the suspension of operations at major Black Sea ports,” and claimed steel production in Ukraine has been halted following airstrikes. 
He claimed that the Russian military took control of more than 1,800 square kilometers of territory and 92 populated areas in Ukraine since Sept. 1, and that its strikes in this period “significantly reduced” Kyiv's capacity to produce long-range weapons. 
Gerasimov added that Russian troops had reached the outskirts of Kramatorsk, the provisional seat of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. 
He went on to claim that fighting between Russian and Ukrainian troops was continuing in Druzhkivka, just south of Kramatorsk, and that Russian forces in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region were five kilometers (3.1 miles) from the southern outskirts of the regional capital. 
Gerasimov also reported on the “destruction” of 2,000 encircled Ukrainian troops in the northeastern part of Kharkiv region. 
Ukrainian authorities did not immediately comment on Putin and Gerasimov's remarks, and independent verification is difficult due to the ongoing war.

articles.title: Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine
Countries along NATO’s eastern flank are growing increasingly concerned about the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine.
Poland has scrambled its defences once again as Russian attacks overnight hit western Ukraine close to Poland’s border.
Poland’s armed forces said on Friday that they had scrambled fighter jets during the attacks and no violation of the country’s airspace was recorded.
It was just the latest such alert as Poland and other countries along NATO’s eastern flank grow increasingly concerned over the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine as Russia appears to be accelerating its tests of regional defences. Later on Friday, Bulgaria’s defence minister said Sofia has requested help from NATO to bolster its defences.
During air attacks across Ukraine overnight, numerous strikes hit the Volyn region, cutting electricity to 370,000 people across the western district, which sits on the border with Poland. Governor Roman Romaniuk reported that two people were injured.
In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a drone attack killed three people and injured five, the regional governor said. In central Ukraine, police said strikes on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number.
Private power company DTEK announced on Friday that it had implemented emergency power cuts across Kyiv due to ongoing strikes.
In Russia, officials said air defences had blocked a Ukrainian drone attack against a heating plant in the Vladimir region.
Ukraine has had significant success in attacking Russia’s energy infrastructure and its oil refineries in particular. However, that strategy has provoked anger from United States President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for pushing up global oil prices.
Russia said it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, 94 of them headed for Moscow.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said the capital’s four airports and St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport had suspended operations.
Ukrainian attacks killed two people in the Russian-controlled Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said.
Concern over Russian activity near NATO territory has grown since the summer as Romania, Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states reported numerous intrusions of drones into their airspace and waters.
That activity appears to be becoming more bellicose. In recent weeks, drones have struck at least seven cargo ships off the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, leaving 25 people dead or missing.
Drones hit two ships off Romania’s coast this week. A hit on a commercial vessel that sank off Bulgaria’s coast on Tuesday prompted Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Friday that while the evidence pointed to Russia, his government does not have proof.
Shortly afterwards, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters that Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and antidrone systems to bolster its defences.
“We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision,” Stoyanov said.
NATO did not immediately respond to a request for comment, the Reuters news agency reported.
Stoyanov said he plans to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO antidrone initiative by the end of October.
Romania’s president has also said that his country has asked for additional equipment.

articles.title: Why Ethiopia and Eritrea’s march to war demands global attention
articles.body:
The distant thunder of drones over Adigrat is not merely another African conflict. It is the sound of a continent’s most fragile peace shattering—and with it, the already slender prospects for stability across the Red Sea corridor that carries twelve per cent of global trade. Barely eight years after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and President Isaias Afwerki embraced in Asmara, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate’s handshake now lies in ruins.
Eritrean troops have crossed into northern Tigray, advancing up to sixty kilometres into Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia has responded with multiple drone strikes targeting those forces, destroying lorries and ammunition, witnesses say, amid reports of civilian deaths. Both nations have severed diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia calls it an “all-out invasion.” Eritrea calls it an “unprovoked war of aggression.” The truth matters less than the trajectory: two of Africa’s most battle-hardened armies are edging toward a conflagration neither can afford, yet both seem convinced they cannot avoid.
The roots of this rupture are not mysterious. They are anchored in geography so cruel it functions as destiny. Ethiopia, home to 130 million people, is the world’s most populous landlocked nation. It depends on Djibouti for over 95 per cent of its maritime trade, paying between $1.5 and $2 billion annually in port fees—a haemorrhage equivalent to the cost of building a Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam every three years.
A nation that once commanded the Red Sea through the ancient port of Adulis now watches its commerce squeezed through a single corridor. This is not merely an economic inconvenience. It is a structural wound that successive Ethiopian leaders have described in existential terms.
Abiy’s response has been to demand sovereign maritime access—specifically, to the Eritrean port of Assab, barely sixty kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Eritrea, which won independence in 1993 after a thirty-year liberation struggle, views this as nothing less than a threat to its territorial integrity and the very meaning of its statehood. Asmara’s information minister has accused Ethiopia of openly working to bring about regime change by sheltering and supporting armed opposition groups. The result is a security dilemma of terrifying symmetry: each side’s defensive measures confirm the other’s worst fears.
Into this vacuum have stepped external powers with interests that have little to do with Ethiopian or Eritrean welfare. Israel has publicly endorsed Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions, with its ambassador describing support for the effort as “clear Israeli policy.”
The strategic logic is cold: a strong, allied Ethiopia provides a non-Arab anchor in a region where Israel seeks to counter Iranian and Houthi influence, and where its recognition of Somaliland has already signalled a willingness to redraw regional alignments. The United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia’s largest investor and a quiet supplier of military technology, forms the other pillar of this de facto axis.
The United States, by contrast, has intervened with uncharacteristic directness. On 14 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Abiy that “the region cannot tolerate more conflict,” demanding respect for sovereignty and an immediate halt to cross-border incursions. Washington has even lifted certain sanctions on Eritrea—a pragmatic pivot driven not by any moral reassessment but by the urgent need to secure Red Sea shipping lanes against Houthi attacks. This is containment dressed as diplomacy, and it carries an uncomfortable implication: accountability for Eritrea’s role in the Tigray war has been quietly subordinated to maritime security.
The regional picture is equally troubling. Egypt and Sudan have aligned themselves with Eritrea, driven by their own existential anxieties over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Cairo views the dam as a threat to its 97 per cent dependence on the Nile. Addis Ababa views it as a sovereign right.
The result is a “river-versus-sea” confrontation in which the Nile and the Red Sea have become inseparable theatres of competition. Ethiopia’s army chief has openly accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the very rebels now fighting federal forces.
The human cost of this geopolitical chess game is already being paid. The 2020–2022 Tigray war killed an estimated 600,000 people. A renewed interstate conflict—this time involving heavy drone strikes, conventional armies, and the potential spillover onto Eritrea’s Red Sea coast—would create a humanitarian catastrophe of a different magnitude entirely. Millions of Ethiopians already face severe food insecurity.
The fragile Pretoria Agreement that ended the Tigray war has dissolved into renewed fighting across Amhara and Afar, with former allies now united in an armed alliance against the federal government. Ethiopia cannot fight a civil war and an interstate war simultaneously without fracturing.
Yet the most disturbing truth is that neither Washington’s pressure nor the African Union’s exhortations have altered the trajectory. The AU, headquartered in Addis Ababa, is structurally compromised—it cannot credibly mediate a conflict involving its host nation.
The Gulf states possess the financial leverage to broker a settlement, but the UAE’s deep ties to Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s alignment with Egypt make a unified mediation unlikely. The window for diplomacy is closing, and it is closing fast.
What is required is not another communiqué. It is a recognition that Ethiopia’s landlocked status is not a moral failing to be corrected by force, but a structural reality that demands a structural solution. The path forward lies in negotiated maritime access frameworks, joint port management arrangements, and regional economic integration that makes war materially irrational.
Ethiopia’s accession to the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System in October 2026 offered a glimpse of what patient, institutional cooperation could achieve. That glimpse is now being extinguished by the roar of drones.
The international community must act with a clarity that matches the urgency. The United States, the Gulf states, and the African Union must coordinate a single, unambiguous message: there is no military solution. But pressure alone is insufficient. The world’s strategic powers must offer Ethiopia a credible economic alternative—guaranteed, legally binding access to Red Sea ports under international law, backed by investment and infrastructure. Eritrea, for its part, must be assured that its sovereignty is not a bargaining chip.
The Horn of Africa has burned before. The world watched then, and the world did too little. It must not watch again. The drones over Adigrat are not a warning. They are a countdown.

articles.title: Future of western security is at stake in Yemen civil war, says country’s former PM
articles.body:
The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.
Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.
Appealing for more western help, Saeed said he had no doubt that the Houthis intended to seize control of all of Yemen, and claimed their goal was “to help Iran to expand the chaos”.
Saeed admitted the lack of coordination among government-backed troops, competition between Gulf states and a slowness to appreciate the implications of Yemen acquiring long-range drone technology had contributed to the pressure facing his government, and its chief backer Saudi Arabia.
“We only have light weapons and Saudi Arabia did not plan at an early stage for this escalation, but it is never too late to regain our position,” he said.
Saeed called on the west to think through the implications of allowing the Houthis to take control of Yemen, arguing the country would never be secure with Houthis on the land.
Saeed is not only an adviser to the Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, he was prime minister between 2018 and 2024 and a former negotiator with the Houthis.
He said: “The battle around Taiz is not just a battle for Taiz, but a broader battle that involves the whole of the western world, and one of the most important maritime straits. The Houthis know controlling Taiz is controlling the straits and it’s the highlands before the straits and the coastal city of Mocha and the Gulf of Aden. If Taiz is lost, access to the strait will be lost. The rest of the country will come later. The Houthi plan is to control the whole of Yemen.”
Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze the frontlines in 2022.
He said existing intelligence showed the Houthis were already seeking to control parts of the south, including the former Soviet camp at al-Sabiha, in the Lahij governorate, and eventually Aden. “The Houthis bleed a lot,” he said, “they suffer a lot, but they always want quickly to use their gains or any collapse to gain more land.”
With some Houthi leaders offering safe passage to armed groups to leave the city, he said for now the Houthis were allowing some fuel and commodities into the urban area of Taiz which houses more than 500,000 people, but in the meantime they were expanding their control of rural areas and smaller major cities.
Saeed said: “In a matter of days there will be a full siege and they will try to enter the city. I know the Houthis. They will show some flexibility until they are ready to control. It will be much worse than the siege of 2015. It will be catastrophic.”
He described Taiz as a modern democratic city untied to tribal culture, and predicted the Houthis would try to impose their Zaydi education, financial and tax systems very quickly, but the citizens would continue to resist. “The loss of Taiz would have a very significant symbolic impact on the idea of the modern state in Yemen and of resisting the Houthi project which relies on tribal networks and extremist religious education.”
Saeed admitted Taiz only had light weapons and the government had not been prepared for the loss of the west coast, allowing the Houthis to attack Taiz from four different axes.
“We have good troops,” he said, “but the problem is the coordination. We needed more communication between the National Shield Forces, National Resistance Forces and the Giants Brigades. It’s been a wake-up call inside the government and the army because not enough happened between the truce of 2022 and the restart of the fighting this year to reorganise the troops. The Houthi ideology solely is to fight.”
He added: “I hope now that the knife has come to our neck, and the Houthis represent a critical threat, the priority would be to come together to defeat the Houthis, and then to discuss other demands and guarantees.”
The exiled leader of the southern secessionist force, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, on Tuesday called for a mobilisation of southern troops against the Houthis, but coupled this with a demand for a referendum on secession within two years. He brought tens of thousands on to the streets in support on Wednesday, but his return would be a bitter pill for Riyadh to swallow.
Saeed said it was not a coincidence that the Houthi attack along the Red Sea coast in September had come when Iran was under heavy pressure.
“Its airplanes and airports cannot operate, 90% of the oil was coming out of Hormuz. That is why they attacked the Saudi east-to-west pipelines. The Houthis, by talking about a Saudi blockade, have found a reason to hit the Saudi oil installations, airports and they want to do it now because the only thing Iran can do is to keep expanding the consequences of the war for America.”
He said Houthi military capability and negotiating power had been transformed over the last decade leading to its ability to target key sites in Saudi Arabia now. “In 2017, the Houthis had nothing but blind missiles to fire at us that missed their targets.” By 2020, he said intelligence existed that Iranian experts operating from the Houthi capital Sana’a were training Houthis and in December of that year, in a devastatingly effective attack, they fired ballistic missiles at Aden airport. The attack left 28 dead and 107 injured, including Saeed himself, newly installed as prime minister. The missile travelled 186 miles (299km).
He explained: “We thought even then they did not have that many missiles, but since then the Iranians have expanded their manufacturing lines.” In January 2022, using missiles, the Houthis attacked Abu Dhabi oil tanker trucks more than 900 miles away.
In October 2022, inside Yemen, they struck the Nushayma oil terminal and al-Dhabba port, severely damaging government finances. By the time the US attacked Yemen in March 2025, he said “it was clear the Houthis had dozens of targeted missiles, land sea missiles and drones. They had become a unified front with Iran, and developed their missile base.”
He warned: “This is a new era of radical terrorism. It is not the old chaotic one of Isis and al-Qaida. It is semi-state actors and militias threatening powerful states with cheap technologies, and smuggled third-party components. The way Iran has invested in the Houthis could become a model for threatening navigation elsewhere. It is a new model of war, without traditional armies, needing different air defences. Gulf countries have to reshape and rethink their defences”.

articles.title: Ousted US general warned before Iran war of missile defense shortages lasting until 2030: Report
articles.body:
Ousted US Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defense stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported Thursday.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began, according to US officials familiar with his assessment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was underway.
The general’s assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
The officials reportedly attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel, and limited defense industry production capacity.
The war with Iran has further strained supplies, according to the report. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with approximately 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict.
READ: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran: Report
The country’s prewar THAAD inventory stood at around 355 interceptors, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that these systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defense — missile defense — that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would demand substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles remains a lengthy process, the report said. The CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take over four years to fulfill, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of 3 1/2 years.
The Pentagon rejected claims of a shortage. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: “Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false.”
He added that Washington retains “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing.”

articles.title: UK Sends Ukraine More Storm Shadow Missiles as US Presses Kyiv to Halt Strikes
articles.body:
Britain is supplying Ukraine with additional Storm Shadow cruise missiles to counter Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure before winter, as London backs Kyiv’s ability to strike targets inside Russia despite US pressure to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed replenishing the missile stocks during their meeting in London on Wednesday, Oct. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
London considers strikes on Russian facilities used to launch attacks against Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure a defensive measure, the sources said.
They pointed to Russia’s increased production of jet-powered drones and missiles, saying Ukraine needed the means to counter the growing threat.
The British position contrasts with that of US President Donald Trump’s administration, which has demanded that Ukraine stop drone attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine resumed those attacks on Thursday, Oct. 15, in response to continuing Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and accused Kyiv of driving up global energy prices, even as Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump told Newsmax in an interview published on Thursday, when asked about Ukraine’s decision to resume attacks on Russian refineries.
Europe Has No Starlink Replacement as Ukraine Faces Satellite Disruptions
However, energy analysts say Trump’s deal to resume Russian diesel exports is unlikely to significantly lower fuel prices, as the main driver of the global price surge has been the US-Israel war with Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Bloomberg’s sources, London does not believe Kyiv should stop striking Russia while Moscow continues attacking Ukraine.
The distinction concerns both the targets and the broader question of Ukraine’s right to respond: the reported British position supports attacks on facilities enabling Russian strikes, while Washington has specifically pressed Kyiv to spare refineries.
Britain began supplying Storm Shadow missiles to Ukraine in 2023. Their use was initially restricted to targets within Ukraine, including Russian-occupied territory. Ukrainian forces first used them against military targets inside Russia in late 2024.
Manufactured by MBDA, Storm Shadow is an air-launched cruise missile designed to strike high-value targets. It flies at low altitude to reduce detection, and the manufacturer lists its range as more than 250 kilometers, or about 155 miles.
Bloomberg also reported that Burnham announced plans in August to share technical information and designs for long-range missiles to support assembly in Ukraine, as establishing that production capability would take time.
