articles.title: Iran reaffirms Strait of Hormuz closure, says passage must be coordinated
articles.body:
Iran reaffirms Strait of Hormuz closure, says passage must be coordinated
TEHRAN — Iranian military officials have reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to uncoordinated maritime traffic, linking any easing of restrictions to 'respect for Iran’s rights' and warning that continued US military presence in the region will deepen insecurity.
Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, deputy coordinator of the Iranian Army, said on Thursday that any vessel seeking to transit the strategic waterway must coordinate its passage with the Iranian authorities who are in charge. His remarks came as Army Chief Commander Major General Amir Hatami and Army Spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia issued separate statements emphasizing Iran’s military readiness and its determination to maintain control over the security environment around the strait.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a ceremony honoring Army nurses, Sayyari argued that the impact of restrictions on maritime traffic was evident in international fuel markets.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If it were open and oil were passing through it, gasoline prices in the United States would not have risen,” he said.
Sayyari outlined the deployment of Iran’s armed forces around the waterway, saying the naval forces of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) maintained a firm presence to the west of the strait, while the Iranian Army operated to its east and extended its presence northward into the Sea of Oman.
He stressed that any passage through the waterway must be coordinated, warning that vessels attempting to transit without such coordination could face consequences.
Hatami links reopening to respect for Iran’s rights
Army Chief Commander Major General Amir Hatami has also made clear that, in Iran’s view, the future of the strait is directly linked to the treatment of the country and its rights.
Speaking at Imam Ali Officers’ University in Tehran on Thursday, Hatami said the Strait of Hormuz had been closed following the outbreak of the war and would remain closed until Iran’s rights were respected.
He attributed the conflict to a ‘fundamental miscalculation by Iran’s adversaries,’ who had underestimated the country’s military capabilities and assumed that it was in a weakened position.
According to Hatami, the Iranian Army and the IRGC responded from the earliest hours of the conflict with extensive strikes against hostile targets. He argued that the adversaries had failed to achieve their military and strategic objectives.
Rejecting US assertions that Iran’s military capabilities had been weakened, the Army chief pointed to continued missile and drone operations and the functioning of the country’s air-defense systems as evidence of its sustained operational capacity.
Hatami also said Iran had taken firm action against vessels that violated its regulations, leaving maritime traffic through the strait severely restricted.
He added that Iran’s armed forces had used the pause in hostilities to repair damage and strengthen their readiness. Iranian ground, naval, air-defense and missile units, he said, remained equipped and prepared to defend the country’s territorial integrity.
Hatami further warned that any attack on Iran’s infrastructure would prompt a response inflicting substantially greater damage on the infrastructure and interests of its adversaries, including Israel and those cooperating with it.
Army says US military presence fuels regional insecurity
In separate remarks on Friday, Army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia said Iran was developing new operational plans that would force hostile US naval vessels to withdraw even farther from the country’s coastline.
Akraminia said Iran’s air-defense capabilities had advanced beyond their prewar and wartime levels, adding that Iranian air-defense units had intercepted several US drones in the country’s airspace in recent weeks. He also said US military vessels had been pushed to distances exceeding 500 kilometers from the coasts of the Persian Gulf.
The spokesman described the US military presence as a central source of insecurity in the region and called on regional countries and the international community to recognize ‘Washington’s role in fueling instability.’
“If America leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, and collective security will be established with the participation of the region’s countries, and the global economy will improve. If it doesn’t leave, we’ll expel it,” Akraminia said.
He added that Iranian forces had rehearsed advanced, coordinated and innovative military operations, while nationwide air-defense coverage had been significantly strengthened.
A strategic waterway with global economic consequences
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most strategically important energy corridors, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Arabian Sea. A substantial share of global oil shipments and significant volumes of liquefied natural gas pass through the waterway, making disruptions a concern for energy-importing countries, shipping operators and financial markets.
Restrictions on traffic through the strait can raise shipping and insurance costs, disrupt energy supplies and add volatility to oil and fuel prices. The effects depend on the scale and duration of the disruption, the availability of alternative supplies and routes, and market expectations about the conflict.
Iran’s latest statements place the waterway at the center of its broader security position: Tehran says passage must be coordinated, its armed forces remain prepared, and any change in the current situation depends on respect for Iran’s rights and the future of foreign military deployments in the region.
The statements also underscore the competing approaches to security in the Persian Gulf. While Washington has emphasized maritime security and freedom of navigation, Iranian officials argue that lasting stability requires regional cooperation and an end to ‘destabilizing foreign military intervention.’
With energy markets and international shipping exposed to developments around the strait, any sustained change in maritime traffic is likely to have consequences well beyond West Asia. For Iran, however, the issue is not solely one of commercial passage: its military leadership has framed the waterway as a strategic lever tied to national security, sovereignty and the outcome of the wider confrontation.

articles.title: Russia strikes nine Ukrainian regions as strain grows between Zelenskyy and Trump
articles.body:
Russia’s heavy bombardment of the power grid before winter sets in has been an annual feature of the war, aiming to wear down Ukraine’s appetite for the fight by denying civilians heating and running water.
Russian attacks on nine regions of Ukraine caused emergency power outages for hundreds of thousands of households and damaged numerous homes, wounding at least 15 people, officials said on Friday, as civilian casualties from Moscow’s full-scale invasion climb steeply.
The latest aerial strikes on civilian targets came as fears mount that a sharp deterioration in relations between Kyiv and Washington this week could leave Ukraine further exposed to Russia’s escalating aerial attacks as the bitter winter approaches.
Russia’s heavy bombardment of the power grid before winter sets in has been an annual feature of the war, aiming to wear down Ukraine’s appetite for the fight by denying civilians heating and running water.
Ukrainian officials have warned Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in coming months.
On Thursday, Ukraine abandoned a brief truce on energy-related targets that it said Moscow did not heed despite US President Donald Trump's demand for a ceasefire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended a summit of European leaders on Friday who share his concerns about Russian aggression and Moscow’s wider plans on the continent.
The officials in Brussels vowed to maintain support for Ukraine and urged the US to put pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
September civilian casualties 85% higher than last year
Russia is blitzing not just Ukraine's power grid but also apartment buildings, public transport, cargo ships, data centres and food stores.
Ukrainian civilians are paying a high price for the escalating Russian attacks, the United Nations human rights office in Kyiv said in a monthly report published on Friday.
At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month, a total 85% higher than in September last year, the report said, noting that intensifying Russian attacks in October already have killed dozens of civilians, including children.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the head of the UN office.
Trump and Zelenskyy barbs raise questions about US support
Tension and uncertainty are gripping Ukraine and Europe after Zelenskyy and Trump publicly made cutting remarks about each other.
On Thursday, Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by the American president and Trump openly declared his dislike of the Ukrainian leader.
Arriving at the EU summit in Belgium, Zelenskyy thanked the 27-nation bloc for its support from what he said were “real leaders.”
“We want to end this war as (quickly) as possible,” Zelenskyy told reporters. “We don’t see now signals from (the) Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That’s why we have to prepare for the winter.”
The public spat between Trump and Zelenskyy raised the spectre of further reductions in US support for Ukraine’s war effort.
Ukraine is desperately short of the US-made Patriot missiles it needs to protect against Russia’s devastating ballistic missile attacks, despite Zelenskyy’s pleading for Washington to send more.
Zelenskyy complained about a breakdown in Western intelligence sharing and sudden restrictions on the use of Starshield, US company SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and military communications.
He also slammed Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, which came despite an international effort to sanction Russia and diplomatically isolate Putin over his invasion.
Trump promised to swiftly end the war, but Ukrainian officials have complained he is trying to bulldoze Zelenskyy into surrendering land to Russia.

articles.title: Zelensky meets Danish PM to discuss air defense and financial stability
articles.body:
Zelensky meets Danish PM to discuss air defense and financial stability
This was reported by the Office of the President, according to Ukrinform.
The leaders discussed in detail the threats posed by Russian escalation, particularly against Ukraine’s energy sector.
“It is clear that Russia has interpreted signals regarding the easing of sanctions as a green light to continue attacking residential buildings, substations, and any other infrastructure that supports normal life. It is now of the utmost importance for everyone in Europe to mobilize to provide additional protection against this brutal terror as winter approaches,” Volodymyr Zelensky noted.
Video: Volodymyr Zelensky / Facebook
The president emphasized that Ukraine’s top priority is air defense—primarily anti-ballistic defense and anything that helps intercept “Shahed” drones.
Volodymyr Zelensky and Mette Frederiksen also discussed how Denmark could provide financial support to bolster Ukraine’s resilience. They agreed that their teams would continue working on this at their respective levels.
As reported by Ukrinform, Volodymyr Zelensky discussed with the Belgian prime minister additional deliveries of F-16 fighter jets and ammunition for them.
Photo: Office of the President

articles.title: Russia pushes its drone war into Volyn Oblast on NATO border, cutting power to 370,000 as strikes creep toward EU
articles.body:
Russia is pushing its drone war westward, into a Ukrainian region that borders NATO. Russian drones attacked Volyn Oblast through the night of 16 October, hitting civilian and critical infrastructure and leaving 370,000 subscribers without power, regional administration head Roman Romaniuk says. Volyn borders Poland, a NATO member, and Belarus, a Russian ally.
Russia’s jet-powered drones keep flying farther west, and now the strikes reach deeper into the center and the EU-facing frontier too. Moscow launched more than 850 Shahed drones at Ukraine in about a day and a half, including a record roughly 360 on the central Kirovohrad Oblast, precisely as a speed cap on Starlink degraded the interceptor drones Ukraine’s air defense relies on.
Moscow escalates its attacks after winning sanctions relief from the diesel deal of US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin and sensing pressure on Ukraine, exploiting the moment its defenses were artificially restricted.
“Russia takes advantage of every such moment and must be held accountable for what it does,” Zelenskyy says, noting the skies had not been clear for a single hour.
A night that turned deadly in the west
In Volyn Oblast, the damage was concrete and lethal. Debris fell on a power line in the central Lutsk community, cutting electricity and disrupting water supply, and the city lost power entirely with public transport halted, Lutsk council secretary Andrii Razumovskyi says.
The heaviest toll came in Manevychi, where a drone hit the private enterprise Agrofrukt LTD, killing one person and injuring eight. By 10:46 AM, the fire there was contained, and residents were asked to seal windows, doors, and vents due to the risk of an ammonia release from a damaged facility.
A capital-to-border map of the same assault
Throughout the day, Russia has struck Kyiv and its region, and the Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Rivne, Kharkiv and Donetsk regions, along with Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Poltava and Ivano-Frankivsk.
By reaching western border regions at once, Russia is widening the pressure on civilians across the country and edging closer to the EU.

articles.title: Israel unlikely to attack Iran before elections – media
articles.body:
Israel unlikely to attack Iran before elections – media
There is a widespread belief within Israel’s political and security establishment that the country will not attack Iran ahead of the October 27 parliamentary elections, Ynet News reported on Thursday.
The report comes after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Army Radio on Wednesday that it would be “inconvenient” to launch preemptive strikes against Iran at this time. He claimed, however, that “Iran’s proxies” were planning to fire rockets at Israel.
“Even if Iran fires missiles at us, they will blame me,” he said, adding that Israel would retaliate against any attack.
Netanyahu sought to dispel speculation following a Channel 12 report claiming that he had urged Washington to strike Iran before the Israeli elections and the US midterms scheduled for November 3.
Axios cited a US official earlier this week as saying that Netanyahu “seems to want to go in again” against Iran. Netanyahu’s office denied the claims.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly hinted in recent weeks that he could resume the bombing campaign if Iran does not accept his terms. American media outlets have reported that the Pentagon prepared plans to use a massive conventional explosive nicknamed the “mother of all bombs.” The White House, however, denied that Trump and Netanyahu had discussed resuming the war.
Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have stalled, with Washington and Tehran accusing each other of making unacceptable demands. Iranian officials have warned that the country is prepared for renewed war if American or Israeli forces launch another attack.
The Knesset election will determine whether Netanyahu can remain in power after more than three years of governing with a coalition of right-wing and religious parties. He has faced accusations of intelligence failures ahead of the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, which triggered Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, as well as criticism over his handling of efforts to secure the release of Israeli hostages. His ongoing corruption trial also remains a political liability.
Neither Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition is assured of securing the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
The US midterms will determine control of Congress for the remaining two years of Trump’s presidency amid an energy crisis exacerbated by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both chambers of the legislature, while Democrats hope to regain control and constrain Trump’s agenda.
A Pew Research Center poll published on October 8 found that 65% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the Iran war, while his overall approval rating had fallen to 30%, its lowest level of his second term.

articles.title: Trump rules out nukes against Iran, keeps strike threat alive
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, saying the United States did not need them, while warning that Washington could launch further strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities as he predicted the war would end soon.
In an interview Thursday with Newsmax, Trump addressed reports that his administration was considering deploying the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iran, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump stressed that the weapon was conventional, not nuclear, describing it as an extremely powerful bomb.
“The mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “This is just an extremely large bomb.”
He repeated the distinction, saying the weapon was a conventional munition despite its destructive capacity.
Asked directly whether he would use nuclear weapons against Iran, Trump dismissed the possibility, saying Washington had no need to resort to them.
“No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to,” he said.
However, Trump left open the possibility of additional American attacks on Iran's nuclear infrastructure, specifically mentioning a suspected underground facility known as Pickaxe Mountain.
“Now, we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there,” Trump said. “We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast.”
The site is suspected of being part of Iran's nuclear program, and Trump's remarks suggested that Washington was considering further action to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Trump indicated that such an operation would not necessarily involve American ground troops. Asked whether U.S. forces would be deployed on the ground, he said he did not expect that to happen.
“No, I don't see that. I don't see that,” he said.
The president also warned that the United States might need to carry out additional military operations if it withdrew before ensuring Iran could never acquire nuclear weapons.
“We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said, suggesting that the prospect of future strikes would remain if Washington believed its objectives had not been achieved.
Despite signaling the possibility of further attacks, Trump predicted that the conflict would end in the near future, citing negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
“The Iran war will be over very soon. It's going to end very soon,” he said.
“One way or the other, it'll end very soon. And oil will go dropping like a rock, and gas prices as well.”
Trump's comments linked his expectations for an end to the conflict with the prospect of falling energy prices, which have been a major concern amid the fighting and uncertainty surrounding oil supplies.
He also claimed that Iranian officials had asked Washington to halt American and Israeli military operations, although he did not provide further details about the alleged request.
“They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them,” Trump said.
His remarks offered little detail about the status of the negotiations, the issues under discussion or the conditions that might lead to a cessation of hostilities.
Trump's prediction of a swift end to the war came alongside his warning that the United States remained prepared to strike additional Iranian nuclear facilities if necessary.
The administration's approach, as outlined by the president, combines diplomatic engagement with the threat of continued military action to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Trump also addressed his relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose government has been involved in the military campaign against Iran alongside the United States.
Asked whether he trusted Netanyahu, Trump gave a blunt response.
“I don't trust anybody, honestly,” he said.
He reiterated his position, adding: “In the world of politics, I don't trust anybody.”

articles.title: Zelenskyy meets Belgian PM De Wever in Brussels during European Council visit
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with Prime Minister of Belgium Bart De Wever on Thursday, where the politicians discussed the delivery of F-16 fighter jets and ammunition for them. In addition, Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a series of meetings with the NATO Secretary General, the Prime Minister of Poland, the President of France, and the King of the Belgians.
"Discussed with Prime Minister of Belgium Bart De Wever the consequences of round-the-clock Russian attacks on residential buildings, energy, and other critical infrastructure of Ukraine... Informed Mr. Prime Minister in detail about Russian terror and our needs. Right now, F-16s are helping immensely to repel attacks by jet-powered Shaheds. We are working with Belgium to receive additional fighter jets as soon as possible. We also spoke about the possibility of additional ammunition supplies for them. Every decision on defense support saves lives. Grateful to the Prime Minister and Belgium for assistance and readiness to support our defense of life going forward," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram.
Earlier on Thursday, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy was granted an audience with King Philippe of Belgium; the president emphasized the importance of supporting Ukraine, Ukrainian air defense, and supplying F-16 aircraft to Ukraine. Prior to this, Zelenskyy held a series of meetings with representatives of NATO, Poland, and France.

articles.title: Bulgaria Asks NATO for Aircraft, Air Defenses and Counter-Drone Systems as Black Sea Attacks Intensify
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Bulgaria Asks NATO for Aircraft, Air Defenses and Counter-Drone Systems as Black Sea Attacks Intensify
Bulgaria has requested additional aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone equipment, and air patrols from NATO as attacks on vessels in the Black Sea intensify, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said, according to Novinite on October 16.
Speaking to journalists, Stoyanov warned that the security situation in the Black Sea was deteriorating, with attacks becoming increasingly frequent. He pointed to recent strikes in Romanian territorial waters as evidence of the growing threats facing countries in the region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have requested aviation, surface-to-air missile systems, counter-drone systems, and air patrols—essentially, the entire spectrum of available assets,” Stoyanov said, adding that the deployment of additional allied resources would also help demonstrate a stronger NATO presence in the region.
However, the minister acknowledged that it remained unclear which capabilities Bulgaria would ultimately receive. He noted that Romania and the Baltic states were facing similar security challenges, while European partners were paying increasing attention to threats in the Black Sea.
“I hope for a swift response and a strengthening of our capabilities,” Stoyanov said.
To improve regional coordination, Bulgaria is also seeking closer cooperation with neighboring NATO members. According to the minister, a meeting involving the defense ministers of Bulgaria, Türkiye, and Romania, alongside the chiefs of defense of all three countries, is expected to take place soon.
The discussions are intended to support the development of a coordinated response to emerging threats and strengthen cooperation among the three Black Sea NATO members.
Despite the requested assistance, Stoyanov cautioned that deploying additional allied forces and equipment would not eliminate all security risks in the region.
“100% security is impossible,” the defense minister said, emphasizing that the objective was to minimize potential threats rather than guarantee complete protection.
Meanwhile, Bulgaria continues to rely on its existing military resources to monitor its maritime territory and respond to potential threats.
According to Stoyanov, the country currently operates two reconnaissance systems dedicated to maritime surveillance, with a third expected to become operational by the end of the year.
The minister said the additional system would introduce technology that had not previously been deployed elsewhere.
The calls for additional security measures follow a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident near Bulgaria’s coast on October 13.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reported that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones overnight, leaving one ship sunk and forcing the evacuation of the entire crew of another after three drones hit its deck and hull.
One of the vessels was the Chelsea 3, a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship sailing under the Maltese flag, which came under attack approximately 18 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian coastal town of Byala.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: EU faces growing pressure to plug Ukraine’s Starlink gap
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — The European Union is under pressure to keep Ukrainian troops fully online after Elon Musk's Starlink was restricted amid volatile U.S. support for Kyiv.
"It was a very dangerous and unpleasant surprise,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters after EU leaders met in Brussels, referring to Starlink speed limitations experienced by military troops in recent days. "We were using Starlink to intercept jet-powered Shaheds [combat drones] that are attacking our civilian infrastructure and killing our families ... When the speed limits were lowered, we became incapable of shooting [them] down."
Ukraine has long relied critically on Musk’s satellite constellation for wartime efforts. Reuters reported Friday that the order to slow Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield service came from the White House, days after Washington pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries, amid soaring energy prices and ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Advertisement
"It is unacceptable for Ukraine’s defense — and therefore Europe’s security — to depend on the goodwill of a single American billionaire or on Donald Trump’s decisions," French centrist Member of the European Parliament Christophe Grudler told POLITICO.
Ahead of Thursday's high-level meeting, European lawmakers had been calling on the EU executive to fast-track Kyiv's access to satellite capabilities already pooled under the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities.
Negotiations between the EU executive and Ukraine over this access have been ongoing since March, with no breakthrough. Norway and Iceland secured such an agreement earlier this year.
"What I don’t understand is why the European Commission and the Member States have not done everything possible to quickly reach an agreement that would allow Ukraine to benefit from it," added Christophe Grudler, who wrote to EU leaders.
He also called on them to speed up work on IRIS² — the EU’s in-house, planned satellite network and full-fledged match to Starlink, which is only expected to come online in 2030.
Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed in a statement that it is "currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate" the country with the EU's Govsatcom program. "The war in Ukraine shows that our security also depends on space. And the EU has been doing quite a lot. We are ready to support Ukraine where we can support Ukraine," he added.
Advertisement
Calls to crack down on dependence on foreign providers and boost alternatives to Starlink also come at a time when legislators are negotiating a series of laws that could tame Musk's ambitions in Europe.
"Ukraine’s dependence on Starlink highlights the vulnerability of European defence systems that rely on U.S. technology, Another reminder that Europe must reduce its dangerous technological dependencies — ASAP," center-right Finnish lawmaker Aura Salla said on social media.
Policymakers across Europe have been joining forces to curb Starlink's dominance in low-Earth orbit, where satellites fly close to Earth to deliver faster connections.
"As legislators, we must ensure that European operators are well positioned in the market and limit the dominance of foreign players," German center-left lawmaker Matthias Ecke said. In Brussels, lawmakers, including Ecke, are backing European telcos gunning for prized satellite frequencies, currently licensed to U.S. operators until next year and eyed by Starlink.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was working bilaterally with EU countries to secure more capabilities, citing France. He also expressed hopes that Starlink restrictions could be lifted. “My partners told me there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities.”
SpaceX — Starlink's parent company — didn't respond to POLITICO's request for comment.

articles.title: Russian strikes reduce Ukrainian capacity to produce long-range weapons — Gerasimov
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. As a result of 12 massive Russian strikes this fall, 30 Ukrainian defense industry companies and logistics centers have been hit, thereby significantly reducing Kiev’s ability to produce long-range weapons, including cruise and ballistic missiles, Russian Armed Forces’ General Staff Chief Army General Valery Gerasimov told President Vladimir Putin.
"In total, [Russian servicemen] carried out 12 massive strikes in September and October, striking 30 military-industrial complex enterprises and logistics centers involved in the production and storage of missiles and strike drones, as well as 14 fuel, energy, and transport infrastructure facilities. As a result, the Ukrainian industry’s capacity to produce long-range weapons, including cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as to procure the necessary equipment to support Ukraine’s industrial and energy sectors has been significantly reduced," he said.

articles.title: Drone strikes in Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation
articles.body:
Romanian warships sail during a Romanian Navy led exercise outside Constanta, Romania, on April 16, 2024. (AP Photo/Andreea Alexandru, File)
A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
The attacks in the two countries’ exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine.
Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube River ports, leaving Kiev increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine’s Danube ports.
In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones on Oct. 14 and 15, one in Romania’s territorial waters.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said on Oct. 15 in Brussels that “two drones” had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. “There will be a reaction from the Romanian state,” he warned.
Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia.
“There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Oct. 15 that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and “the latest attacks on commercial shipping.”
“NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” he said.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.”
A source in Romania’s defense sector, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the incidents, told The Associated Press that the attacks are designed to hurt Ukraine economically and that “Romania is not the target right now.”
“All summer we’ve been hunting all kinds of [drone] debris, water drones, sea drones, air drones, debris in the water, on the beaches,” they said. “If this continues, someone should do something about that.”
The source added they have heard Türkiye “would like to summon all the riparian [Black Sea] states to plan a mission to escort these convoys” through a militarized safe corridor.
“I’m not sure about Turkish, but our Romanian vessels don’t have anti-air defense systems to protect against drones,” they said. “That would be a high risk for the Navy, for military vessels to escort this.”
In July, Romania, Bulgaria and Türkiye expanded the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Force naval pact to “expand the missions to the protection of critical submarine infrastructure,” according to Romania’s Defense Ministry. It would include, it said, a permanent naval presence in Romania’s exclusive economic zone.
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Oct. 14 that the country plans to join NATO’s Drone Edge project by the end of October. Launched in July, the initiative, which Romania also joined, aims to invest over $40 billion in “counter-drone capabilities” over the next five years.

articles.title: U.S. lawmakers reportedly offered Ukraine Starlink coverage inside Russia in exchange for halting refinery strikes. Zelensky was receptive, WSJ says.
articles.body:
U.S. lawmakers reportedly offered Ukraine Starlink coverage inside Russia in exchange for halting refinery strikes. Zelensky was receptive, WSJ says.
A group of U.S. congressmen has proposed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky halt strikes on Russian oil refineries in exchange for an expanded Starlink coverage zone for Ukraine’s armed forces, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The lawmakers raised the idea at a meeting in Kyiv last Friday. Under the plan, the U.S. would extend the Starlink coverage zone 300 kilometers (186 miles) into Russian territory in exchange for Ukraine halting the strikes, allowing Ukraine’s armed forces to destroy Russian launch systems.
Zelensky signaled he was willing to accept the proposal and halt strikes on Russian oil refineries for 100 days, WSJ reported.
The newspaper did not say whether the congressmen were acting as envoys for U.S. President Donald Trump or were advancing the proposal on their own initiative.
Trump has publicly demanded for several weeks that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries. In mid-October, he said Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to an “energy truce,” meaning a mutual halt to attacks on oil refineries.
Ukraine did refrain from striking Russian oil refineries for several days, Kyiv said, but on October 15, Zelensky announced that the strikes would resume because Russia, he said, had continued to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Moscow claimed there had never actually been a moratorium on Kyiv’s part.
Starlink service is currently limited to Ukraine’s internationally recognized territory. The Atlantic reported in August that former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov had unofficially tried to persuade SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink’s coverage zone for Ukraine’s armed forces so Ukraine could strike Russian missile launch systems. Musk refused, warning of the risks of escalation, according to the magazine.
Ukrainian authorities are looking for ways to strike Russian missile launch systems amid a critical shortage of Patriot missiles, which has left Ukraine effectively defenseless against Russian ballistic attacks. Zelensky, who announced yesterday that strikes on oil refineries would resume, stressed that he is willing to soften his position if allies supply Kyiv with more Patriot missiles.
War in photographs. Kharkiv
On the morning of October 16, Russian drones attacked an outdoor market in Kharkiv. Two vendors — a 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man — were killed and 13 other people were injured, authorities said.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Zelensky ‘destroyed’ Ukraine – Trump
articles.body:
Missiles supplied to Ukraine sold on ‘open market’ – Trump
US President Donald Trump has accused Ukraine of selling American-supplied missiles on the black market, questioning the whereabouts of billions of dollars in military and financial aid provided to Kiev under his predecessor, Joe Biden.
In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, accusing him of exploiting Washington’s generosity, while refusing to negotiate an end to the conflict with Russia.
“Where is the cash that we gave to Ukraine? Where is all the equipment? Biden was giving them missiles, and they were being sold on the open market,” Trump said.
Russian officials have repeatedly warned that unchecked deliveries of Western weapons to Ukraine and rampant corruption in the country have resulted in a large amount of these arms ending up in the hands of organized criminal groups and extremist organizations in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America, including Mexican drug cartels.
An RT investigation in 2022 found a variety of Western-supplied weapons such as anti-tank rockets, drones, and small arms for sale on the “dark web.”
According to a report by Small Arms Survey, the Ukrainian authorities intercepted a vehicle carrying 18 US-made Javelin anti-tank missiles and other hardware in Kiev-controlled part of Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic in 2024. The driver lacked the proper paperwork to transport the weapons, which suggested that they could have been intended for sale, it said.
Ukraine has also been rocked by numerous corruption scandals in military procurement involving officials close to Zelensky. In August, the country’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) reported losses of 254 million hryvnias ($6 million) as a result of an alleged embezzlement scheme which revolved around purchases of drones for Ukrainian forces.
Last year, investigators uncovered a $100 million corruption scheme in the Ukrainian energy sector allegedly run by a former close associate of Zelensky, businessman Timur Mindich, who fled the country before he could be detained. Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Rustem Umerov has been questioned as a witness in the case.
Zelensky has faced criticism from the West and street protests in 2025 over his attempts to put Ukraine’s independent anti-corruption watchdogs under the control of the government. The pressure eventually forced him to reverse course.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Biden for providing Ukraine with weapons and funds without preconditions and proper oversight. During Thursday’s interview, the US president compared Zelensky to P.T. Barnum, a 19th-century American showman and traveling circus-owner, known for publicity stunts and sensational attractions.
“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with. Biden gave him billions and billions of dollars,” he said.
Trump also questioned the Ukrainian leader’s willingness to reach a diplomatic resolution to the conflict with Moscow.
“He says he wants to settle but he [doesn’t],” he said, adding: “No, I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country.”
The remarks followed Zelensky’s criticism of Trump’s decision last week to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in order to contain surging energy prices ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections. The Ukrainian leader said he felt betrayed by Washington’s move and defied Trump’s demand to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The US president, meanwhile, made clear that Washington would prioritize rebuilding its own depleted weapons inventories rather than continuing to supply Kiev.
“Once we are really stocked, we will start letting our allies buy them [the arms] from us,” he said.

articles.title: Order limiting Starlink access for Ukraine's military came from within White House, Reuters reports
articles.body:
Order limiting Starlink access for Ukraine's military came from within White House, Reuters reports
An order to implement speed restrictions on Starlink systems for the Ukrainian military came from within the White House, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing U.S. and Western officials.
Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones. It is restricted from using it inside Russia itself.
Pentagon officials received notice from within the White House that the Starshield service — Starlink's military package — needed to be slowed down, two U.S. officials, and another Western official, told Reuters on the condition of anonymity. Officials did not state who was responsible for issuing the order.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from multiple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that "several" military missions severely disrupting amid the restrictions.
read also
Connectivity for Starlink systems used by the Ukrainian military have "been restored and remains operational," a source in the Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
But a source in Ukraine's drone industry who requested anonymity due to the nature of their work told the Kyiv Independent that "in some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not."
While the source of the disruption has yet been publicly confirmed, Ukrainian officials as well as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have pointed towards Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House.
A post on X from Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said.
According to Reuters, a senior U.S. official denied that the request came from U.S. President Donald Trump.
The restrictions came as Ukraine continues to come under significant and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries, something Kyiv views as an essential part of its defense against Russia's invasion.
The Ukraine-U.S. relations continue to hit a low point after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries for the rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts — and his team threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halts the attacks.
read also
Washington then unexpectedly unveiled a deal allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A few days later, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally announced an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise — as Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Personal tensions between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky appeared to unravel in the days following. When asked whether he felt betrayed by Trump for the diesel export decision, the Ukrainian leader answered: "Really, yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings."
In response, Trump described the Ukrainian president on Oct. 15 as "not a good guy for (the U.S.) to deal with," adding that he was "not a big fan of Zelensky."

articles.title: Trump rules out nuclear weapons against Iran, threatens further strikes
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, saying Washington did not need them and emphasising that the "mother of all bombs" was non-nuclear.
Asked during an interview on Thursday with Newsmax about reports that his administration was considering using the bomb against Iran, potentially after the US midterm elections, Trump stressed that the weapon was conventional, not nuclear.
“The mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” he said, describing it as “just an extremely large bomb”.
He reiterated that the US did not need to use nuclear weapons.
“No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to,” he said.
Trump also raised the possibility of further strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities, including a suspected underground site known as Pickaxe Mountain.
"Now, we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there," he said.
"We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast."
Asked whether such an operation would involve American ground troops, Trump replied: "No, I don't see that. I don't see that."
He said withdrawing before ensuring Iran could not obtain nuclear weapons might require further US military action within a year.
"We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon," he said.
‘Iran war will be over very soon’
Trump also predicted that the war would end soon, saying Tehran was negotiating with Washington.
"The Iran war will be over very soon. It's going to end very soon," he said.
"One way or the other, it'll end very soon. And oil will go dropping like a rock — and gas prices as well."
Trump claimed Iranian officials had requested a halt to American and Israeli military operations.
"They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them," he said.
Asked whether he trusted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Trump responded: "I don't trust anybody, honestly."
"I don't trust anybody," he said. "In the world of politics, I don't trust anybody."

articles.title: Developers of Ai-Petri electronic warfare system move away from hardware in favour of AI – media
articles.body:
The developers of the Ukrainian Ai-Petri data transmission and electronic warfare (DTW) system are focusing on implementing artificial intelligence and software to automate the management of the network of counter-UAV systems, since, in the face of massive attacks, a human is unable to quickly coordinate the operation of numerous disparate systems without the use of appropriate intelligent software, according to an article published on the Militarnyi specialized portal.
"The system does not replace the weapons themselves, but rather manages their network – it distributes targets among available assets, assigns frequency channels for electronic warfare operations so as not to jam its own interceptor, and redistributes resources in real time depending on which targets have been shot down and which have just appeared. The key point: situational awareness systems, which simply display the battlefield situation on a screen for the commander, are not the same as combat management systems, which directly make decisions and issue commands to assets. There are quite a few of the former being developed in Ukraine, but far fewer of the latter, and it is precisely these, according to the developer, that are critically lacking," the article reads.
A corresponding system is already operating in experimental mode in Kyiv, Odesa, and Zaporizhia, and is now being launched in Dnipro, but its coverage remains limited. "This is a fundamentally different approach to countering drones. Instead of buying as many individual units as possible, we're building a network where each unit becomes an operational component of a unified system. Part of this architecture has already been implemented in Ai-Petri. The hardware creates a physical effect, while the software determines when, where, against which targets, and in coordination with which other assets this effect should be applied," according to the article.
The article notes that to completely neutralize a single "Kometa" navigation system – which the Shahed UAVs operate – several "Ai-Petri" complexes, arranged in a specific configuration, are required.
As previously reported, MP and leader of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko has invested over UAH 200 million since the autumn of 2023 in the production of "Ai-Petri SV" systems, which have successfully passed testing and are in use by the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Each system includes the counter-surveillance device itself, a pickup truck, a charging station, a generator, and the necessary electronics. In March 2025, Poroshenko announced a contract with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, and on June 29 of that same year, he announced the start of cooperation with the command of the Ukrainian Armed Forces' Ground Forces regarding the supply of these systems to the military. On September 9, 2026, the Ai-Petri counter-surveillance system was unveiled for the first time at the MSPO 2026 security and defense technology exhibition, held in Kielce, Poland.

articles.title: Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
articles.body:
Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
Ukraine could reduce mobilization exemptions for employees of companies deemed critical to the country, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky has said, arguing that employers are exploiting the current system.
The country declared mobilization shortly after the escalation of the conflict with Russia in February 2022, barring most military-age men from leaving the country.
However, approximately 1.4 million Ukrainians currently hold employment-based exemptions from military service, according to Economy Minister Aleksandr Kravchenko.
Speaking during a Q&A session in the Ukrainian parliament on Friday, Koretsky said the government is considering stripping critical-sector employers of the right to exempt 100% of their staff. He cited cases in which companies had significantly expanded their workforces, with all employees automatically shielded from conscription.
“Unfortunately, there are many abuses, and additional exemptions continue to be granted every month,” Koretsky said.
“If you have a 100% exemption, it means you can expand your workforce indefinitely and exempt people from mobilization, regardless of whether they actually work as repair technicians, energy workers or in other roles. Unfortunately, this practice has already become widespread,” he added.
Koretsky said some companies had received blanket exemptions despite not meeting the criteria for being classified as critical. As an example, he cited an unnamed contractor for Ukrenergo, the national power grid operator. “When we looked into the details, it turned out that only 20 out of 100 employees were actually working for Ukrenergo. Yet all 100 were exempted,” Koretsky said.
The prime minister called for audits to determine how many employees at a given company perform tasks essential to its operations and the country’s needs. He added that stricter criteria could be applied to businesses as a whole, with only those supporting Ukraine’s defense capabilities and other essential state functions qualifying as critical.
Earlier this week, opposition MP Yaroslav Zhelezhnyak published what he claimed was a draft of the proposed changes, reducing exemption quotas for defense and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
Multiple lawmakers and businesses have warned that such measures would exacerbate existing staffing shortages in critical industries.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian outlet Strana UA reported on Thursday, citing sources, that relations between Koretsky and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky had deteriorated. The outlet claimed that Zelensky could dismiss Koretsky in the spring of 2027 and blame him for government failures during the winter months.
Koretsky, who was appointed prime minister in a government reshuffle in July, has been linked by local media to disgraced businessman and former close Zelensky associate Timur Mindich, who fled to Israel amid an investigation into an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme involving state nuclear power operator Energoatom.
According to Strana UA, Koretsky has defied Zelensky’s expectations by developing political ambitions, disregarding some of his requests and communicating directly with European partners without Zelensky’s involvement.
Amid mounting battlefield losses and desertions, Ukraine’s conscription drive has been marred by incidents of draft officers forcibly detaining military-age men on the streets, sparking spontaneous protests, clashes and outrage on social media.
While Kiev does not regularly publish figures on its battlefield losses, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed last month that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month. Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed that Ukrainian casualties reached 500,000 in 2025 alone.

articles.title: Bear crash and drone strike cost Russia three more aircraft
articles.body:
Russia lost three tactical and strategic aircraft in the space of a week, a Tu-95MS bomber that crashed after multiple engine failures on a training flight and two fighters destroyed by a Ukrainian one-way attack drone at an airbase five hundred kilometres from Ukraine, according to the latest UK Defence Intelligence update on the situation in Ukraine.
The update said: “Over the course of one week, Russia suffered three tactical and strategic aircraft losses. These airframes have been involved in strike campaigns against Ukraine.
“On 29 September 2026 Russia’s Long Range Aviation fleet lost one of its workhorse Tu-95MS BEAR H on a training flight shortly after take-off in eastern Russia. The BEAR H suffered multiple engine failures before crashing. These aircraft have been used extensively to strike Ukraine over the course of the conflict, almost certainly creating a significant maintenance burden on the fleet.
“On 04 October 2026, a Ukrainian one-way attack uncrewed aerial vehicle strike destroyed a Su-35S FLANKER M multi-role fighter and Su-34 FULLBACK fighter-bomber and a munitions depot at Khanskaya airbase, Russia, 500km from Ukraine.
“FULLBACK aircraft are used on daily operations to launch glide munitions into Ukraine. Analysis of commercial satellite imagery dated 04 October 2026 identified the attack had destroyed two fighter aircraft, cratered the parking apron and the taxiway, destroyed one building and destroyed and damaged two munitions’ depots.
“Russia has lost more than 100 fighter aircraft in the Ukraine conflict since February 2022.”
Russia will find the Bear the harder of the two losses to absorb, because production of the Tu-95MS ended in the early nineteen nineties. They fly the Kh-101 cruise missile strikes that have hit Ukrainian cities through the war, launching from well inside Russian airspace and turning for home without entering contested air.
Khanskaya sits in the Republic of Adygea in southern Russia, well outside the range at which Russian commanders had been willing to disperse aircraft earlier in the war. Ukraine’s long-range one-way attack drones have steadily pushed that calculation back, and airfields that were treated as rear areas have had to adopt the revetments, decoys and dispersal that frontline bases adopted years ago.

articles.title: Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, news agency Reuters reported- citing four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
Reuters reports, citing a US military official, that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade.
Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers.

articles.title: US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
articles.body:
US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
The US and Russia each have more than 4,000 warheads. China is set to catch up with them within five years, Trump says.
The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced.
Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russia in terms of the number of warheads it has – is racing to catch up. He added during an interview with US broadcaster Newsmax that Washington is discussing with its peers a route to “denuclearise”.
China’s nuclear stockpile of about 620 warheads is dwarfed by those of the US and Russia, which each have more than 4,000, but Trump said he thinks China will “catch up” within five years.
“The whole thing is a shame because I’d love to denuclearise if possible,” Trump said. “We’re actually talking to Russia about that, and we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.”
China doesn’t seem willing to disarm, he noted, but said talks have continued. Newsmax reported that Trump spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the subject, but no further details regarding the talks with either Russia or China were revealed.
Russia has the world’s largest stockpile of nuclear warheads, and the US is close behind, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
The two countries together possess an estimated 86 percent of all nuclear weapons globally.
China has the third largest nuclear arsenal, according to SIPRI, having expanded it to 620 warheads in the past year.
Trump’s claims came shortly after the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, an arms control agreement between the US and Russia to limit their nuclear arsenals.
A month after the treaty expired, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the Forward Deterrence Initiative as Russia’s nuclear sabre-rattling during its war on Ukraine has spooked Europe.
Former Australian Minister of Foreign Affairs Gareth Evans told Al Jazeera that the world’s interest in the risk of nuclear weapons has waned.
“[The] world … has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding,” he said

articles.title: Liberation of DPR, security zone, continuation of massive strikes: Putin’s statements
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Russia will continue launching strikes against Ukrainian defense enterprises and logistics centers, Russian President Vladimir Putin said while visiting an auxiliary command post of the Joint Force.
He stressed that the establishment of a buffer zone will not be open to discussion with Kiev and thanked Russian troops fighting to liberate Dobropolye and Alexeyevo-Drushkovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR).
TASS has compiled the president’s key statements.
Russia’s objectives
After Ukraine’s incursion into Russia’s Kursk Region, Russian forces were tasked not only with driving the enemy out of Russian territory but also with establishing a security zone, and this task is being successfully implemented: "Our task is to ensure absolute security of Russia’s border territories in the future and we are not going to make this a subject of any potential peace talks with Ukraine."
Commanders of battlegroups must continue "carrying out tasks in strict compliance with the objectives of the special military operation." "Naturally, it is necessary to continue massive and coordinated strikes against enemy defense facilities and logistics centers."
Strikes against the Kiev regime’s facilities have been effective: "I assess the results positively."
"As for the situation on the ground, naturally, one of the key objectives is the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic."
Successes
Russian forces are advancing along the entire frontline in the zone of the special military operation, and "the pace of their advance has increased significantly."
Russia’s armed forces continue to carry out the objectives of the special military operation: "As has already been mentioned here, in September alone, more than 1,300 square kilometers of territory in Donbas and Novorossiya was liberated."
"Around 6,500 square kilometers of territory and 310 settlements have been liberated since the beginning of this year."
The liberation of Dobropolye in the DPR is an evident success: "Please convey my words of gratitude to all personnel directly involved in the liberation of Dobropolye. I will say more about this when addressing the commanders of the task forces, but I want to emphasize and point out right here: the capture of Dobropolye is undoubtedly a significant milestone in the liberation of Donbas as a whole and a clear success for the Russian Armed Forces. Congratulations to you all."
"The enemy had turned the city into a fortified stronghold in this area, but the coordinated and highly professional actions of Russian assault units made it possible first to encircle enemy forces in the city and then to take complete control of it."
The liberation of Dobropolye "opens a direct route toward the DPR’s borders."
The liberation of Alexeyevo-Druzhkovka and the start of the assault on Ukrainian fortified areas in Druzhkovka and Kramatorsk in the DPR create conditions for "the swiftest possible completion of the liberation of Donbas from the Kiev regime’s combat units."
"Please convey my most sincere words of gratitude to all the personnel who were directly involved in the liberation of Alexeyevo-Druzhkovka for the courage and resilience they demonstrated during this combat operation."
Russian forces successfully encircled a Ukrainian grouping 2,000 troops in the Kharkov Region: "Entrapping a grouping of about 2,000 troops, in an area of more than 400 square kilometers, 460 square kilometers, is certainly no ordinary feat. Taking into account the subsequent elimination of the enemy in that area, this is indeed a success."
"The offensive in the Zaporozhye Region continues at a high pace, with Battlegroups Dnepr and East’s troops advancing successfully."
"A decisive role [in ensuring rapid progress] undoubtedly belongs to our soldiers and officers, who, while carrying out combat missions, act professionally and demonstrate the finest qualities of the Russian military, such as selfless devotion to the Motherland."
Protection of facilities
Air defense combat crews are operating professionally: "But, of course, there is room for improvement in this regard. We need to enhance the effectiveness of our defense of civilian, first and foremost civilian, and, of course, military facilities."

articles.title: Europe Provides Two-Thirds of Intelligence to Ukraine, Says French Foreign Minister
articles.body:
Europe now provides two-thirds of the intelligence Ukraine receives from its partners.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot made the statement in an interview with France Inter.
“Two-thirds of the intelligence provided to Ukraine now comes from European countries, including France,” Barrot said.
His remarks come amid US threats to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine following Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
European countries provide Ukraine with several types of intelligence, including optical and radar satellite imagery, intercepted radio communications, information on troop movements, and warnings about ballistic missile threats.
For example, to help detect ballistic threats, European countries provide Ukraine with information collected by ground-based electronic intelligence systems and long-range ground-based radars. These systems can track missiles after they rise above the radar horizon.
France previously announced a major upgrade of its strategic Nostradamus radar, located in the Eure-et-Loir department.
Unique in Europe, the radar can detect threats thousands of kilometres away, from the North Sea to the Ural Mountains,without mechanically rotating its antennas.
Developed in the 1990s by France’s aerospace research agency ONERA, the system had remained mothballed for an extended period.
Amid growing threats from Russia and Iran, France’s Ministry of the Armed Forces has decided to bring the radar back into operation, investing more than €50 million in its modernization.
The radar works by bouncing high-frequency radiowaves off the ionosphere, allowing it to detect objects beyond the horizon. Its antennas, spread across a 12-hectare star-shaped array, can monitor a volume of several million cubic kilometres, from the ground to an altitude of 250 kilometres.
Meanwhile, Germany also plans to deploy a constellation of more than 100 military satellites in low Earth orbit in the coming years to provide secure communications and track missiles.

articles.title: Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years after election: Report
The Trump administration is backing efforts to form a broad Israeli unity government after this month's election that could keep Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister for up to two years before handing power to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, according to an Israeli media report.
The proposal would exclude far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and bring together Netanyahu's Likud party with Eisenkot's Yashar party, Israel Hayom reported on Friday.
The newspaper cited unnamed US and foreign political officials familiar with the discussions. Neither Washington nor the Israeli parties involved have publicly confirmed an agreed plan.
Israel is due to hold a Knesset election on 27 October.
Polls have suggested neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor the fragmented opposition is guaranteed a stable governing majority, raising the possibility of prolonged coalition negotiations.
According to Israel Hayom, the US and regional governments believe a broad coalition would be better placed to make major decisions on ending regional conflicts and advancing President Donald Trump's wider Middle East agenda.
One unnamed foreign official quoted in the report said a fragile minority government would be unable to make the "major and decisive political decisions" the region required.
The proposed arrangement would allow Netanyahu to remain prime minister for up to two years before Eisenkot succeeded him, according to the report.
During that period, the government would be expected to work towards ending wars on multiple fronts and reaching political agreements with regional states, particularly Saudi Arabia.
The Trump administration has been pushing Riyadh to join the Abraham Accords and normalise relations with Israel.
Washington has linked that effort to other parts of the US-Saudi relationship, including F-35 fighter jets and a civilian nuclear programme.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said, however, that normalisation with Israel would require meaningful progress towards Palestinian statehood.
The issue has also become entangled with Washington's proposed nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, which Trump has said would depend on Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords.
According to Israel Hayom, Saudi Arabia is also seeking a different political configuration in Israel before moving forward.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has recently met several senior Israeli politicians, including Eisenkot, the report said.
The contacts were said to have been handled carefully because of concerns over perceptions of US interference in the election.
But Israeli politicians were reportedly told that Washington and other governments would welcome a broad and stable coalition without far-right parties.
Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has emerged as one of Netanyahu's principal challengers in the election and leads the centrist Yashar party.
The proposed government would also seek to address domestic issues that have deeply divided Israeli politics.
These include demands for an official inquiry into the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 attacks, disputes over the judiciary and the continuing row over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has denied reports that he is directly involved in efforts to engineer a unity government.
He has nevertheless said he wants to avoid repeated elections and see a stable government formed after the vote.
The reported US effort comes as Israel's election remains highly fragmented, with Palestinian parties potentially playing a decisive role if neither major bloc secures a governing majority.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defenses down 114 out of 149 Russian drones launched at Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defenses down 114 out of 149 Russian drones launched at Ukraine overnight
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
As reported, starting at 18:00 on Thursday, October 15, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 149 strike drones, including Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones. Of these, 108 Shahed drones were jet-powered.
The launches were carried out from the area of the Russian town of Oryol, as well as from the temporarily occupied areas of Hvardiiske in Crimea and Donetsk.
The enemy attack was countered by Ukrainian combat aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:30 on Friday, October 16, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or jammed 114 Russian drones, including 77 jet-powered Shahed drones, as well as Gerbera and other types of drones.
Hits by 27 enemy aerial weapons were recorded at 24 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 14 locations.
The Air Force emphasized that Russian UAVs are still present in Ukrainian airspace and the attack is ongoing. Citizens are urged to follow safety precautions.
As reported by Ukrinform, in the Odesa region, enemy strikes damaged private homes, an energy facility, and a household goods manufacturing company. Casualties were reported.

articles.title: Zelensky turns to Europe for backing as ties with Trump deteriorate
articles.body:
Zelensky turns to Europe for backing as ties with Trump deteriorate
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky turned to his European allies on Friday, asking Brussels for an additional €70 billion to fund the war against Russia next year. Zelensky's relationship with US President Donald Trump deteriorated after the US eased sanctions on Moscow as part of a diesel-supply deal.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky urged EU leaders Friday to keep financing Kyiv's fight with nearly $80 billion more next year, as he insisted he was standing up for his country amid a fresh row with US President Donald Trump.
Kyiv's ties with Trump have nosedived after the US leader eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to supply diesel.
Trump branded Kyiv's actions a "disgrace" and said it was easier to deal with Russia's President Vladimir Putin than Zelensky, after the Ukrainian leader ordered his forces to resume strikes on Russian refineries.
Read moreWhy have US-Ukraine relations soured ahead of the midterms?
"I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively," Zelensky told journalists after talks with EU leaders in Brussels.
Asked if he was being made a scapegoat for Trump's domestic woes ahead of the US midterms, Zelensky just smiled.
"This is my answer," he said, after an extended pregnant pause.
The latest breakdown between Trump and Zelensky has fuelled fear that the US leader is siding with Moscow.
Those concerns have been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered Ukraine's ability to counter Russia's intense bombardments.
Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Elon Musk's SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones. It also uses SpaceX's parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, but not for offensive operations.
Tech billionaire Musk – though a virulent Zelensky critic – said his company was not behind the disruption and a US official denied any intervention by Trump.
