"Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," Zelensky said.
In his speech to EU leaders, Zelensky said that he believed that most Americans supported Ukraine's fight against Moscow's invasion.
"At the end of the day, the American people will have their say," he said.
70 billion-euro question
While he grapples with Trump, European leaders put on a show of unity with Zelensky.
"This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions," European Council chief Antonio Costa said.
"Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that "the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US."
"It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today – and explore what additional steps we can take," he said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
But the EU leaders will need to find more than just words to keep Ukraine going.
Zelensky asked the bloc to provide more Patriot missiles to shoot down Russian missiles and come up with an extra €70 billion ($79 billion) in support next year to help Kyiv keep fighting.
"This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back."
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that the figure of €70 billion "has to be covered" and urged partner countries to "step in" and help. Leaders told her commission to come up with a proposal for the financing.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Kyiv's backers will analyse the demand, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the EU will discuss it before the end of the year.
Macron also said Europe was "working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed."
Frozen assets
The EU is currently paying out instalments of a €90 billion loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027.
But the Ukrainian authorities have warned they will still face a major budget black hole as Russian strikes have battered the country's economy.
The talks on new funding have reignited calls for the European Union to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
"The frozen assets are there. That's what should be used for supporting Ukraine," said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs.
But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: The Russian army has launched strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities — Gerasimov cynically reported to Putin
articles.body:
The Russian army has launched strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities — Gerasimov cynically reported to Putin
Kyiv • UNN
Gerasimov reported to Putin on strikes against Ukraine's energy facilities and strategic bridges. He also stated that the production of long-range weapons had been weakened.
Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces Valery Gerasimov reported to Russian dictator Vladimir Putin that the Russian army had begun strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities, UNN reports, citing Russian media.

articles.title: Coercive diplomacy: What does the call between Netanyahu and al-Sharaa really mean?
articles.body:
The phone call between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Syrian interim leader Ahmed al-Sharaa—following months of firing salvos via fighter jets, missiles, and third-party intermediaries, alongside strikes that targeted the courtyard of the Syrian Ministry of Defence and the perimeter of the presidential palace—was no ordinary diplomatic formality. Rather, it was a condensed moment signalling a tectonic shift in the geopolitics and power balance of the Middle East.
When Netanyahu and Sharaa speak directly to discuss sectarian tensions in the Druze-majority province of Sweida, we are not merely witnessing a localised security arrangement dictated by geography and overwhelming force. We are standing before a series of uncomfortable questions shaping the region’s future: Is Syria capitulating entirely to the rhythm of Israeli power, which has established itself as an unyielding arbiter in the new Syrian landscape? Or is this a pragmatic response from Damascus to pressure from an Arab bloc seeking regional normalisation—a bloc that views any effort to rebuild and reintegrate Syria as passing, one way or another, through the neutralisation of active fronts with Tel Aviv?
Furthermore, who granted Israel and Netanyahu the political and international mandate to act as the self-appointed custodian over Syria’s Druze minority?
The most realistic answer lies elsewhere: in a devastated economy, a shattered state apparatus, and a transitional authority that has come to realise that rebuilding Syria requires, above all, zeroing out external hostilities. States emerging from the crucible of war do not enjoy the luxury of managing multiple conflicts at once. Today’s Syria looks far closer to this exhaustion model than to the legacy slogans of traditional “Resistance.”
Yet, the phone call poses far larger strategic dilemmas than it answers: Is this a tactical manoeuvring aimed at preventing escalation and buying time, or the beginning of a structural shift redefining Syria’s place on the regional map? Is Sharaa treating Israel as an unalterable geopolitical reality, or is the entire region entering an era where ideological mantras surrender to the imperatives of economic survival, reconstruction, and stability?
Anticipating an answer requires reading this new Syrian stance not as absolute surrender, but as a tightrope walk driven by a “survival mindset.”
Sharaa lacks the military capacity to engage an adversary that strikes the heart of Damascus with international impunity. Conversely, he understands that total compliance with Israeli terms risks sparking domestic fragmentation and delegitimising his rule regionally.
Hence, the most plausible regional scenario is Damascus moving toward ending the “active state of war” without entering the formal fold of political normalisation—establishing a security framework for borders and minorities that satisfies regional patrons while isolating Syria from radical axes to minimise reconstruction costs.
On the Israeli side, Netanyahu is attempting to engineer an advanced “politico-security belt” reaching deep into Syria’s social fabric.
By asserting proxy guardianship over minority populations like the Druze, Tel Aviv aims not only to secure its northern border, but to institutionalise a model of a “regional patron” holding the keys to stability in broken neighbouring states.
This style of power projection forces any future government in Damascus—whether led by Sharaa or another—to operate within a security architecture drafted in Tel Aviv long before it reaches the halls of the United Nations.
Ultimately, what transpired was not the announcement of a new alliance, but a mutual acknowledgment of a new balance of power. It is an equilibrium in which Netanyahu realizes his security influence remains incomplete without ordering his immediate Syrian backyard, while Sharaa recognizes that reclaiming statehood may require, for the first time in decades, managing relations with Israel through state pragmatism rather than ideological rhetoric.
The significance of the call lies not in its brief duration, but in its role as a barometer for a Middle East where yesterday’s political impossibilities have become today’s negotiating points.
Yet, all these calculations could swiftly evaporate or invert should Netanyahu lose power in the upcoming Israeli elections.
READ: Damascus rejects Israeli politicisation of Syria’s Druze after Netanyahu’s brief call with al-Sharaa
The core dilemma rests not solely within Syria, but in the nature of the Israel that Netanyahu embodies today. Under his tenure, Israel has transformed from a state seeking security-driven compromises into an actor behaving as the region’s absolute power, backed by an unprecedented surplus of self-confidence—perceived by its adversaries as military hubris and by its leadership as earned strategic dominance. Thus, any potential Syrian opening cannot be disentangled from the persona of the man wielding power in Tel Aviv.
Is Damascus reaching out to Israel as a permanent state institution, or is it coercively adapting to an extraordinary “Netanyahu moment” and the hard facts it has established on the ground? This question is no less vital than the issue of normalisation itself. If Netanyahu departs the political stage and Israel reverts to more conventional, less aggressive security calculus, the strategic weight of these contacts may shift overnight. They may well be reinterpreted as fleeting security arrangements dictated by temporary power dynamics rather than enduring strategic realignments.
When the dust settles, we may discover that the true historical event was not the phone conversation between Sharaa and Netanyahu, but the historical epoch that produced the phenomenon of Netanyahu itself—an era that compelled the entire region to redefine power, deterrence, and sovereignty under the weight of a prolonged war that has not yet ended, but will not forever remain governed by the logic of a victor who believes history moves by his will alone.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Sikorskiy reminds Trump that Ukrainians are attacked by Russian missiles, bombs, and drones
articles.body:
Polish Minister of Foreign Affairs Radosław Sikorskiy has sharply responded to statements by U.S President Donald Trump, who earlier in an interview with Newsmax alleged that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is responsible for the destruction of the country and the trauma of Ukrainians.
"We appreciate President Trump’s concern for the victims of the war but in Poland we think that those Ukrainians were injured by drones, bombs and missiles launched by Vladimir Putin," Sikorskiy wrote on the social media platform X.
Earlier, Trump in his interview blamed Zelenskyy for the injuries and deaths of Ukrainian soldiers.
"I watched an interview of a young woman the other day from Ukraine. And she said, 'President Zelenskyy has destroyed our country. President Zelenskyy has taken our men away from us. Our men have no legs, no arms. Our men in many cases in mental institutions or they're," Trump stated.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine has "plenty of targets" in Russia beyond oil refineries
articles.body:
Trump says Ukraine has "plenty of targets" in Russia beyond oil refineries
US President Donald Trump has said Ukraine could strike "plenty of targets" in Russia other than oil refineries and called the Ukrainian campaign against Russian refineries a disgrace.
Source: Trump in an interview with Newsmax, quoted by European Pravda
Details: Trump once again claimed that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries are driving up global oil prices.
Quote from Trump: "Now, if you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he's doing is making the world oil price higher... Well, I think that's a disgrace. There's plenty of other targets. ... There are a lot of targets that you can hit. But when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil and we need that and the world needs that, then he's [Zelenskyy – ed.] not doing a good service for the world."
Background:
- In a post on his social media platform Truth Social on 11 October, Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.
- Since then, there has been no information confirmed by the Ukrainian authorities regarding strikes on Russian oil refineries. Meanwhile, Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian energy facilities.
- On 14 October, Zelenskyy said Russia had shown unprecedented contempt for the US by carrying out a ballistic missile strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure facilities overnight on 13-14 October.
- In an interview with the FT on 15 October, Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine had suspended strikes on Russian energy facilities for three days to comply with US wishes, whilst Moscow had continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure. In this regard, Zelenskyy said the ban on striking Russian oil refineries has now been lifted.

articles.title: Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
articles.body:
Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
Washington’s diesel deal with Moscow has exposed divisions within the West over its anti-Russian stance, as the US shifts toward a more pragmatic approach, former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl has said.
US President Donald Trump announced the agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, easing sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April 2027 in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices. The move marks a departure from the Western sanctions policy imposed on Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
Speaking to TASS on Friday, Kneissl described the agreement as more than a “symbolic breakthrough,” pointing to the 300,000 tons of Russian diesel expected to reach the US and global markets by November.
“The EU says that this undermines the West’s united position. However, one could also say that this marks a shift by the US toward a more pragmatic approach, while the EU continues to pursue a purely ideological line,” she stated.
The agreement has drawn criticism from European leaders attending a two-day EU summit in Brussels this week. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused Trump of sidelining the bloc, telling reporters that “Trump, by doing that business with Putin, stabbed us in the back. We have to do something.”
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, however, welcomed the agreement, arguing that lower fuel prices were essential to Europe’s economic competitiveness. “Any step in reducing fuel prices and to guarantee our competitiveness, we appreciate,” he said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the agreement as a “gift to Putin,” while defending Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed on Friday that the bloc would maintain its sanctions against Moscow despite Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
Brussels’ hardline stance contrasts with that of EU member Slovakia, which remains heavily dependent on Russian energy and has sought to maintain economic ties with Moscow. Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly called for diplomacy rather than continued military support for Kiev.
The dispute has also strained relations between Washington and Kiev. Trump has repeatedly urged Vladimir Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for pushing up global fuel prices.
Zelensky criticized the diesel agreement as a “weak decision” and accused Trump of “betrayal.” Ukraine continued targeting Russian energy facilities, including a refinery in Ryazan Region on Thursday, prompting Trump to condemn the attacks as a “disgrace.” At Friday’s summit, Zelensky sought additional financial and military assistance from European leaders but left empty-handed, with only renewed promises of support.
The confrontation comes as global diesel supplies remain under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to accelerate the release of emergency oil reserves, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, in an effort to ease shortages and bring down prices.

articles.title: Over 300 combat engagements on battlefield in 24 hours – Ukraine's General Staff
articles.body:
Over 300 combat engagements on battlefield in 24 hours – Ukraine's General Staff
A total of 304 combat engagements took place on the front on 15 October.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 16 October
Quote: "According to updated information, yesterday the enemy launched 83 airstrikes, dropping 271 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders deployed 7,059 kamikaze drones and attacked settlements and the positions of our troops 2,551 times, including 76 times using multiple-launch rocket systems."
Details: Meanwhile, Ukrainian aircraft struck a cluster of Russian military personnel over the past 24 hours.
On the Pokrovsk front, Russian forces launched 60 attacks over the past 24 hours, more than on any other front. They attempted to advance near the settlements of Dorozhnie and Molodetske and towards Toretske, Pavlivka, Novopavlivka, Vilne, Kucheriv Yar, Hannivka, Dobropillia, Svitle, Krasnopodillia, Serhiivka and Muravka.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, Russian troops launched one airstrike using three guided aerial bombs and conducted 64 attacks on Ukrainian defence forces positions and populated areas over the past day.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian units repelled 22 Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to attack near Starytsia, Izbytske and Chuhunivka and towards Buzove and Radkivka.
On the Kupiansk front, Russian troops made three attempts to improve their tactical positions, conducting assault operations towards Novoosynove and Shyikivka.
On the Lyman front, Russian attempts to break through Ukrainian defences had been repelled, the General Staff said. Russian forces launched eight attacks towards Novoiehorivka, Olhivka, Druzheliubivka, Lyman and Staryi Karavan.
On the Sloviansk front, Russian forces carried out two attacks towards Orikhuvatka and Mykolaivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the defence forces repelled three Russian attempts to advance near Chervone and towards Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 27 attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted offensive operations near Kostiantynivka and Dovha Balka and towards Rozkishne, Mykolaipillia and Raiske.
On the Oleksandrivka front, Russian forces did not conduct any assault operations.
On the Huliaipole front, the Russians attacked Ukrainian Armed Forces positions 20 times. Russian troops attempted to advance towards Rizdvianka, Dolynka, Hirke and Yehorivka.
On the Orikhiv front, Russian forces made two attempts to attack towards Pavlivka.
On the Prydniprovske front, the Russians did not conduct any assault operations.

articles.title: Yemen coalition says shot down 3 drones over southern Saudi Arabia, Riyadh region
articles.body:
Serdar Dincel
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Friday that it shot down three drones over Saudi Arabia's southern and Riyadh regions amid continued Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
Turki al-Maliki, the coalition's spokesman, said on US social media platfrom X that they also intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea.
The coalition also shot down a ballistic missile targeting the Saudi port city of Yanbu over the past few hours, Maliki added.
The latest incidents follow a wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and energy facilities.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several other provinces since 2014.
The current escalation began in July after a period of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce that started in April 2022.

articles.title: Zelenskyy expects delivery of Swedish Gripen fighter jets shortly
articles.body:
Zelenskyy expects delivery of Swedish Gripen fighter jets shortly
Following a conversation with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reported that Ukraine expects to receive Gripen fighter jets in the near future to complement its F-16s, particularly in destroying Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy and Kristersson discussed Ukraine's needs for protection against Russia's relentless attacks, first and foremost stronger air defence. In particular, Sweden has promised to provide Gripen fighter jets.
Quote: "I thank Sweden for our agreements on Gripen fighter jets. We expect deliveries soon. They will complement our F-16s, particularly in shooting down jet-powered 'Shaheds'."
Details: Zelenskyy and Kristersson also discussed Ukraine's EU membership bid and support for the energy sector as it prepares for winter.
Background:
- Earlier the same day, Zelenskyy and Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo discussed how to protect Ukraine from Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure.
- On 16 October, Zelenskyy called on EU leaders to provide Ukraine with at least €70 billion in additional aid next year for defence, weapons and strengthening resilience.

articles.title: Zelenskyy and Finnish PM discuss Russian strikes and Ukraine's need for shelters
articles.body:
Zelenskyy and Finnish PM discuss Russian strikes and Ukraine's need for shelters
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Prime Minister of Finland Petteri Orpo have discussed how to protect Ukraine from Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy and Orpo discussed Ukraine's need for shelters on Friday 16 October.
Quote: "Together with Finland, we established the Shelter Coalition and now we need to speed up this work. Every Ukrainian city and community must have proper shelters."
Details: The two leaders also spoke about how to protect Ukrainian regions from Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Quote: "We constantly need the means to shoot down missiles and drones to protect people's lives and critical infrastructure. New decisions to support Ukraine will come as early as this month. Finland has always helped us, and we greatly appreciate it."
Background:
- On 16 October, Zelenskyy called on EU leaders to provide Ukraine with at least €70 billion in additional aid next year for defence, weapons and strengthening resilience.
- Earlier that day, Zelenskyy held his first official meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar. The one-on-one meeting took place on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels.
- Following the meeting, Magyar stated that it is both countries' interests to put political and economic relations on a new footing.
- Zelenskyy described his meeting with Magyar as "very good".

articles.title: Trump calls Zelensky ‘more difficult to deal with than Putin,’ says he’s ‘not a big fan’
articles.body:
Trump calls Zelensky ‘more difficult to deal with than Putin,’ says he’s ‘not a big fan’
U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with the right-wing channel Newsmax that he finds it harder to negotiate with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky than with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Trump said. “Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with. He doesn’t want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t. No, I’m not a big fan of Zelensky.”
He again criticized Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he said are driving up global fuel prices. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace. There’s plenty of other targets. … There are a lot of targets that you can hit,” Trump said.
Trump again raised the issue of elections in Ukraine, which have not been held because of martial law. He expressed doubt that Zelensky retains public support amid the ongoing war in Ukraine. “I think you need an election because there’s nobody that’s telling me that the people of Ukraine are satisfied having missiles hitting their apartment building,” he said.
Trump said he still believes the war will “end soon,” because “they actually both would like to see it end.” However, he said, there are certain difficulties. “Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin. And when you have that kind of hatred, it’s very hard to get something settled,” Trump said.
On October 9, Trump agreed with Vladimir Putin on supplies of Russian diesel fuel to the American and global markets. Ukraine and Europe criticized the decision.
On October 11, the U.S. president announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a truce in the energy sector. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the truce announced by Trump “came as news” to him. On October 15, Zelensky said Ukraine had not struck Russian oil refineries for three days but would now resume strikes because Russia had not observed the truce. Russian authorities claim Ukraine never stopped its strikes.

articles.title: Twenty-two US lawmakers demand Trump immediately impose Russia sanctions under Graham Act
articles.body:
Twenty-two US lawmakers demand Trump immediately impose Russia sanctions under Graham Act
Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives have written to President Donald Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Source: Congressman Jim Costa's website; Ukrainian journalist in Washington Ostap Yarysh on Facebook
Details: The letter was authored by House Foreign Affairs Committee member Jim Costa, together with the co-chairs of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus in the House of Representatives: Mike Quigley, Marcy Kaptur, Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson. The lawmakers stressed that the first mandatory deadline for the key sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to take effect expires on 18 October.
They emphasised the need to step up economic pressure on Moscow ahead of winter.
Quote: "As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war. Utilising the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously."
Details: In the letter, the lawmakers also expressed deep concern over the US Department of the Treasury's decision on 9 October to issue General Licence No. 135, which permits transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian diesel fuel into the US.
They called on the administration to immediately revoke this permit and prevent any new exemptions that restore the flow of petrodollars into the Kremlin's war chest.
Furthermore, the House members have asked the administration five questions and demanded written answers by 18 October. They want to know what steps will be taken to ensure the full implementation of all mandatory sanctions, tariffs and bans, and whether the White House intends to delay any provisions or grant exemptions to them.
The lawmakers are also calling for the administration to publish a list of Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and state-owned companies targeted by the restrictions and to clarify whether foreign banks and Russia's shadow fleet operators will also be affected. They are further demanding details of which countries will face secondary tariffs for purchasing Russian energy, what safeguards will be in place for allies, how pressure on Putin will be measured, and why sanctions are being eased despite the existing legislative ban on Russian energy imports.
Among the 22 signatories to the letter are leading representatives of both parties, including Republicans Michael McCaul, Joe Wilson, Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, as well as Democrats Steny Hoyer, Jim Costa, Marcy Kaptur, Josh Gottheimer and Dina Titus.
Background:
- On 17 September, the US Congress passed bill H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation authorises 500% tariffs on Russian goods, secondary tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, and mandatory sanctions against key sectors of the Russian economy.
- On 19 September, US President Donald Trump signed the Graham Act into law, setting the first 30-day deadline for the implementation of its provisions for 18 October.
- On 9 October, the US Department of the Treasury, through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued General Licence No. 135, allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel.
- On 14 October, a bipartisan group of 12 US senators sent a strongly worded letter to Donald Trump, calling the diesel deal with Moscow a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and urging him to immediately revoke the licence and move to full implementation of the Graham Act.

articles.title: Ukraine’s air defenses down 253 Russian drones, nine Banderols during day
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defenses down 253 Russian drones, nine Banderols during day
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
“During the day on October 16 (from 7:00 to 19:00), the enemy attacked Ukraine with 315 strike UAVs (78 of them were jet-powered), Gerbera drones and other types of drones, as well as 15 S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T missiles,” the statement said.
According to preliminary data, during the specified period, Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 253 UAVs (49 of them were jet-powered), as well as nine S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T missiles.
The Air Force added that as of 18:00, about 35 strike drones were still in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine is using Starlink to operate interceptor drones that shoot down jet-powered Shaheds attacking civilians.
